#3039. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3035. Ibotta (IBTA) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Redemption revenue surged 23% as publisher network hit all-time high redeemers.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Ibotta, Inc. (IBTA +2.98%) reported third-quarter performance that exceeded internal expectations for both the top line and adjusted EBITDA. Management attributed the growth to an improved supply of advertiser offers and the continued expansion of the third-party publisher network. The company stated that the business is benefiting from operating leverage as revenue growth outpaced the increase in operating expenses. Management indicated that current planning for the next fiscal year is focused on strategic partnerships and the rollout of new product capabilities to drive sustainable revenue growth.

Operator: Good afternoon, and welcome to Ibotta's Q3 2026 earnings conference call. With us today are Bryan Leach, Founder and CEO, and Matt Puckett, CFO. Today's press release and this call contain forward-looking statements.

Forward-looking statements include statements about our future operating results, our guidance for Q4 2026, and our preliminary outlook for 2027, our ability to grow our revenue and grow margins, our ability to grow supply and demand on our network, factors contributing to our potential revenue growth, our key initiatives, our partnerships, the expected performance and ramp of new publishers, client spending and offer supply, consumer demand and macroeconomic conditions, our capital allocation plans, including share repurchases, and the capabilities of our offerings and technology, all of which are subject to inherent risks, uncertainties, and changes. These statements reflect our current expectations and are based on the information currently available to us, and our actual results could differ materially.

For more information, please refer to the risk factors in our recent SEC filings and our 10-Q to be filed this week. In addition, our discussions today will include references to certain supplemental non-GAAP financial measures and should be considered in addition to and not as a substitute for our GAAP results. Reconciliations to the most comparable GAAP measures are available in our earnings press release, our 10-Q to be filed this week, and our Q3 2026 earnings presentation, which are all available on our investor relations website at investors.ibotta.com. Unless otherwise noted, revenue and adjusted EBITDA comparisons to prior periods are provided on a year-over-year basis. With that, I'll turn it over to Bryan.

Bryan Leach: Good afternoon, everyone. Thanks for joining our discussion of third quarter results. A year ago, we were in the middle of a significant transformation of our business. Today, thanks to our team's hard work, our results reflect a company that is executing well and returning to sustainable revenue growth with attractive margins. I'm pleased to report third quarter revenue and adjusted EBITDA that were both above the high end of our guidance range. Revenue grew 17% year-over-year, building on the return to growth we reported last quarter, while our adjusted EBITDA increased by 43%, illustrating the strength of our financial model.

The revenue growth rate partly reflects an easier comparison to the third quarter of last year, which Matt will address in his remarks. But the underlying driver is the same one we've been talking about all year. Our advertiser offer supply continues to improve. That improvement reflects several factors, including stronger sales execution and a focus on our core value proposition, the growth of LiveLift, the benefits of enhanced first and third-party measurement, robust consumer demand for savings, and the success of our seasonal events playbook, specifically back to school in this quarter. You can see this most clearly in our core redemption business. A year ago, redemption revenue was down 15% year-over-year.

Since then, it's improved to down 5% in the fourth quarter, down 1% in the first quarter, and up 10% in the second quarter. This quarter, redemption revenue grew 23%. Third-party publisher redemption revenue tells the same story. It declined 4% a year ago and has improved consistently, posting a 43% year-over-year increase this quarter. This robust third-party redemption revenue growth was driven by 57% year-over-year growth in redemptions on the digital properties of our third-party partners, a tremendous outcome for them and us. On the demand side of our network, redeemer growth was exceptionally strong. We had an all-time high of 23.6 million redeemers in the third quarter, up 30% year-over-year and up 13% from the second quarter.

We added 2.7 million additional redeemers between Q2 and Q3, our largest sequential increase since the fourth quarter of 2023, a quarter which benefited from the full rollout of Walmart. Consumers are currently under significant pressure, and they're clearly looking for value wherever they shop. Increasingly, they're finding it through Ibotta offers that show up natively in the apps and websites of retailers like Walmart, Family Dollar, Dollar General, Instacart, DoorDash, Uber Eats, 7-Eleven, and others. Of course, more redeemers only create value for us if there are more offers to put in front of them. In the third quarter, third-party redemptions per redeemer growth accelerated to 17% year-over-year, the second consecutive quarter of growth.

When looking at that metric across the entirety of the network, it grew 8%, the first time we've seen that occur since the advent of the Ibotta Performance Network. These results indicate that offer supply is growing faster than redeemer demand, even as that demand accelerates. Our success during back to school was a significant contributor to our offer supply growth. Back to school is one of the most important moments of the year for many of our clients. Shoppers are stocking up and making every dollar count, and brands want to win share while volume is at its peak. The investments we've made in our revenue organization over the past 18 months are showing up in various ways.

First, we've grown the number of key relationships within our clients. In the third quarter, we increased the number of client contacts per meeting by 44% year-over-year. This metric has increased sequentially every quarter since the third quarter of 2025. Second, we're serving a larger percentage of our clients' brand portfolios. In Q3, we increased our penetration of brands per enterprise account by 7% year-over-year. Third, and finally, we are more involved in our clients' planning processes, with more active preferred partnerships today than this time last year, with our clients indicating an intent to spend more. These preferred partnership agreements give us improving visibility on the forward revenue potential.

To make all this more concrete, I'd like to share an example. One of the world's largest food manufacturers was once a significant Ibotta partner, but had reduced its investment with us over the past few years. Through deeper strategic engagement and an expanded publisher network, we've rebuilt that relationship. In the third quarter, this client returned to our list of five largest clients for the first time in years, investing more than 10x as much this quarter as it had in all of 2025. Like many leading food manufacturers, this client is focused on restoring volume growth and regaining market share as quickly as possible.

Our verticalized sales structure has given us the industry expertise to support those objectives, and our expanded network lets them reach consumers across multiple channels, ranging from mass to grocery to dollar to convenience and last-mile delivery. Working with the client's brand, revenue growth management, and sales teams, we have moved them from individual brand campaigns to multi-brand occasion-based programs. Our conversations with this client about 2027 planning are well advanced, and they're focused on a longer-term, more strategic approach to consumer incentives. We also continue to play a leading role in the industry conversation about how promotions should be planned and measured.

Over the past few months, our team has been on stage at Groceryshop with Danone, at ADWEEK House with Mondelēz and Pernod Ricard, and at the Brand Innovators summit with McCormick. Our test-versus-control approach continues to be regarded as an important breakthrough in methodology, and our partnerships with independent measurement companies back that up. Danone's recent experience with LiveLift highlights the relevance of that conversation. With a traditional temporary price reduction, a brand must plan weeks, if not months, in advance. It chooses an offer value and duration upfront, and the promo runs as planned, whether it's working or not.

With LiveLift, Danone was able to launch a campaign within days and see how its Ibotta campaign was performing while it was still ongoing. It used that information to adjust offer values across products, and over the following 10 days, Oikos and Activia were able to scale with a cost per incremental dollar that was more than 30% more efficient than before. Over the course of the pilot, the campaign moved more than 1.5 million incremental units and generated more than $3 of incremental return for every dollar invested. Circana measured our results independently. Oikos outperformed the yogurt category sales lift benchmark by 1.4x, and the featured Light + Fit four-pack exceeded it by 4.8x.

In both cases, most of the lift came from new households buying the brand, not from existing buyers buying more. Danone's head of strategic insights, planning, and connected commerce described in-campaign optimization as, quote, "A distinction that's changing how we think about where the next dollar goes, not just how the last one performed," end quote. Turning to our publisher network, Giant Eagle went live during the third quarter. Since switching to the Ibotta Performance Network, its customers have access to nearly 3x as many coupons as before, a result Giant Eagle has highlighted on its own website.

We believe that reflects the breadth of our national offer content and the strength of our relationships with the brands that fund it. At Giant Eagle, we also manage the retailer's own shopper programs, which allows us to apply the work we've been doing on targeted and merchandised offers. That work is helping us to drive higher redemption rates and generate more value, both for our clients and our publishers. 7-Eleven went live in October across the 7-Eleven and Speedway apps, with 7NOW expected to follow, and redemption activity is beginning to ramp up gradually.

The convenience channel is where many of our CPG clients sell single-serve and smaller pack sizes, and it's particularly important for our snacking and beverage clients. We've had significant inbound interest from clients who are encouraged by this incremental opportunity to reach C-store consumers. It's still early days, but we expect to gain a better sense for the opportunity as we head into 2027. Most recently, during the fourth quarter, our digital offers went live at Festival Foods, a regional grocer in Wisconsin that was acquired by Schnucks in 2025. We continue to work closely with Walmart to expand the visibility and accessibility of manufacturer-funded offers throughout the shopper journey.

During the quarter, we partnered on customer engagement initiatives to drive greater awareness and adoption of Walmart Cash while advancing opportunities to integrate offers more deeply into Walmart's digital and in-store shopping experiences. Last quarter, I said that we look forward to building on our momentum in the back half of the year. Our third-quarter results show we're doing just that. Redemption revenue growth has accelerated every quarter this year. LiveLift continues to grow. Our redeemers have increased 30% year-over-year. Our network is larger and more diverse than it has ever been, and our team is executing well. We're carrying that momentum into the fourth quarter and into our planning for 2027.

Before I turn it over to Matt, I'd also like to highlight a recent change to our board of directors. In September, we welcomed Tony Weisman to the board. Tony is the former Chief Marketing Officer of Dunkin' U.S. and former CEO of Digitas North America. He brings more than 30 years of experience helping the world's largest brands with go-to-market strategy, digital transformation, and AI-driven marketing. His perspective will be valuable as we continue to expand the reach and impact of the Ibotta Performance Network. At the same time, Thomas Lehrman has stepped down from the board after more than a decade of service.

Thomas was an early believer and investor in Ibotta, and on behalf of the entire company, I want to thank him for his guidance and the many, many contributions he's made along the way. With that, Matt will walk through our results and outlook in more detail.

Matt Puckett: Thank you, Bryan, and good afternoon, everyone. It's great to be able to share details of our third quarter financial performance, another quarter where our teams delivered strong results relative to our plans. We are pleased with the continued momentum in the business and particularly gratified to see the business deliver an increase in adjusted EBITDA this quarter. This is now the fourth consecutive quarter in which we've delivered top- and bottom-line results above the high end of our guidance range. Just as importantly, our return to growth last quarter has been followed by a meaningful acceleration this quarter, with total company revenue up 17% year-over-year.

We delivered revenue and adjusted EBITDA that were respectively 11% and 83% above the midpoint of the guidance range that we provided on our second quarter earnings call, as the stronger revenue performance led to an outsized impact on profit, a direct result of the operating leverage in our business. Now, to share the details of our top-line results in the quarter. Revenue was $97.8 million, up 17% versus last year. Within that, redemption revenue was $88.5 million, up 23% year-over-year, driving the stronger-than-anticipated performance in the quarter. Our revenue team is executing our go-to-market playbook at a high level.

This includes taking advantage of seasonal opportunities such as back to school, and leveraging the growing scale of the Ibotta Performance Network to secure greater offer supply from our clients. LiveLift revenue remains on track relative to our expectations, once again growing both year-over-year and sequentially versus Q2. Third-party publisher redemption revenue was $70.7 million, or up 43% versus last year, accelerating meaningfully versus the prior quarter's increase of 27%. Direct-to-consumer redemption revenue was $17.9 million, down 22% year-over-year, and similar to recent quarters' results. Where consistent with our expectations, redemption activity shifted to our third-party publishers.

Ad and other revenues, which represented 9% of our revenue in the quarter, were $9.3 million, right in line with our expectations, and down 17% versus last year. We continue to see pressure on ad revenue as a result of lower direct-to-consumer redeemers, which is being partially offset by growth in other revenue. Turning now to the key performance metrics supporting redemption revenue. Total redeemers were 23.6 million in the quarter, up 30% year-over-year. Third-party publisher redeemers grew by 34%, driven primarily by organic growth with existing publishers benefiting from improved offer supply.

To a small extent, the quarter was also impacted by the launch of Uber in the second quarter of this year, and the launch of Giant Eagle this quarter. Redemptions per redeemer were 4.9, up 8% versus last year. This is the highest that metric has been since the fourth quarter of 2024, and as Bryan mentioned, the first time it has grown year-over-year since the advent of the IPN, another outcome of the strong results this quarter. The driver of this increase was improving offer supply, which was only partially offset by the mix of redeemers, specifically the growth in third-party redeemers, which have a lower redemption frequency as compared to our direct-to-consumer redeemers.

Third-party redemptions per redeemer were 4.4, up 17% year-over-year. For the first time in 12 quarters, direct-to-consumer redemptions per redeemer grew, up 4% year-over-year. Redemption revenue per redemption was $0.76, representing a 13% decline versus last year, driven by the mix of redemption activity as well as strategic pricing actions. This quarter, we saw strong growth in food and beverage, particularly lower-priced items, which have a lower MSRP, and thus a lower resultant redemption revenue per redemption. I will add, and as I have said before, when considering our model and the absence of any meaningful cost per redemption, our strategic pricing actions are focused on growing redemptions and maximizing redemption revenue. That is how we win.

Bringing it all together, total redemptions were 116.4 million, up 40% versus last year. This acceleration in growth versus Q2, again driven by increased offer supply, was highlighted by 57% redemption growth with our third-party publishers. Moving down the P&L, non-GAAP cost of revenue was up $2.3 million, or 14% versus a year ago, including an increase in both technology and publisher-related costs. This resulted in a Q3 non-GAAP gross margin of 80.7%, up approximately 60 basis points versus last year, and up 140 basis points sequentially versus Q2. Non-GAAP operating expenses were up 15% versus last year and were 60.2% of revenue, a decrease of approximately 150 basis points year-over-year.

Non-GAAP operating expenses were slightly favorable versus our prior expectations, as we realized certain timing-related benefits and modest spend efficiencies in the quarter. Within that, non-GAAP sales and marketing expenses were up 21% versus the prior year, driven by a planned increase in labor, higher variable compensation expense, and a continued investment in third-party lift studies, partially offset by lower marketing expenses. Non-GAAP research and development expenses increased by 15%, driven by higher variable compensation expense and AI-related costs. Lastly, non-GAAP general and administrative expenses, an area of the P&L where we are benefiting from operating leverage and cost control, decreased by 1%, while depreciation and amortization increased by approximately $1.5 million.

We delivered Q3 adjusted EBITDA of $23.8 million, growing 43% year-over-year. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 24.3%, up about 440 basis points versus last year. We delivered non-GAAP net income of $16 million and non-GAAP diluted net income per share of $0.62. Our non-GAAP net income excludes $15.4 million in stock-based compensation and includes a $4.2 million adjustment for income taxes. We ended the quarter with $149.9 million of cash and cash equivalents. In Q3, we spent approximately $14.4 million repurchasing approximately 400,000 shares of our stock at an average price of $36.39. We had 26 million fully diluted shares outstanding as of September 30th.

As of the end of the quarter, we had $52.9 million remaining under our current share repurchase authorization. Cumulatively, we are pleased with the value creation of our share repurchase program to date. As of the end of the third quarter, we have spent $347.1 million since the program's inception to repurchase 10.4 million shares at an average price of $33.24. Finally, on cash flow, in Q3, benefiting from the stronger earnings, we generated $16.8 million in free cash flow, a bit ahead of our expectations. Stepping back and looking at the year-to-date result, we've generated $48.1 million in free cash flow, an increase of 9% versus last year. Now, shifting to Q4 guidance.

We currently expect revenue in the range of $94 million-$98 million, representing approximately 8% year-over-year growth at the midpoint. We expect Q4 adjusted EBITDA in the range of $15 million-$17 million, representing about a 17% adjusted EBITDA margin at the midpoint. With that, let me provide some context and additional color on our outlook. The sustained improvements in our go-to-market execution that Bryan described continue to pay off. Together, the performance of our product offering, including LiveLift, along with strong consumer demand for value on our network, have driven four straight quarters of improving revenue trends. We believe that positions us well to deliver continued growth in the fourth quarter and into 2027.

There are a couple of dynamics that we are navigating as we project the Q4 results. One is specific to the comparisons, shifting contributions of our revenue streams over time, and the second is relative to the actual business drivers and impacts. Relative to the first, and recognizing our guidance implies a slower rate of year-over-year growth in Q4 than in Q3, our two-year growth rate is relatively comparable across the two quarters. It is also worth noting that Q3 was our easiest comparison of the year, as the third quarter of 2025 was the low point in our redemption revenue results. On top of that, our seasonality between Q3 and Q4 is changing.

Historically, our ad and other and D2C businesses have been more heavily weighted toward the fourth quarter. As those businesses become a smaller percentage of our total revenue, the typical step-up from Q3 to Q4 is becoming less pronounced. Specific to our assumptions on business drivers, our back-to-school programs were extremely successful in Q3. While we could see similar strength during the holiday season, we are maintaining a conservative planning posture, given that we have only just completed October, which is typically the smallest month of the quarter in terms of revenue, and the holidays are still ahead of us.

Importantly, our team has shown it can move quickly to capture opportunities, and we are poised to do that should it occur. Looking beyond the fourth quarter, I also want to share some preliminary thoughts on 2027 revenue. The progress we have made across the business over the past several quarters, along with the impact we expect from work still underway, gives us increasing confidence that we are returning to a period of consistent and sustainable revenue growth. Based on our initial planning, we project at least mid-single-digit revenue growth in 2027, which will continue to be highlighted by relatively faster growth in our core redemption revenue business. We will share more detail about this next quarter.

Lastly, our balance sheet remains strong, and we continue to generate healthy cash flow. That gives us the flexibility to keep doing what we have done consistently over multiple quarters, investing in the organic growth of the business and our key strategic priorities, while opportunistically returning cash to shareholders through our buyback program. As we prepare to close out the year, we are pleased with how much ground we have covered. We have meaningfully increased the offer supply available on our network and demonstrated improved go-to-market execution. We have seen our product capabilities deliver effective outcomes and be well received by the market.

We have grown our redeemer base at existing publishers and brought new partners like Uber, Giant Eagle, and 7-Eleven onto the IPN. We see plenty of opportunity ahead to build on these gains and create even more value for our CPG clients, retailer partners, and consumers. With that, operator, let us please open up the line for Q&A.

Operator: For today's Q&A session, we will be utilizing the Raise Hand feature. If you would like to ask a question, please click on the Raise Hand button at the bottom of the screen. Once prompted, please unmute yourself and begin with your question. We will now pause a moment to assemble the queue. Thank you. Our first question will come from Alex Vegliante with Goldman Sachs. Your line is now open. Please go ahead with your question.

Alex Vegliante: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my question. Congrats on a good quarter. I just wanted to ask about LiveLift. You mentioned that it's tracking in line based on your expectations and up year-over-year and sequentially. Maybe just an update on what the progress is there, the adoption rates by your clients, and any continued investments that you need to make in order to accelerate that adoption, whether it's continued third-party lift studies or your go-to-market efforts. Thank you.

Bryan Leach: Thanks, Alex. Appreciate it. With regard to LiveLift, we're pleased with how that's tracking. We mentioned the example of Danone in my remarks, using that product and finding terrific results. Certainly, the partnership with Circana has been helpful in corroborating the incremental sales results that we're able to pass along. I think just to remind everyone, the things that make LiveLift, the first is that we make a projection of incremental sales, typically a range. Second is that we measure incremental sales using a sophisticated statistical method. Third is that we then optimize based on what we found, so that the campaigns can achieve their objectives more effectively.

We're continuing to see clients that use that give us very positive feedback, introduce other brands to the LiveLift product. As far as ongoing investment, we're continuing to refine the models that do the projections and do the recommendations and optimizations. That's an ongoing thing. The more campaigns we run, the more data we gather. As we get more data from our publisher partners and build next-generation models, we expect that more and more types of campaigns will be eligible, for instance, campaigns that don't run as long in terms of the number of weeks. But we're seeing very positive reception to that.

The other thing is that LiveLift will be powering a new generation of products at Ibotta that are going to be rolling out next year. I spoke a little bit about that in the last call, but the idea is that instead of just having a model that can do those three things, having a set of tools at your fingertips that allow you to do those things is even more powerful. That will be something we will be talking more about in 2027.

Alex Vegliante: That is great. Thank you.

Operator: Your next question will come from the line of Mark Mahaney with Evercore ISI. Your line is now open. Please go ahead.

Mark Mahaney: Okay, thanks. I will throw out two questions. On that 2027 revenue guidance, I think you said at least mid-single digits. Just go through again why it would come out like that. I would have thought it would have been a little north of that, given the recovery, the improved performance, and the results, frankly, of the second half of this year. Are there particular factors that I know comps get tougher, but there is a real recovery here. Just talk through that a little bit. Secondly, just on one metric, how should we think about revenue per redemption going forwards? Is there a stabilization in there? If you could just talk about that metric. Thank you.

Matt Puckett: Yeah. Hi, Mark. I will take both of those. As it relates to 2027, I mean, first of all, it is pretty early, and we are providing a preliminary projection. As you will well know, this will be the first time actually since we have gone public, since post-IPO, that we have provided really any forward view beyond the next quarter. We thought right now it was really important to signal confidence that we have got based on the growth that we have seen over the last number of quarters and the performance and the results that we are driving with our partners. Certainly, the confidence is buoyed by the progress that we have made.

That said, we are not going to get out over our skis at this point. We certainly gave you what we think is a floor. We said at least mid-single digits. Could it be faster in 2027? It could, and certainly some of those things will be a function of continued go-to-market execution, which has been really good. Could that drive more growth next year? It certainly could. I think we are just being careful. The other thing I would say is, Bryan talked about the progress that we are making with LiveLift, but really the product roadmap generally.

We are not currently assuming a significant impact from those product enhancements as they roll out over the next several quarters, given it is still pretty early. We will have more to say on this next quarter and as the next year progresses. So, stay tuned. As it relates to pricing and the redemption fee itself, overall, our goal is to drive more redemptions and more redemption revenue. That is the number one priority, and we really want to deliver on clients' objectives. In some cases, to achieve client objectives, we identify opportunities for strategic pricing actions. You can know those are always done in the service of driving more revenue for Ibotta.

Some of the downward trajectory we have seen in recent quarters, and particularly in the third quarter, is a function of offer mix. As we are successful in driving increased promotions on lower-priced items, which results in lower redemption revenue per redemption, I talked about that on my prepared remarks. By the way, we saw that in Q3, particularly in food. It will likely continue. It is not easy to predict what happens to redemption fees over time, but if we feel like we can accelerate growth, whether it is short-term, medium-term, or long-term, we will, and you might see that number move lower as a result.

I think the last thing I would say on that, really important from a financial perspective and from our financial model, given that we really have no cost per redemption, certainly no variable cost per redemption, driving incremental revenue is a great outcome, and that is what we are focused on.

Operator: Your next question will come from the line of Bernie McTernan with Needham & Company. Your line is now open. Please go ahead with your question.

Bernie McTernan: Great. Thanks for taking the questions. Maybe just to start, Bryan, would love to get what your initial reaction was of the announced CART and DASH merger. Anything we should be contemplating on potential top-line impact and bottom line? And then second, redemptions this quarter at 116.4 million, that was almost 20% above the prior peak. So just want to see if that's the right kind of ceiling we should be thinking about going forward for redemptions, and maybe your line of sight into that ceiling next year. Thank you.

Bryan Leach: Thanks, Bernie. Yeah, I'll tackle the first one first. So the merger, yeah, I mean, we don't have a lot more information than anybody else. Our understanding is that they're going to be keeping these two services distinct and that our offers will obviously be available to users of both of those services.

We have a really terrific relationship with both Instacart and DoorDash, and I think this provides an opportunity for us to, once the merger is actually complete and gone through regulatory and so forth, to actually apply some of the best practices and learnings from one environment to the other environment, which whether that—yeah, there are a lot of different ways in which we can think about how that could be the case. But for instance, to maximize the redemption rate and the awareness, making sure that all the different touch points where you could interact with this type of digital promotion will be available.

As far as other than that's all I can say on that until I know more, I suppose. I'm not sure I fully understand the redemption ceiling question. I mean, we don't view this as some kind of arbitrary ceiling for our business. I mean, we feel like if we continue to execute in the ways that the sales team has been going to market, make it easier to launch offers on our platform, we absolutely can grow redemptions and redemption revenue beyond what we've achieved this year. And I would expect no less from our company. So unless I missed something, the answer is no magic ceiling.

Bernie McTernan: That's great. Thanks, Bryan.

Operator: Next up will be Ken Gawrelski with Wells Fargo. You may now go ahead with your question.

Ken Gawrelski: Thank you. Could you talk a little bit about how durable the unlock in supply, advertiser supply was in the quarter? Clearly a nice driver, and to see that expansion in redeemers, or in redemptions, I should say, suggests an unlock of some supply. Could you talk a little bit more about the durability in the near term, into the fourth quarter? But as you look into 2027, could you talk about any kind of durable unlocks of supply? And I'll stop there and maybe have a follow-up, please.

Bryan Leach: Sure, Ken. You can always have a follow-up, my friend. To the first question, I would say, we offer a level of scale, a level of sophisticated measurement, and a level of speed that these companies are realizing they cannot find elsewhere. If you need to grow market share quickly and you need to make a dent with an investment, and you also want to trust that is being done in a way that third parties can validate and that is rigorous from a measurement standpoint, so you can continue to lean in based on those results.

I think you are seeing a lot of people who may have piloted LiveLift come back and spend more, introduce new brands to Ibotta broadly, but especially to our latest tools. I think in terms of some other durable wins, there are new pockets of redeemers that are available. We have grown redeemers significantly, as you point out, and I think those are durable gains.

You are talking about new ways in which publishers that we currently have are building awareness of this offering, so interacting with it in more places on their website or in-store, thinking about how we will be able to build on that by making sure that it is part of their agentic algorithms, for example, their in-store shelf tag, tying in with those sorts of things. I think those are very durable, and honestly, we are on the front end of those benefits. You get new types of budgets.

For example, when we launched Giant Eagle, being able to bring in access to their shopper marketing offers, their Giant Eagle exclusive offers is a wholly new budget for us that will be durable going into next year. That increases the redemptions and the number of redeemers, of course. I just think, scale and proof beget scale in the sense that we will hope to add even more momentum on the redeemer side, diversify even further the publisher base in our network, and I think that gives us more surface area, different types of customers.

For instance, the launch of 7-Eleven and Speedway, that is something that touches the convenience channel for the first time and brings in a different kind of customer. I think we gave this example of a top client of ours that went away almost entirely and is now back to being a top five client. I do not think they are going to suddenly, knock on wood, but I do not think they are going to suddenly go away again. I think we addressed their concerns around measurement and proof, and now we are building together in a really strong way based on that trusted relationship and having proven results.

You should get more momentum when you prove that what you say you can do has actually happened. I think in those senses, I feel really good about the durability of these gains.

Ken Gawrelski: Thanks, Bryan. Just one follow-up on the same point.

Ken Gawrelski: Could you talk about, maybe if you could weigh in on how much of this is competitive share gains in an existing budget pool versus your ability to unlock new budgets? You touched on it a little bit in your previous answer, but I would love it if you could just weigh in, and I think it would help us a lot in thinking about the growth rate potential of the company as we look over the next 12-24 months. Thank you.

Bryan Leach: Yeah. No, I think Ibotta really is in a unique position in the way that we go to market. There are some other companies that have specific relationships with specific retailers and provide the rails to power principally their shopper marketing retailer-specific offers. But those are fixed budgets that we are not really growing because we are taking share from them or otherwise. We are getting in there and we are proving that, first of all, you do not have to take a dollar from anywhere if what you are doing is driving top line and not eroding margin.

If you can show that you are delivering profitable revenue growth and paying back with very conservative measurement inside of a 60-day period on a cash-on-cash basis, people will go and find that money the same way they will when they have a set constraint on AppLovin, for example, and they like the iROAS or the payback period of that. They want as much of that as possible, and I think that mindset is only possible now that we have the proof to show what that incremental sale is on a rolling basis.

And they can say, "Gosh, this is actually something we have not seen before in terms of, I want as much of this subject to this constraint," what we have called sometimes the outcomes era. There are situations where we've seen that we are able to pull dollars out of media or out of other promotion budgets, and we are helping companies creatively find those dollars in order to fund our programs. But I think those are not what I would call competitive share gains.

Those are growing the number and types of people inside of an organization, whether it is the revenue growth management team, whether it is the media agency, that are actually really intrigued by our scale, speed, and sophisticated measurement. So, I think that is a bullish signal from the standpoint of, I think, where your question is coming from.

Operator: Your next question will come from the line of Andrew Boone with Citizens. Your line is now open, and you may ask your question.

Andrew Boone: Thanks so much for taking the questions. I wanted to stay on Ken's line of questions. Bryan, what we are all trying to understand is kind of where demand came from. In prepared remarks, you talked about stronger sales execution, focus on core value prop, growth of LiveLift, enhanced measurement, demand for savings, and then the seasonal benefit. Is there a way that you can rank those things for us to just better help us understand where demand came from for redemptions?

Bryan Leach: Yeah, that's a really great question. I think that the way I would say that is, number one is just delivering. Delivering for our clients, calling our shot, running a program, it performs or outperforms, and then they go and find more money. They come back and say, "Yep, here's some extra dollars in the third quarter. We're really pleased with how this went in the second quarter." I'd say second, and behind that lies a trust. A trust not just because of the results, but because of the relationship. The fact that we understand their business, we are more upstream in their planning process.

I mentioned that we have more visibility into these preferred partnerships than we have had in the past. I think that's another way of answering Ken's question in terms of durability. Because we're more upstream in the planning, we're further in advance, and we're not sort of still reaping the negative consequences of sort of some of the poor execution in late 2024, early 2025, before we executed our reorganization. Now what we're seeing is the dividends of good execution in 2025 paying off when that program that was scheduled as part of the planning process is there for back to school. So you get a really vibrant back to school program.

I think there are some competitive tensions between our clients as well, where you see, "Gosh, this is now at a scale where I'm seeing my competitor move the needle in their market share. What is going on? Who do I call at Ibotta? How do I make sure I'm participating in an intelligent use of my promotional dollars?" So you've got some of those healthy dynamics that are going on as well. I think the other things you mentioned are definitely important. I think that the third-party partnership with Circana continues to be a huge validator and unlock.

I think you combine LiveLift with Circana, and you kind of go in and directly anticipate the objections or critiques that may exist, and you help really reframe that mindset around, "I want as much of this as I can get," rather than, "As much as I need to do in order to satisfy a retailer's demands." I think the fact that the publishers are leaning in various ways, helping to further improve measurement, helping to further improve targeting, helping to further improve awareness visibility.

When you can talk about how now all of a sudden it's going to be something you can see on digital shelf tags or on digital end caps or in-store mode, it's going to be personalized, it's going to be part of agentic solution. These are all the things they're thinking about, and I think they view our team as kind of out in front as thought leaders, helping them make better decisions in the age of AI. So I think it's those things for the most part, honestly, Andrew, but there are little puts and takes.

Obviously, back to school is always a particularly good event for us, especially in the food category, in categories where we really needed to bring back customers, and we did that. So I think those are where it's coming from. I think you're going to see a whole other wave of tailwinds in 2027 when we roll out this next generation of products. I think that's going to be the next big inflection point, but we got to see how long that takes, and that'll be an iterative process.

Andrew Boone: Bryan, I wanted to ask about the move toward more always-on budgets. It sounds like you guys are getting to measurement faster in 2026. As we think about 2027, the progress across the product roadmap, is there a way that you guys can accelerate what is always on and get to measurement and ROAS faster? Is that part of the roadmap? Can you just speak to kind of your progress there? Thank you.

Bryan Leach: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, this is fundamentally a statistical exercise. So you need to find enough data that allows you to make statistical claims that are significant between populations that are exposed and not exposed. Think of a test versus control type of approach. This really is a breakthrough, a major breakthrough in sophistication. It's the gold standard. To do that, you need a certain amount of data, and you need a certain amount of accuracy from your model, which is based on how many examples you've run through the model in the past.

So the longer you're running a campaign, the more frequently that product that's featured is being purchased, the more quickly you develop signal, the more accurate your projections can be, and the more effective your optimization strategy can be. We are making good progress on that. We've really improved dramatically, I would say, over the course of the last 18 months, our ability to accurately project how long a campaign will last, including also improving our ability to project the performance of that campaign. So, as clients see that, they develop confidence, and then they say, "Okay, we understand how this works. This is a range. As the campaign goes on, we get more and more and more precision.

The range narrows." That's just never been a conversation that's happened in the promotions industry before. The conversation has literally been, "Here's how many clips I'm giving you. Think that'll satisfy the merchant?" End of conversation. To actually have a conversation about profitability, incremental sales, performance, to even get to a place where it would make sense to be always on is itself a major move that has taken much of the last year to effectuate. Now we're sort of speaking the same vocabulary, getting in there and saying, "Okay, we're going to shoot for this. We all agree upfront that if we hit this is something we would keep doing," right?

We qualify the sale that way on the front end. That way, when it happens, you're in a much better spot versus you ran a campaign, and then you sent a recap deck, and now you're debating over whether or not the methodology is valid or not. You get a lot more credibility when you kind of say, well, we don't know. We're going to tell you exactly how we're going to measure it upfront. This is our best guess as a range, and then we will tell you as soon as we find out. There'll be no time to interpret that or anything like that. It'll just be showing up, and then we'll all react to it.

It's not going to be a Soviet election where it's a hit 99% of the time. It'll work the great majority of the time, and sometimes when it doesn't work, we'll adjust. You might be too efficient, leaving profitable revenue on the table, or you might be not efficient enough and needing to make the offers a little less generous, sacrifice some volume of incremental sales in order to get to your profitability goals. I think that this kind of consultative approach where we really talk about the margin structure of their products at the SKU level beforehand is really paying dividends in terms of trust, and I think that's really what underpins willingness to switch to always on.

Operator: Your next question will come from the line of Ron Josey with Citi. You may now unmute and ask your question.

Ron Josey: Great. Thanks for taking the questions. Bryan, with that comment to both Andrew and Ken, just talking about budgets, perhaps the mix shift or the move to always on. With budgets unlocking here, just talk to us a little bit more about the publisher network. I think you had some pretty good comments on Giant Eagle when that went live. You saw more coupons than before. I wanted to hear a little bit more both about the publishers that have the offline component, but of course, the internet native ones as well, not necessarily the combination of the merger that we've seen, but just the adoption of these tools. Thank you.

Bryan Leach: Thanks, Ron. Yeah, I mean, I'm really proud of our team, led by Amir, our Chief Business Development Officer, and everybody's been working hard to add publishers to our network. We've added Uber, we've added Giant Eagle, we've added 7-Eleven, and we're just starting to roll those out, ramp those up. It takes a while for consciousness of these programs to kind of permeate. But it's also the work we've done with the publishers we do have, Instacart, DoorDash, Dollar General, Family Dollar, Walmart, and making sure that we are meeting their needs, and where we're missing the mark, we're immediately correcting ourselves and getting them what they want.

The fact that Giant Eagle was willing to go onto their own website and say, "We've just tripled the number of offers we have," many of which are in the most critical food categories, not so top-heavy on beauty products, for example, that's a really big deal in terms of the validation we think that provides of our network to the next publisher that we want to add. "Hey, listen, don't take our word for it.

It's right over here." These are people saying, "I switched from a competitor who I'd been with for a decade to the Ibotta Performance Network, and overnight got the feedback from our shoppers that, 'Hey, this is great,' at a time when we really care about value and decide where to shop based on value." I think that's a really, really important validating proof point. I think that as we become better partners to our publishers, we can point to all the ways in which that kind of consultative relationship is benefiting them.

For instance, thinking through the future of agentic shopping, how do we position you both to have our content taken into account by whatever agents you may be building on your own experience, but also to make sure that you are positioned well to receive traffic from other agents that may be considering offers as a primary determinant of what products to put into a basket? These are just things that make us more and more sticky, more and more valuable. As far as the last mile or online publishers, I mean, I think that we've really been intentional about our approach. We focused on getting all three of the big last-mile providers, Uber, Instacart, and DoorDash.

That's really valuable because a huge portion of the growth that's happening in consumer goods is happening in online purchases. In some companies, it's 200% of their growth. They know, okay, in one environment, I can set a campaign that's rational based on my strategic objectives, and those can evolve in the course of a year, but that will then allow me to really capture market share and have a competitive advantage in those environments. That's, I think, really powerful. We know that a lot of them are tech-forward, therefore, helping us out building these really sophisticated test and control approaches to measurement, which I think the industry has really never seen before.

They're helping us solve this offline signal, this offline conversion problem that has plagued the CPG industry from an advertising perspective since the advent. There's never been reliable offline signal the way that we're building it right now. We're now focusing more on core grocery, so you see things like Giant Eagle and newer frontiers like convenience coming into our network, and I think that is being well received, especially by those clients that really care about, for instance, beverage, snack, that care about some of those new areas, surface areas that we're putting out there.

It also, you find that in different organizations, there can be different budgets for e-commerce or for last mile that are reserved and that we now have access to in a way that, had we not added them, we might not have. Those are some ways in which I think we've done a good job on the publisher growth strategy thus far this year.

Ron Josey: That's great. Thank you, Bryan.

Operator: As a reminder, if you would like to ask a question, please click on the Raise Hand button at the bottom of your screen. Once prompted, please unmute yourself and begin with your question. Next up will be Nitin Bansal with Bank of America. Please unmute your line and ask your question.

Nitin Bansal: Thank you for taking questions. Bryan, can you provide an update on the health of your key verticals, like where growth was stronger or weaker versus your initial expectations entering the quarter? If you can also share some color on how the current macro backdrop is impacting consumer activity and promotional supply on the platform, if you are seeing any changes in the budget allocation or consumer patterns that could serve as a leading indicator for the trends in 2027. Thank you.

Bryan Leach: Thanks, Nitin. I think we saw broad-based strength across our CPG business. I would call out ongoing strength in the food category. We have seen emerging brands be a source of strength. Health and beauty continues to be a really great area for us, sometimes because they have a little bit better margins to work with. Broad-based, I am really proud of the entire sales team that we have got out there with our verticalized sales structure that Chris put in place. I think there is not a pocket of our organization that has not raised their game in terms of execution. I am excited about that.

I would say in terms of the macro backdrop, I think there is always a demand for intelligent deployment of resources to grow market share profitably. It does not matter whether you are facing pressures from tariffs or supply chain or for whatever reason, you do not want the only way you can grow market share be a very blunt instrument like a one-size-fits-all rollback of price that hurts your margins, or an unmeasurable blunt instrument like certain types of upper funnel media that you really have no good basis for knowing whether or not they made a difference.

When you can come up with something that provides a way out of this problem where you say, "Well, what if I told you could grow your top line and grow your market share, protect against private label, but actually do that in a way that is either margin neutral or margin accretive?" Most people kind of look at you like, "Well, that's not possible." When you can show them that with math and science, it is possible, that's really exciting, and they kind of go, "This could be the ticket that I've been really looking for." I don't think—every time I get the macro question, I say the same thing, which is these are non-discretionary purchases, and we are a fundamental part of almost 24 million—23+ million redeemers every quarter, and that's a significant base of consumers that is appealing in all environments.

As far as overall attitudes toward promotions, though, I will say that our being here as a thought leader, driving substantial investments through Luke and his team on R&D, actually putting the work in to say, "We've come up with a better mousetrap. Hey, here's a tool that's going to allow you to diagnose opportunities in your business using the latest trend data. Here's a tool that's going to help you quickly design the optimized promotion against your specific strategic objectives. Here's a set of tools that make it easier for you to deal with invoicing and back and forth or have a more self-service interface." This is not typical in our industry.

I think what you're starting to see is Ibotta is not viewed as a promotions company per se, but as a solutions provider upstream in their strategic planning process, a platform that can help them really grow their business at scale. That is, I think, starting to pay off. It takes a while to change that mindset, but I think we're starting to see the benefits of that. That will persist in the future regardless of the interest rates or the level of inflation, et cetera.

Operator: This concludes the Q&A section of the call. I would now like to turn the call back to management for closing remarks.

Bryan Leach: Thank you. I appreciate everyone's ongoing support and interest in our business. We've had a lot to prove over the last year. We said we were setting out to turn around, reorganize, rethink, reinvent certain aspects of our go-to-market, certain aspects of our product, to really listen to our clients and build things that make a difference in their businesses. And I am incredibly proud of the trend line and the trajectory that our team has achieved. I'm also grateful for the questions and being pressed to become a more predictable business.

I think we have better forecasting, better ability to provide the kind of guidance that hopefully the investing public is looking for, and I want to thank Matt and his team for doing a tremendous job of giving us that level of visibility. With that, I appreciate it, and thanks, everyone.

Operator: Thank you for joining today's session. The call has concluded. You may now disconnect.

#3031. Canada-India $5.5 billion bank takeover attracts opposition from workers, politicians

Canadian firm Fairfax Financial Holdings' proposed $5.5 billion takeover of IDBI Bank is facing pushback from employees of the Indian state-owned lender and political parties in the country.

On Sunday, the United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees called for a two-day "nationwide" strike against the sale of the bank to Fairfax. The workers' union also expressed "grave concerns" about the transparency of the sale and valuation process, according to a post on X.

It is demanding that the government "cancel the privatization process" and instead focus on strengthening the bank while protecting public investment and employees' interests.

Last week, Rahul Gandhi, India's leader of the opposition, extended support to the IDBI Bank employee unions opposing the takeover by Fairfax. "Public banks are not assets to be sold off, they are tools to build the nation," Gandhi said in a statement on Thursday.

He added that the sale of over 60% stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax goes against the commitment of previous governments to hold a 51% stake in the state-owned lender.

Nirmala Sitharaman, India's finance minister, in her response said the public sector bank was handed to the government in "poor shape" and was revived through "professionalism, prudence" and recapitalization of more than 250 billion rupees ($2.6 billion).

"The IDBI Bank is now poised for its next phase of growth," the finance minister said. The government has previously said that the next phase of growth will be driven by a strategic investor.

The Indian government on Oct.14 said the sale of over 60% of the share in IDBI will mark the largest foreign direct investment transaction in India's financial sector. Fairfax made a bid to pay 81 rupees per share for IDBI against the average fair value set at 75.99 rupees apiece.

On Monday, shares of IDBI opened at around 79 rupees per share.

However, Indian media outlet Businessworld on Thursday reported that government officials had suppressed the valuation of IDBI to make Fairfax's offer seem attractive. The Ministry of Finance has defended its procedure, adding that the bidding process was a "double blind" as the bidder did not know the valuation and the valuators did not see the bids.

The Indian government has been divesting stakes this year as it pushes to keep the country's growth engine running amid deepening fiscal pressures. It sold shares in several companies, including Cochin Shipyard, Indian Railways Finance Corp, NHPC and Coal India. In August, it got $3.3 billion for a 6.5% stake in the country's top life insurer, Life Insurance Corporation of India.

Kosmos Energy Ltd. (KOS -13.33%) reported progress on its strategic objectives including production growth, cost reduction, debt repayment, and portfolio advancement. Management emphasized the successful completion of the infill drilling program in Ghana and the stable operational performance of its liquefied natural gas project offshore Mauritania and Senegal. The company successfully executed a farm-down of a development project in the Gulf of America to bring in a new partner and reduce capital obligations. Following the extension of its reserve-based lending facility, the company stated it is now focused on managing long-term bond maturities. Management noted that the current operational strategy prioritizes reservoir management and high facility uptime to sustain production levels ahead of future drilling campaigns.

Operator: Good day, everyone. Welcome to the Kosmos Energy's Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. As a reminder, today's call is being recorded. At this time, let me turn the call over to Jamie Buckland, Vice President of Investor Relations at Kosmos Energy.

Jamie Buckland: Thank you, operator, and thanks to everyone for joining us today. This morning, we issued our Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Release. This release and the slide presentation to accompany today's call are available on the Investors page of our website. Joining me on the call today to go through the materials are Andy Inglis, Chairman and CEO, and Neal Shah, CFO. During today's presentation, we will make forward-looking statements that refer to our estimates, plans, and expectations. Actual results and outcome could differ materially due to factors we note in this presentation and in our U.K. and SEC filings. Please refer to our annual report, stock exchange announcement, and SEC filings for more details.

These documents are available on our website. At this time, I will turn the call over to Andy.

Andrew Inglis: Thanks, Jamie, and good morning and afternoon to everyone. Thank you for joining us today for our Third Quarter 2026 Results Call. I will begin today's call by reviewing the progress we have made against the four goals we laid out at the start of the year before giving an update on each of our business units. I will then hand over to Neal to talk through the financials before I wrap up with closing remarks and a look towards 2027. We will then open the call up for Q&A. Starting on Slide 3. When we released our full year 2025 results in March, we laid out four key objectives for Kosmos in 2026, which is shown on the slide.

I am pleased to say through the first 3 quarters of the year, we have made excellent progress against all of them. We have seen strong year-on-year production growth from our core assets, namely Jubilee and GTA. We delivered significant absolute and per barrel equivalent cost reductions year-on-year, with a specific focus on operating costs. We delivered the majority of our net debt reduction target and are on track to achieve the 20% reduction target for the year, a target we increased with our first quarter results in May. We have continued to advance our high-quality growth portfolio, particularly in the Gulf of America, with minimal capital input.

By delivering this agenda, we expect to end the year with a more resilient and more valuable company, a company with higher production, lower costs, and lower debt, with significant upside from our hopper of future growth opportunities. We will also have higher exposure to elevated commodity prices as we enter 2027, which Neal will cover later in the materials. I'd now like to focus on the progress we're making in each business unit, starting with Ghana on Slide 4. We've seen a lot of progress in Ghana this year with an active drilling campaign that has delivered in line with our expectations and highlighted the potential of this mid-life asset.

The key to delivering Jubilee's full production potential going forward is demonstrating operational delivery, in particular reservoir management in the periods between drilling campaigns. In the third quarter, Jubilee gross production was 84,500 barrels of oil per day, an increase of around 17% versus the previous quarter, reflecting the new wells that came online in late 2Q and during the third quarter. Specifically, in August, the J50 producer well came online, and then in September, the J73 water injection well completed the program. Our annual guidance for Jubilee was 70,000 to 80,000 barrels of oil per day, with year-to-date production through end 3Q around 75,000 barrels of oil per day.

With the latest drilling program now complete, the partnership focuses on improving management of the reservoir to mitigate decline. This will require daily focus on operational delivery, namely sustained water injection or voidage replacement above 120%, continued production system optimization, adding gas lift to the west side of Jubilee, and high FPSO uptime of around 98% or above. As we look ahead, we're pleased to have contracted the Faye Kozack rig from Noble for the 2027/2028 drilling campaign of up to 10 wells, with the rig due to arrive in mid-2027.

The first new wells in the program will benefit from the most recent 4D seismic, with the ocean bottom node survey, or OBN, expected to play a major role in planning and high-grading the wells for the second half of the program. In Ghana, we have a government that wants to get things done. Last month at the African Energy Week in Cape Town, I shared the stage with the Chairman of the African Energy Chamber and Ghana's Energy Minister to talk about what we're doing as a partnership to help drive energy prosperity in Ghana. It was a productive and valuable discussion.

One of the key takeaways was if companies like Kosmos can help the country win through long-term investment, lower cost associated domestic gas, the transfer of knowledge and skills, then Kosmos will win, too. Ghana is a case study on how a government and a company like Kosmos can work together to get things done for the benefit of all stakeholders. Turning to Slide 5. GTA continues to perform strongly. During the third quarter, gross LNG production was around 2.44 million tons per annum equivalent, in line with expectations, with higher seasonal temperatures through the summer months as previously guided.

The partnership lifted 8.5 gross LNG cargoes, slightly ahead of guidance, which brings the total number of gross LNG cargoes lifted to the end of the third quarter to '27. The condensate cargo that was due to be lifted at the end of the third quarter was lifted in early 4Q due to bad weather in the region that prevented an earlier lifting, with Kosmos receiving just under 400,000 net barrels of condensate. For the year, the strong operational performance means we are on track to achieve the upper end of our 32 to 36 gross LNG cargo guidance. The three gross condensate cargoes for the year have now all been lifted.

Looking ahead to the expansion of the project, Phase 1 plus is making good progress with the construction of the onshore pipeline in Senegal well underway. The bottom image on the slide shows the first piece of the gas pipeline being laid in September. RGS, the operator of the gas pipeline, reported that the first phase of the onshore pipeline connecting the GTA hub to the 230 megawatt Gandon power plant is now over 25% complete. Further segments of the onshore pipeline connecting additional demand centers to the south are due to commence construction in 2027, with commissioning targeted for 2029.

As I said in my comments on the previous slide, our focus above ground is just as important as the work we do below ground. It is a core part of the Kosmos skill set as we work with the governments and national oil companies to maximize the value of the projects we undertake together. The last 2 months, we spent time with the presidents of both Mauritania and Senegal to talk about the future, as can be seen in the top image on the slide. I'm pleased to say we have a shared vision for the future that prioritizes lower-cost domestic gas alongside the LNG exports from Phase 1 and future phases.

This lower-cost domestic gas will replace higher-cost imported diesel and LNG and help both countries achieve their gas-to-power and gas-to-industry goals over the coming years. If the countries succeed in these goals, then Kosmos will also succeed. We look forward to advancing these goals in the future. Turning to Slide 6. Production in the Gulf of America for the third quarter of approximately 14,100 barrels of oil equivalent was in line with expectations, helped partly by the lack of storm activity during the quarter. This reversed in early 4Q, and Neal will talk about this in more detail shortly. During the quarter, we successfully completed a highly competitive farm-down on Tiberius, bringing Navitas into the project as a 33.33% partner.

Following the transaction, Kosmos will remain as operator with a 33.34% interest, with Oxy, owner and operator of the nearby Lucius facility, holding the remainder. As detailed on our last earnings call, the consideration was a mix of upfront cash, carry for future development CapEx, and future milestone payments. The carry is expected to cover all of our Tiberius CapEx through 2026 and fund our share of the development through the first half of 2027. Tiberius is a low-cost, high-margin development, and we now have an aligned partnership to move forward, with first oil expected in the second half of 2028. Elsewhere in the Gulf, our strategic exploration alliance with Shell is working well.

The partnership is now preparing to drill the Trailblazer ILX well in the first half of 2027, with Transocean's Deepwater Pontus rig contracted. Trailblazer is a 4-way structural trap in the Norphlet, on trend with several other discoveries, such as Shell's Appomattox field. In a success case, the discovery could be tied back to the nearby Appomattox facility, which has available capacity, with Kosmos designated development operator. Beyond Trailblazer, there are several other high-quality opportunities in the Norphlet that we expect to advance as part of the Shell Exploration Alliance.

We are excited to be getting back to exploration in the Gulf and doing it in a capital-efficient way that allows us to test meaningful resource opportunities at a relatively low cost. I will now turn it over to Neal to take you through the financials.

Neal Shah: Thanks, Andy. Turning now to Slide 7, which looks at the financials for the third quarter in detail. It has been another strong quarter for the company, with production higher year-on-year and OpEx falling sharply in line with the targets Andy mentioned at the beginning of today's presentation. All of the line items for the quarter were in line with our guidance, except for DD&A, which was slightly higher than our guidance range due to a minor accounting change to the depletion rate in Jubilee for the quarter, with our full-year DD&A guidance unchanged. Also, tax per barrel was lower in the quarter, reflecting the mark-to-market derivatives loss that offset some of the revenue during the quarter.

Excluding the mark-to-market, tax expense was in line with our expectations. Looking ahead to Q4, net production is expected to be lower quarter-on-quarter, driven by a combination of lower Gulf of America and Ghana production. In the Gulf, fourth quarter production is impacted by planned maintenance at Delta House, the host facility for the Odd Job field, a workover at the Kodiak field, and downtime associated with Hurricane Isaias. In Ghana, with the drilling campaign now complete, the partnership is focused on reservoir management to mitigate decline at Jubilee before the next drilling campaign begins in mid-2027. Also in the fourth quarter, there will be financing costs of around $20 million related to the extension of the RBL.

Turning to Slide 8. Cost reduction has been a big theme across the company this year, particularly on operating costs after similar initiatives on CapEx and G&A last year. We are making a lot of progress, and the charts on the slide show how far we have come year to date. The top left chart shows that absolute operating costs have fallen by almost $150 million in the first 9 months of the year, a reduction of around 26%. OpEx per barrel has fallen around $12 per barrel, a reduction of around 37% on a per-unit basis.

This focus on cost management and a higher commodity price backdrop has seen EBITDAX almost double in the 9 months ended September 30 to almost $800 million, which has translated into robust free cash flow with more expected in the fourth quarter. We now expect around $300 million of free cash flow in 2026, net of any hedging impact, which is expected to be around $200 million for the year, demonstrating the cash flow potential of the business. As we look forward to 2027, our hedges have been put in at much higher levels than 2026, giving us greater exposure to higher prices with a lower cost base.

Turning to Slide 9, it has been a busy year for financing, and I am pleased to report we recently closed the reserve-based lending facility extension to April 2033. The facility amendment and extension is another demonstration of the company proactively addressing its maturities and the continued confidence in Kosmos' portfolio from the banking market. I would like to thank our banks for their continued support, many of whom have been with Kosmos for well over a decade. On liquidity, the strong cash flow performance in the third quarter meant we exited Q3 with around $570 million of available liquidity. We expect this to strengthen further in the fourth quarter.

On hedging, we continue to be active, adding what are likely to be the final hedges for our 2027 program. As mentioned on the previous slide, we have been able to achieve a higher average floor and a much higher average ceiling on the collars we have put in place for next year, giving us more exposure to the upside in a higher price environment. On the debt, in 3Q, we utilized our free cash flow to repay $50 million of the 2027 bonds, $15 million of the GOA term loan, and $25 million of the RBL.

In Q4, with the RBL now complete, we plan to prioritize our free cash flow towards our bonds with a view of addressing our 2028 maturities next. Finally, on leverage, with the strong year-to-date EBITDAX performance and significant debt reduction, leverage is moving towards 2x by year-end, a significant turnaround in only 12 months. With that, I will hand it back to Andy.

Andrew Inglis: Thanks, Neal. Turning now to Slide 10. As I said in my opening remarks, we have four key objectives for 2026: grow production, lower costs, reduce debt, and advance our quality growth portfolio with minimal CapEx in 2026. This slide shows the progress we have achieved year to date against those goals. Production for the first 9 months of 2026 is up 14% versus the same period last year without adjusting for the sale of EG. As Neal said, absolute operating costs are down 26% the first 9 months of the year, driving a reduction in OpEx per BOE of around 37%.

We delivered a reduction in net debt around 70% versus year-end 2025 and are well on track to achieve our 20% target. We are advancing our growth portfolio with the Tiberius farm-down, continued progress on GTA expansion, and the exploration alliance with Shell in the Gulf of America, which will drill the Trailblazer well in the first half of 2027. Turning now to Slide 11 to conclude today's presentation. We have been clear on our targets for 2026 and are delivering on them. As we approach the end of the year, we are turning our focus to 2027, where we have a lot to look forward to.

We have a deep opportunity set across the portfolio, and in 2027, we plan to continue to invest selectively in our highest quality growth options while maintaining the capital discipline we have displayed this year. Jubilee is a world-class mid-life field, and with regular drilling and excellence in reservoir management to mitigate decline, there is a huge amount of value to chase in the future.
