Finally, we remain focused on enhancing the company's financial resilience, paying down more debt, targeting year-end 2027 net debt of around $2 billion at strip prices, while addressing the rest of our near-term maturities.

We are working hard to deliver stronger and more valuable Kosmos, and look forward to delivering on these plans to support long-term value creation for our investors. Thank you, and I would now like to turn the call over to the operator to open the session for questions.

Andrew Inglis: Yes. Thanks, Charles. I want to start really with back to where current performance is in Jubilee. As we mentioned in our prepared remarks, we ended the drilling campaign in September. Charles Meade: That's helpful elaboration, Andy. Andrew Inglis: Yes, I think it's slightly reverse. I think the alliance with Shell is about establishing the equities upfront. We're pleased to be working with, obviously, with Shell. Bob Brackett: Okay. Very clear. Then sort of below the water, Trailblazer is fairly far west of some of those thickest of those aeolian deposits. What is the sort of confidence that those aeolian dunes extend that far west? Are they imageable? Is that a key risk as well?

Neil Mehta: I just wanted to get your perspective on the progress around deleveraging. Certainly in this type of commodity price environment, you guys have done a lot on the balance sheet. So just give us a mark-to-market on where you are and you are happy with, how you are thinking about the progress that you have made, and you are happy with how it is shaping up?

Andrew Inglis: Okay. Neil, my Neal, why don't you have a go at that one?

Neal Shah: Yes. Neil, thanks for the question. It's clear, again, we have been clear around what we wanted to do in terms of tackle the near-term maturities, create some space, increase liquidity, and bring down leverage. Again, I think we are in a good place, particularly with where Brent is at this point to continue to benefit from that, both as we sort of exited 3Q, but also into early 4Q, where prices have remained quite strong. So, we feel good about sort of exiting the year at sort of less than $2.4 billion from a debt perspective. Then, as we mentioned on the call, targeting to get to sort of around $2 billion by the end of 2027.

So I think, yeah, that sort of squares where we want to get to from a net debt or leverage perspective. I think from a maturity perspective, the next thing we clearly sort of voiced is our expectation is to manage the 2028 maturity, and there are a couple different ways we can tackle that. But once we address that, we basically have, call it three and a half years without any meaningful maturities. Again, that will be a huge amount of progress in a short amount of time. Again, the team has done a huge amount of work on that, and we have got a bit more to go, but I think we are in pretty good shape.

The market has been supportive, and things are headed the right way.

Neil Mehta: Yes. Neal, once you get to that target, how do you think about what you do with the excess cash? What are the different options that you have? Do you have a long-term debt target in mind? Are we starting to think about return of capital? Or what is the optimal balance sheet, and what is the approach to excess cash once you hit your target?

Neal Shah: Yes. Again, I think in the near-term, which again, I think, yeah, we would qualify as through 2027, is getting to that sort of less than $2 billion first, right? Then, if we are generating anywhere sort of north of $1 billion to $1.5 billion of EBITDA, we are sort of at a one and a half-ish times of leverage area. Again, I think that remains the first sort of objective. Beyond that, again, I think it will be a combination of then looking at additional debt paydown, and then either funneling the capital towards growth projects, or towards capital returns. So, that sort of framework has not changed.

Again, I think, that is really a decision probably towards the end of 2027 as we get closer to that target. Again, we have a number of growth opportunities, which again, in a more constructive commodity price environment, they make sense to accelerate forward. If the share price is weaker and we're in a bit of lower environment, we may lean more into the return side of the equation. Again, I think it's a good question. Again, we're not quite there yet, but after the next 12 months or so, that's certainly the right question to ask.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of David Round with Stifel.

David Round: Andy, can I just come back to the priorities before the next Jubilee drilling campaign, or Ghana drilling campaign? Can you just talk a bit more about how important those four projects are to your production levels? I think uptime probably speaks for itself, but any context on the other three items would be good. If I do think of these as specific projects, whether there are any timing milestones to look out for.

Andrew Inglis: Yes, David. Look, I could say it's really just about daily operational excellence. Ultimately, it's about managing the reservoir pressure, which is about voidage replacement. Our view is probably to have that well above 120% to manage the decline effectively. We've been a little short of that through 3Q, and it's really about now ramping up the reliability of the water injection equipment and ensuring that we deliver that. So it's not really a project, but it's a daily grind of operational excellence.

The second item is really about production optimization, and I think some of you have heard me say there's 168 set points as you look at all of the well intervals across the producing wells and injectors on Jubilee. It's the constant normalization and optimization of those settings, again, to take advantage of the increased water injection areas of increased pressure, and therefore maximizing the delivery. Again, as I've said, I think on previous calls, AI now is making a difference there, given the number of variables that you're optimizing around. We're seeing it have quite a significant impact. The final one, which is gas lift on the west, is in your project sort of bucket, I think.

It's reconnecting a riser so that we can introduce gas lift to the west side of Jubilee. That project's ongoing at the moment and will probably come in towards the end of this month. But altogether, those are the things that are part of our armory now to maximize the production from the field through the end of the year, and then exit at the maximum rate, and then continue with that through the first half of 2027.

Mark Wilson: A couple of questions from me. First, just to carry on from that RBL extension. Excellent to see that. Neal Shah: Mark, let me just take your first one, then I'll hand it over to Andy. Just in terms of a refinancing, again, I don't think we'd be looking at anything out of the ordinary. Andrew Inglis: Yes, Mark. Yes, no, absolutely. It's interesting, isn't it, comparing the lower 48 to the internationals. I'd say one of the big drivers in the lower 48 is access to inventory. Then clearly, the second big issue then is all around the synergies from those match-ups. When it comes to the international space, you look at Kosmos today, the R/P is well over 20. It's all about the organic self-help that actually gets us there today. As Neal's talked about, really every question has been around building the resilience of the balance sheet. Ultimately, it's about lowering the breakeven, taking cost out of the business, and then improving our margin.

So, the answer is, I agree with the thesis, but for Kosmos, it has to be around something that genuinely addresses the ability to create a more valuable company, because there's another access to capital, and there's a greater cash flow potential. So, that's the basis on which we would evaluate any opportunity.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Stella Cridge with Barclays.

Stella Cridge: Thanks for all the updates and the comments on the debt side. I just wonder if I follow up with one question on bonds. Obviously, you noted about the pricing in the market at the moment, obviously interest rates have moved higher, made raising debt a bit more expensive for everyone. But the one bond that has performed quite well has been your GTA bonds, which were issued perhaps before the price rally in Brent. I am just wondering, where do they sit within your thinking about the whole capital structure?

Is that a bond that you might think about refinancing at some point to lower the cost of debt, or are you just perhaps a bit more focused on the near-term maturities for the moment?

Neal Shah: Yes, Stella. I mean, clearly we put it in place at the beginning of the year to manage the 2027 maturities. It's got some time on it in terms of it's a five-year note, but clearly it's at a higher coupon than what we'd like to manage. Again, I think, yeah, we were at a pivotal point in GTA in terms of it just starting up. It's now been online for running at full rate for over a year. We'd expect it to do a pretty meaningful contribution to EBITDAX this year for the company as well. Again, I think there's been a huge amount of de-risking the asset.

I've always thought secured debt at GTA makes sense within our capital structure on a long-term basis. That note, again, I think should be lower priced at a regular time in the capital structure. It's got a 30-month call period, so again, I don't think we can call it until mid-2028. Again, I think it'd be something we could look at extending or modifying once we get to the end of the no-call period.

Operator: Your next question comes from Erik Borthen with Fearnley Securities.

Erik Christian Borthen: Congrats on a great quarter. Thanks for the update on the bond refi and outlook there. Just to follow up on the sort of growth and M&A initiatives. Your partner at Tullow at Jubilee is struggling a bit. Could you be looking at sort of increasing your stake there come sort of 2027?

Andrew Inglis: Yes. Thanks, Erik. Look, I hope I'm being clear today that our primary focus in Ghana is seeing sustained strong performance from the assets, and in particular, Jubilee. I talked in answer to David's question around the things that we need to do to improve the performance of the field, and that's clearly what we're focused on today. If there is a process which creates an opportunity to deepen our position in Jubilee, whether that's sort of directly through a deal or indirectly through preempting a deal, then it's something that we would consider in the future. But today, we're not getting distracted by that.

It's all about a focus on the daily operations, improving the flow across the items that we discussed earlier. If there is an opportunity in the future, as I said, whether directly or indirectly through preemption, we could look at it.

Erik Christian Borthen: Also, just on the 2028 maturity, you said the GTA bond is priced on the high side. With your 2031 unsecured being priced double digits, is there a threshold we should look at to gauge where it will be an attractive opportunity for you guys?

Neal Shah: Yes, Erik. What I'd say is, again, as we reduce the amount of total debt that we have, both on the RBL and the bonds, we expect the pricing to come in. We've seen a huge compression in the credit spreads, and while they're still low double digits, we still think there's room to go. Again, I think clearly, in my mind, our credit should be single-digit paper. I think, to the extent we can get the, we've moved the credit rating back to single-B. We need to move the credit rating of the issue back to single-B as well.

That should open us up to a pretty large financing market, allowing us to issue paper where we want to on a recurring basis. Again, I think we've got some luxury.

Operator: Since there are no further questions at this time, I would like to bring the call to a close. Thanks to everyone for joining today. You may now disconnect your lines at this time, and thank you for your participation.

#3026. Democratic Rep. Stevens endorses Republican Rogers over rival El-Sayed in Michigan Senate election

Michigan Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, in a stunning move, endorsed Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday.

Stevens lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed earlier this year, but since then had backed his candidacy.

Her endorsement of Rogers came after days of rising tension with El-Sayed and his campaign over an inflammatory ad by a political action committee, Rebellion PAC, which depicted a couple debating whether they could afford groceries due to U.S. support for Israel.

El-Sayed's campaign has said it was not involved or affiliated with the ad.

The stunning endorsement was announced two days before Election Day, when voters will decide which party will control Congress for President Donald Trump's final two years in the White House. The outcome of the Michigan Senate race could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate, where Republicans currently hold a slim majority.

"Hey Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said I'm no longer welcome in his campaign, and I should stay away, and he's right," Stevens said in a video statement on X.

"And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," she said.

"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign. I do not stand with Hasan Piker, who gets trafficked on our college campuses," said Stevens.

Piker is a controversial political commentator who has campaigned with El-Sayed.

El-Sayed, standing with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., outside a church on Sunday, dismissed Stevens endorsement of his opponent.

"I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," El-Sayed said. "There are families that are preparing to send their kids to schools tomorrow that look like they did 50 years ago. They're worried about what they're going to feed their kids for lunch. They're worried that if one of their kids gets sick, they're not going to be able to pay the bills. Those are the things that matter."

Rogers and El-Sayed are vying for a seat set to become vacant after Democratic Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek re-election.

In recent weeks, a deepening rift has worsened between El-Sayed and Stevens. At the center of it is U.S. support for Israel, which was a major issue in the primary contest.

Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel; El-Sayed has called the country's conduct in Gaza after the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attacks by the radical group Hamas a genocide.

Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, endorsed Rogers before Stevens' flip-flop, citing what he said was rising antisemitism.

"I'm sorry people are upset," Stevens told reporters at a press conference in Detroit, standing with Rogers, whom she had attended church with Sunday morning.

Staffers in Stevens congressional office quit following her endorsement.

"As of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself," Justin German, Stevens' chief of staff for eight years, said in a statement obtained by MS NOW.

"We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens' decision to support Mike Rogers," German said, adding that he was speaking on behalf of the team "in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate," German said.

Stevens had the endorsement of much of the Democratic establishment during the bruising primary, making her endorsement of Rogers even more stunning.

She was the preferred candidate of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, who on Sunday reiterated his support for El-Sayed and accused Republicans of Islamophobia.

"Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors," Schumer said. "We Democrats [are] equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans."

In a later post to X, Schumer called her endorsement of Rogers "a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens."

Peters and Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin both disavowed Stevens for her endorsement.

"[A]nyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good," Slotkin said in a post to X.

Curtis Hertel, the chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, appeared to suggest that Stevens had been kicked out of the party.

"Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future," he said in an X post.

In a Truth Social post, Trump praised Stevens' endorsement.

"Congresswoman Haley Stevens, a Highly Respected Democrat, who narrowly lost in the Primary to Abdul Mohamed El-Sayed, and who has been breathlessly wined and dined by the Dumocrats to help in their Michigan Campaign for the United States Senate against Mike Rogers, has just ENDORSED Mike Rogers for Senate!" the president said.

"Her following is huge, and the level of respect from the People of Michigan, especially our African American and Jewish populations, is virtually unparalleled," he said.

#3024. Palantir: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

The company's shift to enterprise workflows over generic productivity tools reveals why its pricing power may compound as corporate adoption accelerates.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 2, 2026, Palantir (PLTR -3.13%) announced quarterly revenue of $2.3 billion, representing 96% year-over-year growth as enterprise demand accelerated. The company's shifting revenue mix demonstrates that corporate software adoption is eclipsing government contracts as the primary expansion engine. Three key takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

U.S. commercial revenue surged 148% year over year to $984 million, surpassing government revenue in the region for the first time. Private enterprises are shortening evaluation cycles and expanding deal sizes as demand for operational software tools accelerates across corporate workflows.

Management emphasized that generating measurable return on investment (ROI) requires embedding technology directly into operational workflows rather than chasing individual employee productivity gains. The company's Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) targets core enterprise execution to deliver quantifiable economic results.

Customizing open-source models on proprietary operational data inside the company's ontology, its central data mapping architecture, enables clients to achieve high performance without transferring proprietary knowledge to external model providers. Fine-tuning smaller models lowers compute costs while maintaining domain advantage.

Commercial software adoption is accelerating across corporate enterprises. Palantir relies on its operational software architecture to integrate deeply into client infrastructure, maintaining pricing power while management monitors enterprise contract conversion velocity.

Deploying tailored operational systems enables the business to compound cash flow as enterprise buyers pivot from generic language models to customized enterprise workflows.

#3022. 2 Unstoppable Quantum Computing Stocks to Buy Hand Over Fist Before the Next Rally

IonQ's revenue rose 287% and Rigetti's 185% last quarter, but both carry steep valuations. Here's how the two compare on risk and fit.

Quantum computing is moving closer to mainstream adoption, creating exciting opportunities for investors. With that, IonQ (IONQ -6.22%) and Rigetti Computing (RGTI -5.16%) are two promising companies making strides in quantum computing. And looking ahead, if adoption accelerates, both stocks could be well-positioned for the next major rally.

Let's start by looking at what IonQ is building.

IonQ is building a comprehensive platform that spans quantum computers, networking, and cybersecurity. That broader strategy could give it several ways to benefit as quantum technology moves closer to commercial adoption.

One of IonQ's biggest advantages is its trapped-ion approach, which is said to deliver highly accurate quantum operations. That matters because the company is working to develop more powerful and reliable quantum computers, thereby enhancing the performance and scalability of its systems.

The company's recent technical milestones are also encouraging.

IonQ demonstrated the industry's first end-to-end real-time quantum error decoder, which could make larger quantum systems more reliable. The company also demonstrated a quantum memory-enhanced interconnect, which is an important step toward connecting separate quantum processors.

IonQ is also strengthening its manufacturing capabilities. As an example, it completed its acquisition of SkyWater Technology, a U.S.-based semiconductor foundry. This gives the company greater control over the hardware manufacturing process, helping it improve production, develop specialized chips, and scale its technology more efficiently.

The commercial opportunity is also gaining traction. IonQ reported strong revenue growth in its second quarter, supported by demand across its broader quantum platform. In fact, revenue climbed 287% year over year in a record quarter.

On top of that, its partnerships with organizations like Nvidia, Sandia National Laboratories, and Anduril highlight its role in other industries, including artificial intelligence (AI), scientific research, and national security.

But of course, IonQ remains a speculative investment at this stage, as quantum computing has yet to achieve widespread commercial adoption. The company also faces many technical and execution challenges before it can become profitable. Valuation is also a concern, with the stock trading at about 42 times its price-to-sales (P/S) ratio.

Aside from IonQ, another company is taking a different approach to scaling quantum systems.

Unlike IonQ, Rigetti uses superconducting qubits, which run using electrical circuits cooled to extremely low temperatures. One of the biggest advantages of this approach is its fast gate speeds, which allow quantum operations to run much faster. The company believes its technology can provide a practical path toward building more powerful quantum systems.

Its chiplet strategy is also a key advantage. Instead of relying on a single massive chip, Rigetti combines smaller processor units into a larger system, and the company has already demonstrated this approach with its Cepheus-1-108Q system.

Meanwhile, Rigetti has also been fulfilling orders for on-premises quantum systems, including its Novera-based machines and the 108-qubit system program for India's Center for Development of Advanced Computing. These deployments matter because they give universities and research institutions direct access to quantum hardware.

And the initiatives seem to be working. Rigetti's second-quarter revenue, for example, grew 185% year over year, though from a small base, all while Rigetti works to build a more commercially scalable business.

More recently, however, Rigetti established a dedicated systems delivery organization and appointed new leadership to oversee operations and technology development.

Still, the company faces meaningful risks in its operations. Rigetti remains an early-stage business with limited commercial revenue, significant operating losses, and a long development path. The stock also trades at about 278 times its P/S ratio, so if future growth doesn't exceed investor expectations, Rigetti could see steep losses.

But despite the risks, can IonQ and Rigetti still deliver massive upside?

IonQ and Rigetti offer two ways to invest in the quantum computing race.

With an expanding technology stack and growing commercial adoption, both companies could be poised for the industry's next growth phase. If they execute on their roadmaps and benefit from accelerating demand, their stocks could still have plenty of upside.

IonQ looks like the more conservative of the two, with a broader platform and lower valuation. Rigetti is the higher-risk, higher-reward pick, given its early stage and steep valuation.

Rick Orford has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Hewlett Packard Enterprise, IonQ, and Nvidia. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3021. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3018. Kimberly-Clark Acquires Kenvue. Here’s What Investors Need to Know Ahead of Its Nov. 5 Earnings Report.

The enterprise value of the monster deal was estimated at almost $49 billion.

On Monday, one of the largest acquisitions of 2026 closed, almost one year to the day after it was first announced. This is Kimberly-Clark's (KMB +0.29%) purchase of consumer healthcare company Kenvue. The two companies said in their original announcement that Kenvue's enterprise value was a cool $48.7 billion or so.

That's immense, even when considering the huge size of both Kimberly-Clark and Kenvue (formerly a business owned by healthcare giant Johnson & Johnson (JNJ -0.97%)). So it'll result in significant changes to the storied Kimberly-Clark. Let's explore what that means for that company's stockholders, particularly since we're days away from its third-quarter earnings release.

In the press release on the closing of the acquisition, Kimberly-Clark and Kenvue wrote that it "brings together two iconic American companies to create a combined portfolio of complementary products, including 10 billion-dollar brands, that touch nearly half the global population through every stage of life."

This isn't much of an exaggeration. Millions of homes in this country stock products from one or both companies. The hygiene-focused consumer goods titan Kimberly-Clark is the company behind Kleenex tissue and Huggies diapers, to name only two familiar product lines. Kenvue, meanwhile, purveys everyone's favorite headache remedy (Tylenol), the Johnson's Baby product suite, and Listerine mouthwash.

In other words, at a stroke, Kimberly-Clark will be not only a significantly bulked-up consumer goods giant but also the No. 1 company in the industry focused on health and hygiene products. That makes for quite a daunting economic moat.

The deal is a mix of cash and stock. Kenvue investors were to receive $3.50 per share in cash and almost 0.15 of a share of Kimberly-Clark's equity per each of their Kenvue shares. Kenvue's stock was delisted before market open on Monday.

The ownership structure was estimated at 54% held by existing Kimberly-Clark investors, with Kenvue stockholders owning the remainder.

An enterprise value near $50 billion is huge, even for a Kimberly-Clark-sized business. The company said that much of the funding for the cash portion of the Kenvue purchase was raised through a $4.9 billion senior notes flotation and the sale of a 51% stake in its consumer paper and business-to-business (B2B) hygiene products business to Brazil's Suzano (SUZ +0.11%).

The two companies believe they can achieve annual run rate synergies of $2.1 billion within three years after the acquisition's close. This is probably achievable given the adjacent -- at times overlapping -- nature of their product lineups and geographies.

Beyond its extremely familiar leading brands, Kimberly-Clark is renowned for its impressive streak of dividend raises. It's a Dividend King, meaning it has hiked its payout a minimum of once per year for at least half a century. Its current streak is 54 years, but, understandably, some investors are worried about the dividend's future. The financing commitments are heavy with this deal.

Yet Kimberly-Clark's stated goal for years has been to maintain its Dividend King status. Besides, Kenvue isn't its first swallow of a peer company. What I think the company will do is what it's done in the past following large acquisitions: declare incremental raises for a period of years to conserve capital for buyout-related expenses. I don't think any investor should worry about management losing that hard-earned crown.

One shareholder-pleasing activity that has been jettisoned for now is Kimberly-Clark's share buybacks, which the company once effected regularly. And at a monster scale; in 2024, for example, they totaled $1 billion. These tapered off quickly around the time of the acquisition announcement last year and fell to $0 in 2026. We can expect the same for at least a few years.

It's important to note that, because the acquisition closed on Monday, Kenvue's recent results won't be included in Kimberly-Clark's third-quarter numbers (although we shouldn't be surprised if the new owner provides them anyway to show what a clever deal it engineered). In addition to digesting the usual figures, growth rates, valuations, etc., investors should pay close attention to any management updates on financing the acquisition, maintaining the dividend raise streak, and -- if the subject comes up -- an eventual restoration of share repurchases.

From what we've seen of the acquisition so far and of both companies’ performance, I’d say it’s a good move, even at that eye-watering price. The pair are more complementary than many big companies tying the knot, and, to repeat, that goes not only for product lineups but also for their geographical footprints. I think the anticipated synergies are achievable, and the Kenvue-infused Kimberly-Clark will be a global powerhouse and a tough competitor. I also think it will maintain its vaunted Dividend King status, which is especially encouraging given its high-yield dividend currently pays out at 4.7%.

Eric Volkman has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool recommends Johnson & Johnson. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3017. Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout

Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.

The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week, shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.

"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."

Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.

The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.

"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.

Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.

Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.

The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.

While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.

What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.

"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."

— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

Record Q3 results driven by data center AI momentum and industrial market recovery.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Lattice Semiconductor Corporation (LSCC +2.66%) reported record results for the third quarter, driven by accelerating momentum in data center AI infrastructure and a recovery in industrial markets. Management stated that the company is transitioning into a sustainable, secular growth entity with a target of over 30% annualized growth over the next five years. The integration of AMI has expanded the company's addressable market into secure firmware and rack-scale management solutions. The company reported record bookings and a backlog that currently extends into 2028, supported by increased FPGA attach rates in heterogeneous server architectures. Management noted that operating leverage remains a primary focus, with earnings growth expected to consistently outpace revenue growth as the business scales.

#3014. Fanatics takes bigger NHL design role with all-32 team Hometown Remix jerseys

Sign up today for the CNBC Sport Newsletter

In most professional sports arenas, rinks and stadiums across the globe, the gear that fans are now wearing to games is made and designed by sports merchandise giant Fanatics. But that isn't always the case for the jersey that the players are wearing on the field, ice or court.

On Monday, Fanatics and the NHL debuted the Hometown Remix program, a collection of uniforms and apparel for all 32 NHL teams. The new designs and look of each jersey is focused on each team's city and fan base. It marks the first time that Fanatics has designed and developed a league-wide jersey program for one of its leagues partners, which include the NFL, NBA, and MLB.

For some leagues, such as the NFL, while Fanatics may manufacture jerseys that fans buy in stores, other consumer-focused products and even what coaches wear on the sidelines, what players wear on the field may be manufactured and designed by a different company. In the case of the NFL, that is Nike. In MLB, while Fanatics manufactures player jerseys, Nike designs them.

Fanatics has been a partner of the NHL since 2005, mainly focused on retail and e-commerce. But in 2023, as the league's jersey deal with Adidas lapsed, Fanatics expanded its partnership to include on-ice uniforms and authentic jerseys.

When that deal began alongside the 2024-25 season, it marked the first time that Fanatics branding appeared directly on an official player jersey in a professional game, a massive evolution for the company.

The new collection takes that a "giant step forward in our partnership with the NHL," according to Andrew Low Ah Kee, CEO of Fanatics Commerce, the company's merchandise business arm.

"What's exciting to me about it is that not only is it all 32 teams, it's actually that Fanatics is singularly responsible and accountable for the design and execution of the program in partnership with the [NHL] and the clubs," Low Ah Kee said. "Whereas we work with Nike and others on other leagues and different programs."

Low Ah Kee said the process for this collection began when its expanded deal with the NHL took effect in 2024, and Fanatics' design team has been working across the league, its teams and players since.

Some of the process itself hasn't been totally new: Fanatics has designed jerseys in conjunction with the NHL and some of its teams for tentpole events like the Winter Classic, Stadium Series and the 4 Nations Face-Off. However, not every NHL team has participated in one of those events.

But Low Ah Kee said doing it in the NHL, which he said has the "most complex construction of any sports jersey out there," while also adding new design elements, highlighting unique aspects of each team's fans and local culture, has been a big moment for Fanatics.

"I don't think this will be a capstone, but this is certainly a big milestone in the relationship that we have," Low Ah Kee said.

Brian Jennings, NHL senior vice president and chief partnerships and club strategy officer, said the league appreciates the legacy and reverence that hockey jerseys — often called sweaters — hold for fans of the sport. At the same time, Jennings said the league has been excited to create new designs around a league-wide platform that celebrates local team culture.

"Each market and city is unique … we love to celebrate that uniqueness," Jennings said.

Jennings said that each team will wear its jersey for a set of games throughout the remainder of this season, providing opportunities to highlight the designs and storytelling.

While this is just set to be a program for the 2026-2027 season, Jennings said that if a team wanted to integrate some of the logos, colors or designs into a future alternate jersey or other products, the NHL and Fanatics would be open to it.

This Hometown Remix collection is also setting the groundwork for future league-wide efforts with Fanatics, Jennings said. "In an ideal world, we'll start to ideate immediately around what is another version," he said. "Once we have the ability to collect some insights, what was successful, what wasn't, what do we want to turn the volume up on … we want to keep the design integrity really, really high and delight and excite fans."

Jennings said these moments do boost the business side as well. While he declined to provide specific targets, he pointed to the bump that the league and teams see when new jerseys and merchandise are released for special event games like the Winter Classic. He also noted the follow-on effects on things like ticket sales and sponsorship activation when teams host special theme nights or special jersey matchups. "It creates a lot of excitement for the clubs that they can market around," he said.

Low Ah Kee said Fanatics is "very aware" that the launch of this league-wide program is happening just ahead of holiday shopping season. At the same time, this collection of jerseys is "limited supply," he said. The prices of these jerseys do vary slightly from some of the traditional NHL jerseys due to some of the unique production features, Fanatics said.

Pricing on Hometown Remix jerseys with custom lettering and numbering are $275 for a premium jersey and $500 for authentics (same as worn on ice by players).

Both Jennings and Low Ah Kee acknowledged the challenges that come with launching new designs of beloved team jerseys: the somewhat unpredictable fan response.

Jennings said that there are so many unique design elements, not just on the front of the jersey but down to the hockey socks that the players wear and how certain parts of the jersey are embossed and raised, that he believes that "fans will really respect that fact."

"The debate about the design will always be ongoing, but I think they'll see the quality come shining through," Jennings said.

When these new jerseys hit the ice on players' backs, it'll come with the Fanatics flag brand on it as well, and Low Ah Kee said while that is a point of pride for the company, it's also a reflection that Fanatics is "accountable for the quality of the garments, the manufacturing of the garments, the design of the garments," he said.

"The protagonists in the story are the fan and their team; we're the supporting actor, and we know that," Low Ah Kee said. "Our job is to think about how do you make that better. Hometown Remix we hope is going to be a really great way for fans to express their love of their cities, their clubs and their markets overall, and we hope people have fun."

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 12 â 0 vote:

The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.
