#3011. Vertex (VRTX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Revenue grew 12% as newer products like CASGEVY and JOURNAVX ramped up significantly.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Vertex Pharmaceuticals Incorporated (VRTX -1.02%) reported a 12% revenue increase for the third quarter and raised its full-year revenue guidance to a range of $13.15 billion to $13.25 billion. Management noted that growth was balanced between the domestic and international cystic fibrosis franchises and new contributions from the heme, pain, and rare endocrine portfolios. The company established its fourth commercial pillar through the $9.0 billion net cash acquisition of Crinetics Pharmaceuticals and is preparing to launch a fifth in renal medicine following the upcoming Nov. 30 PDUFA date for povitacept. Non-GAAP operating expense guidance was revised to approximately $6 billion to support the integration of Crinetics and the commercial scale-up of recent product launches.

Operator: Good day and welcome to the Vertex Pharmaceuticals Third Quarter 26 Earnings Call. All participants will be in a listen only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then 1 on your touch tone phone. And to withdraw your question, please press star then 2. Please note this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Ms. Susie Lisa. Please go ahead.

Susie Lisa: Evening, all. My name is Susie Lisa, and as the senior vice president of relations, it is my pleasure to welcome you to our third quarter 26 financial results conference call. On tonight's call, making prepared remarks, we have Dr. Reshma Kewalramani, Vertex CEO and president, Charles Wagner, chief operating officer and chief financial officer and Duncan McKechnie, chief commercial officer. Given the January 1 transition by Charles to the COO role solely, please note that this is his last quarterly earnings call and is successor, Jonathan Pool, our current SVP of finance, will join us for our Q4 26 call in February. We recommend that you access the webcast slides as you listen to this call.

The call is being recorded, and a replay will be available on our website. We will make forward looking statements on this call that are subject to the risks and uncertainties discussed in detail in today's press release and in our filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. These statements, including without limitation, those regarding Merck marketed medicines for cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, beta thalassemia, moderate to severe acute pain, and acromegaly, our pipeline, the recently completed acquisition of Crinetics Pharmaceuticals and the expected benefits of that transaction, and Vertex's future financial performance, are based on management's current assumptions. Actual outcomes and events could differ materially.

I would also note that select financial results and guidance that we will review on the call this evening are presented on a non GAAP basis. I will now turn the call over to Reshma.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: Thanks, Susie. Good evening all, and thank you for joining us on the call today. I am pleased to note that Vertex achieved another quarter of excellent commercial results and pipeline advancement. Third quarter total revenue grew 12% year on year. Revenue growth was nicely balanced coming from both The US and international, from CF and from our 2 more recently launched medicines, CASGEVY and JOURNAVX, as well as a contribution from PALSONIFY for the month of September post close of the Crinetics acquisition. Rare endocrine is now our fourth commercial pillar. And with the PDUFA date later this month for povitacept in immunoglobulin A nephropathy or IGAN, we plan to soon establish our fifth in renal.

Before turning to the R&D update, I want to acknowledge Charles's final and 30 first earnings call as CFO. Charles' leadership, integrity, judgment, and intellectual rigor are unparalleled. He has deftly helped lead our transition from a CF only company with $4 billion in revenue in 2019 to a company soon to be commercialized in 5 disease areas, with more than triple the revenue with our guidance for over 13 billion in 2026. I look forward to continuing to work with Charles in his role as COO, driving forward the Crinetics integration and our key priorities as we grow and scale the company. I can think of no better successor to Charles than Jonathan Pool.

Our SVP and current head of finance, who will take over as CFO on 01/01/2027. Moving now to the R&D update for the quarter. I will cover 4 disease areas CF, endocrinology, both rare endocrine disorders and type 1 diabetes, and renal in detail. But first, let me start with quick highlights. from 4 other programs. In severe sickle cell disease and transfusion dependent beta thalassemia, we were pleased to have recently received approval for CASGEVY in patients ages 2 to 11 in the US, UAE, Bahrain, as well as in patients ages 5 to 11 in the UK.

In pain, along with the strong growth in prescriptions, we are also seeing fast growth in the body of compelling JOURNAVX real world data emerge, such as a recent paper detailing 80% of freedom from opioid use following total knee replacement when the pain management regimen included JOURNAVX. In chronic pain, both phase 3 studies in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy remain on track to complete enrollment by the end of this year. And for us to be able to share results by mid-2027. In myotonic dystrophy type 1 or DM1, we remain on track to share interim results from the Galileo global phase 1/2 clinical trial of VX-670 before the end of the year.

And in generalized myasthenia gravis, we have completed enrollment of the Aetna Phase 2 dose ranging study of povitacept and expect to share proof of concept data in the first half of 2027. Moving on to the more detailed R&D review, starting with cystic fibrosis. We see ALYFTREK as the most effective medicine approved for CF. With once daily dosing, ALYFTREK can treat up to 95% of people with CF, and in our trials, more than 75% of ALLE treated patients ages 12 and older achieved sweat chloride levels in the range of CF carriers. That is to say, ALYFTREK-treated patients are achieving sweat chloride levels associated with no manifestation of CF disease. nor reduced life expectancy.

On the regulatory front, we continue our work to expand to treating younger patients and have initiated global submissions for ALYFTREK approval in children ages 2 to 5. Lastly, in CF, an update on our next generation 3.0 correctors. We studied VX-828 as part of a triple combination in a cohort of 8 people with CF and as a dual therapy in another cohort of 8. All 16 patients had FMF mutations, which is a more challenging population to treat than patients with FF mutations. In this, FF the VX-8 28 dual combination did not alter sweat chloride relative to the Trikafta baseline.

In the triple combination versus a baseline on Trikafta, the 28 delivered a 6.6 millimole per liter reduction in sweat chloride at day 28 and a 9.4 millimole reduction through day 28. The VX-828 regimen is oral once daily with a good safety tolerability, and DDI profile. In short, these are excellent results. However, given the very high bar set by ALYFTREK, we intend to wait for all the data from the next gen 3.0 family before determining next steps, namely advancement into pivotal development. VX-581 and VX-272, the other next gen 3.0 correctors are currently in first in human studies, and the NexGen 4.0 molecules are in late preclinical development. Moving to our newest pillar, rare endocrinology.

With the Crinetics acquisition now closed, for Palsonify, and Duncan will provide details on the ongoing U. S. Launch. On the R&D side, the most advanced molecule after Palsonify is Atumelnant in congenital adrenal hyperplasia or CAH. Which has orphan drug designation in the US, EU, and Japan, and where the phase 3 pivotal trial is well underway. The primary efficacy endpoint for this Phase 3 study is the proportion of patients achieving the combination of normalization of androgens and physiologic glucocorticoid dose levels. This is the true goal in CAH therapy. And it is what was demonstrated in the phase 2 trial. It is also what no other CAH medicine to date has attempted to achieve.

In adult CAH, we are targeting completion of enrollment in the phase 3 study in Q1 2027. The study then calls for 32 weeks of dosing. In pediatric CAH, Atrumelnant is in a phase 2 dose ranging study. Our goal is to rapidly advance the pediatric program into pivotal development following planned regulatory interactions. In addition, the adaptive Phase 2/3 global study of Atumelnant in ACTH dependent Cushing syndrome is already underway outside the US and was recently granted orphan drug designation in The US. We have planned engagements with the FDA to confirm their expectations for this program and look forward to updating you in the coming months. Let me now turn to T1D.

After careful analysis, we have chosen to prioritize acceleration of VX-017 as our lead program. Recall, VX-017 is an allogeneic off the shelf glucose responsive insulin producing fully differentiated islet cell therapy. It has a similar target product profile to Zemila Cell but is designed for people with all blood types. This doubles the eligible patient population to about 120 thousand people. The potential to bring transformative benefit to even more patients is the key reason to focus on VX-017 given the resource intensity, complexity and manufacturing demands of cell therapy programs. We have already begun dosing patients with VX-017 in a Phase 1/2 study.

Our near term goals are to demonstrate proof of concept, and to scale up manufacturing with the goal of moving to pivotal development next year. Finally, we continue to progress our serial innovation work in T1D. Focused on improved immunosuppression and on generating hypoimmune islets with the goal of making this potentially curative therapy available to even more people. Turning now to renal where we have 4 programs in mid and late stage development. Starting with Pove and IgAN, we are both excited and ready for our PDUFA date on November 30th, just weeks away. Duncan will address our launch readiness.

We just wrapped up a sparkling ASN annual meeting with the RAINIER Phase III interim analysis Presentation and publication in the New England Journal of Medicine supporting what we believe is a differentiated potentially best in class profile for povitacept in IgAN. Simply put, Povitacept will offer a trifecta of excellence in efficacy, tolerability, and patient centric administration features. I will focus tonight just on the patient centric features. The commercial presentation of povitacept is clearly differentiated with a small volume 0.46 mL once every 4 weeks subcutaneously dosed via auto injector at home.

On this point, this advantage is reflected in the poster presented by If et al. at the recent ASN of a qualitative survey study of about 25 adults with IgAN in the US. That revealed 96% of patients preferred an auto injector relative to injection via a prefilled syringe and 80% preferred dosing every 4 weeks versus weekly. Our ambition is to launch povitacept globally. To that end, we have already completed our filing for potential accelerated approval in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, where it has been granted breakthrough status. We estimate KSA represents an incremental 7 thousand-patient opportunity.

And we are planning forward for our regulatory submissions in other regions, including Europe and Asia, when the study completes and the 2-year eGFR data are available. On povitacept in membranous nephropathy, our OLYMPUS Phase 2/3 pivotal trial is ongoing with Phase 3 enrollment and dosing well underway. at the selected dose of 80 milligrams subcutaneously every 4 weeks. Recall this study has a 104-week endpoint. On anoxaplin in AMKD, we have 2 pieces of news since our last earnings call. First, to recap the exciting results from the AMPLIFIED study.

In cohort 1 of patients with AMKD and modest proteinuria, treatment with anaxaplin on top of optimized standard of care led to a 42.7% reduction in urine albumin to creatinine ratio or UACR. At week 13 compared to baseline with a 44.7% reduction. This is remarkably consistent with the treatment effect previously shared in the Phase II data in AMKD published in the New England Journal of Medicine. In cohort 2 of people with AMKD in type 2 diabetes, treatment with anaxaplin led to a 17.3% reduction in UACR. And a 25 point 4 percent reduction in UPCR at week 13. Of note, the majority of patients in both cohorts did not have a diagnosis of FSGS.

Anaxaplin was generally safe and well tolerated with no serious adverse events related to anaxaplin. All adverse events were mild or moderate in severity. We look forward to discussing these results with regulators in the context of the AMPLITUDE study next year. The second key milestone was that we completed full enrollment in the pivotal AMPLITUDE Phase 2/3 trial and we are fully on track to share the results from the interim analysis of AMPLITUDE early next year. If positive, this interim analysis will support potential accelerated approval in the US. Rounding out on renal enrollment in the VX407 AGLOW phase 2 study in ADPKD completed enrollment and we are now on track for study readout next year.

With that, I will turn the call over to Duncan for a commercial update.

Analyst: Thanks very much, Reshma. Our commercial story continues to be 1 of excellence in launch execution across CF, heme, pain, and most recently, rare endocrinology. Through the first 9 months of the year, our ongoing launches of ALYFTREK, CASGEVY, and JOURNAVX have generated over $2 billion in revenue led by over 1.7 billion in ALYFTREK sales and more than 350 million in combined CASGEVY and JOURNAVX sales. To give you a brief overview and put Q3 revenue, patient, and prescription growth in context, In CF, we delivered $3.3 billion in revenue with strong switching to ALYFTREK and over 18 thousand patients benefiting from ALYFTREK around the world.

In heme, CASGEVY achieved $99 million in quarterly revenue with approximately 200 infusions completed since launch and a fourth consecutive quarter with more than 100 patient initiations. In moderate to severe acute pain, JOURNAVX reported over $58 million in revenue. More than 1.6 million patients have now been treated with JOURNAVX in The US, and JOURNAVX is now the number 1 prescribed branded oral analgesic in the US. And in rare endocrinology, Palsonify contributed $10 million in revenue for the month of September following the close of the acquisition. For the full third quarter, Palsonify revenue was approximately $24 million. I will now cover these disease areas in more detail starting with CF.

The Q3, $3.3 billion in global CF revenue represents 8% year-over-year growth. Global growth overall was led by ALYFTREK, which delivered $706 million in worldwide sales in Q3. In the US, ALYFTREK sales year to date have now surpassed $1 billion. In both the US and outside The US, ALYFTREK sales continue to build primarily from patients switching from Trikafta and new patients with rare mutation. Outside The US, we now have ALYFTREK reimbursement in 31 countries. Looking ahead, our CF growth drivers remain consistent and clear. Label expansions in rare mutations, penetration into younger age groups, additional geographies, and by the underlying survival benefit of patients on CFTR modulators.

Turning to CASGEVY in severe sickle cell disease and transfusion dependent beta thalassemia, where $99 million in Q3 revenue reflects 30% sequential growth. We have infused twice as many patients in the first 9 months of 2026 as all of 2025. Since launch, we have initiated over 750 patients worldwide on CASGEVY, and with 4 consecutive quarters of initiation numbers exceeding 100 patients we now have patients at all stages of the treatment journey. We have also continued to enhance the patient journey shortening the overall time from referral to infusion, and decrease the number of mobilizations.

We have excellent visibility into the number of infusions which is when we recognize revenue, for the rest of this year as well as into 2027. That said, infusion timing reflects patient choice with some expected seasonality in Q4 so I would encourage you to focus on the strong annual performance rather than any single quarter. CASGEVY will contribute meaningfully to our greater than $500 million non CF revenue goal this year and is on its way to achieving its own blockbuster potential. With generics in moderate to severe acute pain, we are building a franchise for the long term and are focused on the following critical markers of success.

Broad payer coverage, prescription growth, breadth and depth of prescribing, the addition of JOURNAVX to hospital pathways, and revenue. These are the building blocks of a sustainable, long term, multibillion dollar pain business. Let me start with prescriptions because that is the best indicator of underlying physician and patient demand. In the third quarter, JOURNAVX prescriptions totaled over 750 thousand up more than 40% sequentially from Q2 2026. At the end of Q2 2026, we are well on our way to achieving our guidance of more than 3x the number of prescriptions in 2020 versus 2025. Prescriptions continue to split roughly 50/50 between hospital and retail channels.

Third quarter JOURNAVX revenue of $58 million, up 18% quarter-over-quarter, reflects continued high gross to net with the patient support savings program remaining on. Let me walk you through the revenue growth dynamics. A significant driver of gross to net is continued utilization of our patient support program. We have chosen to leave the PSP in place and extend it into 2027 so that people who are prescribed JOURNAVX but whose plans do not yet cover it can receive the therapy. Accordingly, when we sunset the PSP mid next year, we continue to expect gross to net to stabilize at a level close to other mass market brands in the range of 50% to 60%.

In addition, in Q3, gross to net and revenue were both affected by the onetime impact of securing broad Medicare Part d access in July. As that access came online, previously uncontracted prescriptions to contracted rebated pricing resulting in a 1-time reset in net revenue. This is in line with our overall strategy to secure broad sustained access across commercial and government plans so we can successfully convert physician practices to JOURNAVX for all their patients. This quarter marks our first opportunity to speak about Palsonify as part of Vertex following the deal close at the beginning of September, and we are pleased with the launch trajectory to date.

Let me briefly describe the disease, the unmet need, and frame the key metrics at this stage in the launch. Acromegaly is a symptomatic disease that affects approximately 20 thousand patients in the US and a similar number in the 5 largest European markets plus Japan. Although surgery is the first line of treatment, only 40% to 50% of people achieve durable remission, so the majority of patients need lifelong treatment. In the US, they are treated by approximately 3 thousand endocrinologists. Until the launch of Palsonify, the main option has been monthly injections with somatostatin receptor ligands or SRLs delivered using large gauge needles. These treatments have 3 limitations.

Firstly, they can cause painful injection site reactions at the beginning of the month. Secondly, the efficacy tends to taper off in the latter part of the month leading to breakthrough symptoms such as joint pain, swelling and fatigue, and thirdly, the recurring logistical challenges and burden of chronic depot therapy. The unmet need is therefore significant. The ideal treatment for patients would be a highly effective, easy to take, well tolerated, oral medicine that provides sustained control of the disease and 1 that has a broad indication for both naive and switch patients. This is the exact profile of Palsonify as the first and only once daily oral SST 2 selective agonist.

As we integrate the Crinetics business, there are 3 areas of focus for the success of Palsonify, building on the excellent base of 80% reimbursed coverage. Firstly, build a broad base of repeat HCP writers for Palsonify; secondly, drive growth in both the new and switch settings; and thirdly, deliver on our revenue goals. We are very pleased with the progress that the Crinetics team and now the integrated Vertex team are making against these goals. Approximately 500 endocrinologists are writing Palsonify, and there was a significant increase in the number of repeat writers in Q3 compared to the first half of 2026. Palsonify now has the leading brand share of over 40% among patients initiating or switching therapy.

And lastly, we see continued strong growth in patient enrollment. Leading to $10 million in revenue in September, $24 million in Q3, and approximately $60 million for the first 3 quarters of 2026. Our focus is on excellence in execution to further accelerate the US performance and prepare for international launches. Let me conclude with an update on our commercial readiness for povitacept in IgAN. Reshma has already highlighted the trifecta of efficacy safety and patient centric dosing of povitacept. Put simply, with the PDUFA date just days away now, we are 100% ready, and we are incredibly excited to bring povitacept to patients with IgAN. Our field team is fully hired trained and ready to go.

Over 90% of the team have deep nephrology experience, and many of them have been engaging with nephrologists in IgAN disease education activities since early this year. We also know that the patient experience is of supreme importance in biologics, and IgAN is no different. Based on years of providing comprehensive patient support to our CF patients, we have built a people based and tech enabled patient support program to facilitate patients to get their povitacept as fast and as easily as possible. In addition, our payer conversations continue to proceed very well. Payers understand the significant unmet need, are very familiar with povitacept's clinical profile, and have responded positively to its differentiation and overall value proposition.

We have had many engagements with nephrologists over the last few months, including at the excellent ASN Kidney Week meeting last month. They are looking for treatments that meaningfully and rapidly reduce proteinuria, have a favourable tolerability profile and offer convenient dosing, alongside a seamless treatment experience built on access and patient support. Our discussions with physicians over the last quarter have increased increasingly revealed the importance of dosing frequency, dose volume and viscosity and method of administration. We continue to believe that in addition to an excellent efficacy and safety profile, the low dose easy to use, at home auto injector will be an important differentiator for povitacept. I will now turn the call over to Charles.

Charles F. Wagner Jr.: Thanks, Duncan. Vertex delivered strong third quarter results with total revenue growth of 12% year-over-year, reflecting revenue growth of 10% in the US and 16% internationally. Results include an approximate 1 percentage point favorable impact from foreign exchange and 10 million of revenue from Crinetics following the close of the transaction. Globally, CF revenue grew 8% year-over-year with 5% growth in the US and 12% outside the U.S. or 10% on a constant currency basis. On a non-GAAP basis, third quarter gross margin was 85.6%, On a GAAP basis, gross margin of 84.7% includes intangible asset and inventory step up amortization resulting from the purchase accounting for the Crinetics acquisition.

Turning to Q3 operating expenses, which include approximately $60 million of Crinetics operating and integration related expenses in September. Third quarter non GAAP R&D expense was $936 million, an increase of $74 million or 9% year over year. Approximately $30 million of the increase was attributable to Crinetics. Non GAAP s g and a expense was $556 million, an increase of $187 million or 51% year over year. Nearly 80% of the incremental spend was to enhance our commercial capabilities. Within the increase in commercial spend, the biggest drivers were povitacept in renal and JOURNAVX, and then Palsonify. $30 million of the incremental SG&A spend is related to Crinetics.

We also recorded $41 million in acquired IPR&D expense in Q3, including a $28 million upfront payment for new business development agreement with AbCellera. During Q3, we incurred approximately $50 million in non operating costs associated with the Crinetics transaction financing, including higher interest expense due to the new bank loans and other related costs. In addition, interest income was $15 million lower than it otherwise would have been as a result of lower cash balances after the acquisition. Our third quarter non GAAP effective tax rate was 18%, up approximately 40 basis points compared to Q3 25. Third quarter 26 non GAAP net income was $1.21 billion and third quarter 2026 non-GAAP earnings per share of $4.76.

Turning to the balance sheet. We ended the quarter with approximately $9.8 billion in cash and investments, following the close of the Crinetics acquisition. Note that we raised $4.5 billion of term loans to fund a portion of the acquisition currently bearing interest at approximately 4.8%. Even with a busy period for BD, we also deployed approximately $120 million during the quarter to repurchase roughly 250 thousand shares. Year to date, we have repurchased approximately 2 million shares for $921 million. Our strategy for capital deployment remains unchanged with the priority on investing in innovation, including external innovation, and an additional allocation for share repurchases. Now turning to guidance.

Total revenue guidance, we are raising our prior range of $13.1 billion to $13.2 billion to a revised range of $13.15 billion to $13.25 billion. The increase reflects the addition of Crinetics, which we expect to contribute $40 million to $50 million to full year 2026 revenue. The underlying drivers of our revenue outlook are unchanged. Continued CF performance, including the ongoing ALYFTREK launch together with growing contributions from heme, pain, and now rare endocrinology. We continue to expect more than $500 million in revenue from CASGEVY and JOURNAVX with additional contribution from 4 months of Palsonify. Consistent with prior guidance, our outlook continues to include an expected full year benefit from foreign exchange of roughly 150 basis points.

Given our visibility into the drivers of our business and with just 2 months of the year remaining, we have a high degree of certainty in our revenue guidance range. We continue to expect full year gross margins slightly below 86%. On operating expenses, we are revising our prior combined non GAAP operating expense guidance of $5.65 billion to $5.75 billion to a revised estimate of approximately $6 billion. The standalone Vertex business remains at the high end of our prior range, and the increase in guidance is attributable to the inclusion of approximately $250 million of Crinetics operating expenses and integration related costs.

This updated operating expense guidance reflects continued investment in our late stage clinical pipeline and the commercial infrastructure supporting our launch and revenue diversification. For the full year of 2026, we expect total nonoperating costs of $105 million related to the financing of Crinetics including higher interest expense and other related costs. In addition, interest income is projected to be approximately $60 million lower than it otherwise would have been as a result of lower cash balances after the acquisition. Please see slide 23 of the earnings presentation for full details on the impact of Crinetics upon Q3 results and full year 2026 guidance.

We continue to expect our full year non GAAP effective tax rate to be between 19.5% and 20.5%. In summary, Vertex delivered strong third quarter results with 12% revenue growth and increasing revenue diversification beyond our leading CF business. The integration of Crinetics is well underway, and with the strong commitment of the Crinetics team, we are accelerating commercial, clinical, and valuable preclinical programs. Our continued leadership in CF, the increasing contribution of CASGEVY and JOURNAVX, momentum in rare endocrinology, and with the PDUFA date for povitacept in IgAN on November 30th, we are on the verge of launching our fifth commercial pillar in renal. I will now ask Susie to begin the Q&A period.

I will now ask Susie to begin the Q&A period.

Susie Lisa: Thanks, Charles. Chuck, can you please open it up to questions?

Operator: Will do. We will now begin the question and answer session. If you are using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. If at any time your question has been addressed and you would like to withdraw your question, please press star then 2. And today's first question will come from Cory Kasimov with Evercore. Cory Kasimov: And Charlie, congrats on the new role. it is very well deserved. So I guess how frequently did patients actually fall below the IgG threshold or require treatment interruptions? And what do those data support or potentially indicate in terms of monitoring requirements in the commercial label? Thank you.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: Hey, Cory. it is Reshma. Let me take that 1. With regard to the citizen's petition, thereabout 200 or so of these that happen every year. About 80% or so of them are from named individuals or companies, and about 20% of them are anonymous. This 1, as you know, was anonymous. If the question behind your question is how do we feel about the label, Where are conversations with the agency? Everything that you would expect to be happening with the FDA is happening. And we are really looking forward to our PDUFA date.

On the specific of how can we think about what values IgG levels can achieve The bottom line is, before this wave of B cell modulating therapies, the way a lot of folks thought about IgG levels were from congenital diseases of immunologic basis. And that is where a lot of these values came from. So in this day and age, what numbers could IgG levels get to? I think the best examples to look at are the clinical trials. In our example, we studied over 500 people We measured every 4 weeks. If the IgG was going to go down, we certainly would have found it because we looked and we considered a single excursion, to be worth noting.

I would say the most important point to think about is infections. And on that note, there are no opportunistic infections, as you know, in the povitacept program. The SAEs of infection are balanced. it is exactly 0.5% in povitacept and 0.5% in the placebo group. And the rest of the infections are mild to moderate. You put this together, and you can see why we are so excited about, the PDUFA date. that is very helpful, Reshma. I appreciate it. You bet. You bet.

Operator: The next question will come from Jessica Fye with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Jessica Fye: Hey, guys. Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. Can you help set expectations for what would represent a win coming out of AMPLITUDE on both proteinuria and eGFR? Thank you.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: Yep. Just on the AMPLITUDE study, that is the 1 that is completed full enrollment and it completed the interim analysis cohort enrollment last year. Setting us up for the interim analysis early 2027. A win would be a statistically significant result on the GFR slope. And I say that because, of course, we are going to measure proteinuria and GFR. But our agreement with the FDA, on what would be acceptable for accelerated approval is GFR. that is where they are on the disease, AMKD. I expect the phase 3 to look a whole hell of a lot like the phase 2 in terms of proteinuria. But the key element here is GFR.

And it is a statistically significant difference between the anaxaplin-treated group and the placebo on top of standard of care. Now, I will not share with you the, power analysis and such, but that is what we are looking for because GFR is what the accelerated approval agreement with the FDA is based on.

Operator: The next question will come from Salveen Richter with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Salveen Richter: Thank you. Good afternoon. Just a follow-up on Cory and Jessica's questions. With regard to povitacept, can you speak to your comfort and history with the manufacturer? And then with regard to anaxaplin, can you just walk through further for the reasons for confidence into the 48-week interim data early next year specifically how we get comfortable thinking about the separation between drug and placebo at that time point? And just the read through from some of the data sets that you have generated to date? You bet.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: So, Salveen, let's do Pove first, and then let's get to anaxaplin. On povitacept, the specific question you had is how is it going with manufacturing? We have been with the same manufacturer. All through phase 3 and through to the lead-up for our PDUFA date. We feel really good about where we are. And as you know, in addition to the review of, safety and efficacy, ClinPharm there is also a review of the manufacturing package. All of the interactions that you would expect us to be having with the FDA are occurring. So overall, I feel very good about where we are.

Moving then to aanaxaplin but staying within renal, 1 way to think about the anaxaplin program and GFR because to date, in both the original phase 2 a study that we published in the New England, that was the 1 that had the 47.6% reduction in proteinuria. And the more recent amplified results, which were from the more cohort 1, the more modest proteinuria, that 1 was a 44.7% reduction in UPCR. I think the best way to think about that in terms of GFR, which is the end point we have agreed upon with FDA is in these 2 ways.

1, substantial reductions in proteinuria in homogeneous proteinuria kidney disease have timing and, again, been linked to improvements in GFR. that is 1 general statement. Maybe a second way to look at this is by talking about IgA nephropathy. We used to talk about IgA nephropathy as a fairly indolent disease. But as you can see from the placebo arm of IGAN trials, those patients are losing about 5 cc's per mL per year. Right? AMKD is a rapidly progressive disease, so more than that. 6, 7, 8 cc's per mil per year. And the FDA themselves have said in IGAN, that they are going to be comfortable accepting 1-year GFR differences.

So when I put that all together, it adds to my confidence level of what we are going to see with Amplitude. But I would say those are 2 ways to think about, anaxaplin in AMKD.

Operator: The next question will come from Geoffrey Meacham with Citibank. Please go ahead.

Geoffrey Meacham: Guys, thanks for the question. I also want to offer up some congrats to Charles. Just have a couple of quick ones. On povitacept, Reshma, you mentioned data should continue to mature post approval, including the 2-year eGFR data. I guess the question is how much of a factor do you think this will play in your competitive position ultimately was not sure if you looked at this as maybe a tipping point in terms of what the payer and physician community is going to look at the second 1 real quick on pain, I know it looks like the trials are continuing to enroll midyear data next year.

Maybe just at a high level, give us some context for kind of what you think at this point a win would look like kind of in DPN for versus suzetrigine? Thank you.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: Yeah. Let's do DPN first, and then I will split the Pove question with, Duncan. On DPN, we are fully on track to complete enrollment in both the 2 Phase 3 suzetrigine trials and on track to complete the enrollment in the VX-993 DPN trial. That would put us for results somewhere mid of next year And a win would be the suzetrigine arm beating placebo treatment in the 2 DPN studies. You know, in 1 of the studies, we have a gabapentin arm to give us context, but a win would be beating placebo. that is the regulatory-enabling endpoint. On povitacept, I will just give you a top line comment.

We are gonna go to the 2-year eGFR full completion of the trial as originally designed because our ambition is to launch povitacept around the globe. The FDA has, said that they are comfortable with 1-year GFR. But other regulators have different, expectations. So that is why we are going to full, completion. And I do think the results, are fully mature at that point, and that is another advantage for all of us to fully mature 2-year data. Duncan, do you wanna talk a little bit about differentiation, GFR, and the povitacept launch in The US?

Analyst: Indeed. Hi, Geoffrey. So we thought about this question quite a bit. As you can imagine, we have discussed it with nephrologists and I would encourage you to think about it this way. Nephrologists already had a very strong level of conviction in the connection between proteinuria and EGFR, in IgAN. And I would say the data that has come out from the April BAF inhibitors over the last couple of months has only served to strengthen that conviction. So we believe on the basis of that, povitacept continues to have best in class potential. Through its excellent efficacy profile, impact on proteinuria hematuria, and Gd-IgA1 in just 36 weeks.

As well as being well tolerated and as Reshma alluded to in her prepared remarks, an incredible profile from a patient point of view with a low volume, low viscosity at home once a month auto injector. So when we have been engaging with nephrologists on this topic, which we have done a lot over the last couple of months, including of course, ASN week. They are very excited in the profile of povitacept and looking forward to trying it post approval. So we are very happy with where we are at. Great. Thank you.

Operator: The next question will come from Evan Seigerman with BMO Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

Evan Seigerman: Hi, Thank you so much for taking my question. So we are seeing some good traction with Jornavix. But you are keeping the PSP on through the rest of the year and now pointing to gross-to-net around mid-2027. You help us think about kind of the bridge between prescription growth and eventually reported revenue as the PSP rolls off and whether you expect revenue growth to inflect as normalization occurs? Thank you so much.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: Sure thing. Duncan, maybe you could take that 1 for us.

Analyst: Yeah. So just to step back a little bit, Evan. Just to make a. Couple of points and then I will dive into the PSP program gross to net and revenue. We are very pleased with the performance of JOURNAVX This is hard work. We are changing decades of ingrained prescribing behavior and seeking to convert practices over to the use of generics. So 750 thousand prescriptions in 1 quarter, 1.6 million Americans treated, the number 1 oral branded analgesic, that would all indicate that we are making great progress.

As far as the gross to net is concerned, I would make the comment that obviously negotiated agreements to secure access for the full population with payers are important to the long term sustainable growth of the product. And so it is important that we are able to get those plans in place. For example, the 2 Medicare Part D plans that came in place in July this year. At this point, we have about 82% managed lives covered. But that does mean that there are patients who are yet to be covered, and we want to make sure that those patients have a great experience. So we are taking the strategic decision to keep the PSP program switched on.

We will sunset it by the middle of 2027. And at that point, you can expect, as we have said before, gross-to-net to stabilize at the sort of normal oral branded level of 50 to 60% and revenue growth to grow commensurately. Great. Thank you.

Operator: The next question will come from Brian Abrahams with RBC Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

Brian Abrahams: Hey, good afternoon. Thanks for taking our question and congrats to Charles from us as well. On the povitacept launch, it sounds like you guys have had great engagement with physicians and payers. And then just secondarily, a ALYFTREK conversion looks like it is been picking up steam in last few quarters. Just wondering the right way to think about the continued trajectory there. You bet.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: Brian, I am going to ask Duncan to comment on both.

Analyst: Let's do a second question first, and then we will go back to povitacept. Yes, Brian. ALYFTREK has been driven predominantly by new reimbursement agreements out Obviously outside The US, we have had another slew of those agreements in Q3. And it is also being driven by the new rare mutation indications which obviously offer a de novo patient population to the CF modulator class, writ large in some cases and certainly ALI specifically. So those are essentially the 2 main drivers of ALYFTREK growth over the last couple of months which we are particularly happy with. In terms of povitacept, and a couple of comments there.

Firstly, as with, say, CASGEVY, and we will be providing you with the metrics that we think are most useful to look at in our earnings call at the beginning of 27. I would say you make a great point. The physician enthusiasm for the new BAF inhibitor or APRIL/BAFF inhibitors has been incredible, and that is certainly driving success in the market. And the numbers are a little bit unclear at this point, but let's say let's say. sorry, not povitacept. VOXZALL and Truqap and Taclonex closed the year with about 3 thousand patients on medicine, which is probably roughly where they are going to end up. That leaves us with 163 thousand yet to go.

So with the level of nephrology enthusiasm for advanced therapy and treating early in the disease, For the nephrologist, enthusiasm for povitacept specifically, both its clinical profile and the patient experience and that vast number of patients who still need treatment. Remember 75% of patients with IgAN have a proteinuria above 1 gram. We think there is a huge opportunity here. Thanks.

Operator: The next question will come from Michael Wei with UBS. Please go ahead.

Michael Yee: Hey, guys. Michael Yee at UBS. 2 questions on anaxaplin. Reshma, you made some great comments about some of the previous data we already know in Phase 2. I guess 1 new thing that has come out is obviously some of the IGAN data that shows significant eGFR benefits even at 9 months on just a couple mL per minute deltas and similar proteinuria reductions you are seeing with anaxaplin. So my question is, given the significant benefits you are seeing and given a 12-month time point, our math suggests that a 2 mL per minute benefit should be stat sig. Just wanted to understand your view about the IGAN data and how that translates here.

Given the deltas you see? And the second question is, on PARASOL, I think the working group has been trying to push proteinuria as an endpoint. Was there any color that you got out of their working group how that may be an accelerated endpoint. Thank you.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: Yeah. Mike, first, let's do PARASOL. PARASOL is a very important and influential group. You know, they have come together multiple times over time and work with the FDA to evolve endpoints. And FSGS and their work with the agency, I do think help to move the agency to a proteinuria-based endpoint. We are members of the broader PARASOL community. The thing that I am paying most attention to is the community clearly seem interested in moving to a proteinuria endpoint for AMKD? And at the same time, the FDA and our agreement is indeed with GFR. So, given that, we are focused on GFR. On your math for GFR, I will not argue with your math. Seems reasonable enough.

The thing to say, Mike, is I think what we are learning from the example of IgA nephropathy, because there is so many different classes now that have been used in IgAN, it matters not only that you get the proteinuria down. It matters how you get the proteinuria down. And decreasing proteinuria by way of APRIL/BAFF inhibition has more beneficial impact on GFR than perhaps other methods of reducing proteinuria.

And the thing that I take away from it is targeting the underlying cause of disease is always a better move than going upstream or downstream. it is actually another reason I have confidence in Amplitude because it is another example of a proteinuria kidney disease where we are targeting the underlying biology. So I think both in the dimension of quantity of protein reduction, but also the how. The quality of protein reduction. In IgAN, APRIL/BAFF,, upstream in the forehead hypothesis has beneficial effect. I think that is what we are gonna see with amplitude because anaxaplin is equally targeting that underlying cause. Perfect. Thank you.

Operator: The next question will come from Tazeen Ahmad with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Tazeen Ahmad: Hi, thanks for taking my question. Let's go back to the CF franchise for a second. You just give us your thoughts, Reshma, on how the data for VX-828 compared to your expectations just based on the preclinical data that you looked at? And then if you think about the other CFTR modulators that you have, where do you think is the biggest unmet need at this point? And where is the most room for improvement over what you have with ALYFTREK. Thanks.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: You have such a good question, Tazeen. What is the unmet need? So let me just take a step back and tell you about VX-828 and then where we are going. If you look. And I think we provided it on the slide If you look at the range of outcomes, the decrease in sweat chloride, certainly, the range of covers, our expectations. On sweat chloride reduction that is. But it is obviously a small study. It says n equals 8. The reason we are not advancing VX-828 in and of itself Although the results are excellent, if you were at a different company, you would just be over the moon with results like this. Right?

At 28 days, we are more than 6 points of sweat chloride improvement. And through 28 days, we are catching 10 points of sweat chloride. Those are good numbers. Especially when you take into account it is versus Trikafta. This is not versus a placebo baseline. So those are excellent results. And it is once a day, good DDI, favorable safety. The thing for us is we have 3 medicines in this NG 3.0 family. And we want to pick the best 1. We are gonna have the results from the other 2 medicines, VX-571 and VX-272, next year. When we have all of those results, we will pick the 1 that is best suited to move forward.

And if you say, what is the residual unmet need? I think Tazeen, that is a very, very hard question to answer because when we look at the data with ALYFTREK, we are almost superimposable onto the Gaussian distribution of sweat chloride of normals, of non-CF people. So really, it is a matter of now not almost being superimposable, but being fully superimposable. So a little bit more sweat chloride, more patients getting to less than 30. that is what we are looking for.

Analyst: Hey, thanks so much. Can you talk a bit more about your decision to file on 2-year eGFR data? I know you were going to make a decision. I was anticipating sometime next year. It sounds like you are making the call now. And just from a statistical perspective, if a patient on placebo starts another APRIL/BAFF drug during that kind of 1- to 2-year window how are they actually accounted for statistically? Are they included in the eGFR final analysis? Thank you.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: Yeah. I just wanna make sure I understood your question about the decision for 2-years. I think you were saying why continue to 2-year GFR. Did I understand correctly? Right. Why make the calls now? Because I know you had previously talked about regulators in a global setting 1 or 2-year data, but we already knew that. So what led to the decision to go forward to 2-year today? Yeah. Obviously, we can decide if we wish to cut the data and do a 1 year cut. We could do that at any time.

But our decision to, indicate that we are going to continue to 2-years is because people have asked us the question, including our clinical trial sites, about what our goal is and how we see this. So to allow preparation for everyone, we have let folks know that our intention is and our ambition is global filings, and that is gonna require 2-year GFR because ex US, not all the regulators have agreed to 1-year GFR. So that is the rationale for that.

With regard to how our patients manage, there are clear rules in the statistical analysis plan that not only the FDA, but global regulators have set forward for management of dropouts, missing data, and how to handle if patients are no longer in the study. So we are simply going to follow the rules that are very clearly laid out. I will not go through all of them in excruciating detail, but they are in excruciating detail.

Terence Flynn: Great. Thanks so much for taking the question. I guess 1 more on anaxaplin. I was just wondering on the amplified data. I know there is been some questions about the breadth of response in the moderate proteinuria cohort. So just maybe, Reshma, you could provide a little bit more detail just want to ensure that there was not a small subset of FSGS patients that was driving that proteinuria reduction that was broader based. Maybe you could talk about kind of the response rate across the population in that Cohort 1. Thank you.

Reshma Kewalramani FASN: Yeah. So Terence, on Cohort 1, that let's call it the modest proteinuria group because this was the 0.3 to 0.7 UPCR proteinuria cohort. The majority of patients did not have FSGS. So they did not have a biopsy, and they did not have FSGS, which you would expect because their proteinuria is modest and you are correct. The response therefore was not driven by an FSGS cohort because there were not many of them. Most people in the study were non FSGS patients.

And, if you ask me if I was feeling good about, the filing, all included, including manufacturing, I would say yes. I feel good about the filing. Beautiful. Thank you. You bet.

#3008. Fed will vote on rates less often. What that could mean for borrowers

After the Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady last week, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced plans to reduce the number of rate-setting votes over the next two years. That move could potentially extend the timeline for everyday Americans to see borrowing costs adjust, some experts say.

"Fewer Fed meetings in 2027 could mean consumers wait longer to see relief when borrowing costs are elevated," said James Vrachas, executive director at advisory firm Post Oak Group.

Americans may feel somewhat removed from the Fed, but the central bank's moves have a ripple effect on many types of consumer products, including the borrowing rates for credit cards, home loans and auto financing.

For example, most credit cards have variable rates tied to the prime rate, which moves with the Fed's benchmark. However, even with the central bank holding rates unchanged, credit card rates are edging higher as issuers protect themselves from risk, according to LendingTree.

Card issuers are mitigating their exposure from borrowers who may fall behind on payments or default in the face of stubborn inflation in everyday expenses, said Matt Schulz, LendingTree's chief credit analyst.

Generally, card issuers are slow to bring rates down, unless prompted by the Fed's actions, said Schulz: "Issuers will tinker with rates a bit at the margins at other times, but the big moves tend to only come when issuers are pushed."

On Oct. 28, the central bank voted to keep the benchmark borrowing rate at the current target range of 3.75% to 4% as policymakers deliberated next steps with inflation remaining well above the Fed's 2% goal.

The Fed will keep meeting eight times a year, Warsh said at the news conference following the October meeting, but next year, one of the eight meetings will not entail a vote on interest rates or include a post-meeting statement. The "strategy" meetings will increase to two the following year, leaving just six opportunities to adjust rates — with the exception of emergency meetings, if necessary.

"For consumers, that could mean longer periods of uncertainty around borrowing costs," said Jordan Ricciardi, a senior wealth strategy associate at UBS. "Our clients looking to buy a home, refinance a mortgage or finance a business could be impacted as fewer scheduled opportunities means the Fed isn't as quickly responding to changing economic conditions."

With fewer scheduled opportunities to adjust rates, that means borrowing rates could remain stubbornly high even if economic conditions begin to improve, Post Oak Group's Vrachas also said.

As it stands, financial institutions can adjust rates whenever market conditions warrant, regardless of the Fed's meeting schedule, he said. In the meantime, though, many consumers may continue to face elevated borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans and credit card debt, among other financial products.

"For consumers, the bigger concern isn't necessarily fewer meetings, but whether lenders pass along lower borrowing costs as quickly as they pass along increases," Vrachas said.

Consumers may be even more impacted by the lack of transparency, economists say, as Warsh implements measures to curtail so-called forward guidance, or how the Fed signals its future rate moves.

Although economic conditions have become more complicated and information is more widely available, "Warsh keeps his proverbial cards closer to his chest than his recent predecessors have," said Mark Hamrick, an economic analyst and founder of The Hamrick Brief, a weekly newsletter.

"I wouldn't expect consumers to see the universe of market rates change simply because the Fed votes less often," he said. "But the public may have less opportunity to hear from the source about how and why the Fed is making the decisions that shape what they pay to borrow and what they earn on their savings."

In the interim, "the best protection for consumers remains shopping around, particularly for the highest yields among savings accounts and [certificates of deposit]," Hamrick said.

As long as the Fed keeps rates unchanged, some top-yielding online savings accounts are offering interest rates as high as 4% or more, Bankrate data shows. "That's one of the upsides of an elevated interest rate environment: savers can earn meaningfully higher yields," Hamrick said.

#3006. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

#3003. Defense, healthcare, crypto and AI: How the midterm election could affect stocks

Lockheed Martin gets about 70% of its sales from the U.S. government. Medicaid accounts for three-quarters of Molina Healthcare's premium revenue. Coinbase is waiting on Congress to finish writing the rules for cryptocurrency.

For some of the biggest U.S. companies, Washington is part of the business model. Now, the midterm election could change who holds the leverage.

A Democratic victory in either or both chambers of Congress would grant the party new leverage to investigate companies, challenge federal spending and demand legislative concessions. But their reach would have limits: President Donald Trump would retain his veto and broad authority over tariffs, immigration and federal regulation.

Historically, stocks have performed well under divided government. Under Republican presidents, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 23% in the year after midterms when Congress was split, compared with 16% when Democrats controlled both chambers, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis published Thursday. Analysts often attribute the pattern in part to congressional gridlock limiting sweeping policy changes.

Still, some analysts caution against assuming that pattern will repeat.

"We don't think that blueprint holds up this time around, and we still see plenty of reasons to be constructive on the U.S. equity market," said Ariana Salvatore, head of U.S. public policy research at Morgan Stanley.

For investors, the midterm election could reshape which businesses preserve their advantages in Washington, particularly in industries such as defense, healthcare, banking and artificial intelligence.

"There are some policy changes that might be market moving, at least for certain segments," said Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist at LPL Financial.

Control of either the House or Senate would give Democrats committee gavels and subpoena power, allowing them to demand documents, compel testimony and haul executives before public hearings.

On Oct. 21, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sought records tied to Trump's White House ballroom from donors including Cisco, Salesforce, ServiceNow and Kraken. Apple and Nvidia each committed $25 million to the project, according to records obtained by The Washington Post.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., has separately sought records involving tariff exclusions, including communications involving Apple's former CEO, Tim Cook, as Democrats investigate whether Trump used trade policy to reward political allies and donors.

While donations do not prove wrongdoing or favorable treatment, congressional probes still carry risks: subpoenas consume executive bandwidth, reveal internal communications and generate unpredictable news coverage. Few CEOs relish the idea of sitting at a witness table before lawmakers and television cameras.

"It creates volatility because you get a negative headline," said Monica Guerra, Morgan Stanley's head of policy and geopolitical strategy, who expects Democrats to cast a wide net for their probes.

Democrats have signaled interest in Trump family businesses, government contractors, firms tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s 1789 Capital, and companies associated with Elon Musk and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency.

Then there is the most basic power Congress has: deciding where the money goes.

Trump's 2025 tax cuts and spending law, known as One Big Beautiful Bill, is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion through 2034, according to a KFF analysis of Congressional Budget Office estimates. KFF is a nonpartisan nonprofit that provides health policy information. Meanwhile, new work requirements for Medicaid enrollees are scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, or earlier in some states, while tighter state budgets could mean fewer people are covered and greater pressure on provider payments.

Molina Healthcare generated $32.2 billion, or 75% of its 2025 premium revenue, from Medicaid, according to the company's annual Securities and Exchange Commission filing. In the same filing, Molina warned that losing government contracts or failing to renew them on favorable terms could materially reduce premium revenue.

A Democratic-controlled chamber could not repeal the 2025 law on its own but could use must-pass budget negotiations to seek funding changes or delays to some cuts.

"They're probably going to push back on those Medicaid cuts," Buchbinder told CNBC, noting that preserving coverage could help stabilize enrollment for Medicaid insurers and patient volumes for hospitals.

Hospitals face their own squeeze: fewer insured patients can mean more uncompensated care, while state budget pressure can reduce reimbursement rates, according to KFF. Congress created a $50 billion rural health fund over five years to cushion some of the blow, but KFF and medical providers have said the money would not fully offset the broader Medicaid reductions.

Democratic gains could still cut both ways for healthcare. The same lawmakers seeking to protect Medicaid funding could also intensify scrutiny of insurers, hospitals and drugmakers over prices, coverage and profits.

Defense contractors face a fight over which weapons and programs Congress keeps funding. The White House has requested $1.5 trillion for national defense in fiscal 2027, with a focus on replenishing weapons, bolstering readiness and covering other needs, some tied to the Iran war.

The White House is separately seeking an $87.6 billion supplemental appropriation from Congress for fiscal 2026, driven primarily by military operations related to Iran.

A Democratic Congress could challenge some Iran- and Israel-related spending while pushing for more aid to Ukraine. However, bipartisan consensus on China deterrence, nuclear modernization and missile defense could protect other major programs, according to multiple analysts.

For contractors, the difference could mean billions of dollars in orders.

Lockheed Martin, for example, recently reached a framework agreement with the Pentagon covering 850 F-35 fighter jets over a decade. But the agreement is not yet a finalized contract: Congress must authorize the multiyear purchase and provide the funding.

"You want to be a stock picker and not just ride the whole sector," Guerra told CNBC, pointing to areas such as shipbuilding, autonomous systems and missile defense as likely winners.

For crypto companies, the midterms could determine whether Trump's regulatory shift becomes durable law or remains vulnerable to the next administration. The industry's push for permanence stalled in September, when the Senate failed to advance the Trump-backed Clarity Act, a sweeping market structure bill.

Shares of Coinbase and stablecoin issuer Circle fell as much as 11% when the measure failed.

Getting a bill through the next Congress could come at a price. Democratic gains would give the party more leverage to demand stricter consumer safeguards, limits on yield-bearing stablecoins and tighter scrutiny of Trump's crypto businesses.

"In some ways, the industry doesn't really care who got elected," said Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research. "They just want to know what the rules are going to be for the coming year."

Federal regulators estimate their proposed capital overhaul would cut requirements for the largest banks by roughly 4.8%, potentially freeing billions for lending and shareholder payouts. The Federal Reserve writes the rules, but Senate control shapes who fills future vacancies, and congressional committees can pressure regulators through hearings and investigations.

"It's at the regulatory level where stuff can happen that matters," Buchbinder said.

AI may be the messiest political trade of all.

Trump has made rapid data center construction an economic and national security priority. Morgan Stanley expects hyperscalers including Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta to spend more than $1 trillion on capital projects in 2027, even as the buildout faces growing backlash over electricity bills, water use and infrastructure costs.

CNBC's All-America Economic Survey from October found that 63% of registered voters oppose having a data center within 10 miles of their home, compared with just 13% who support one. The level of opposition is higher from Democrats than Republicans.

That friction has already reached Congress. In September, the House voted 417-3 to require state regulators to consider making large data centers cover the additional electricity infrastructure costs needed to serve them. The measure stalled in the Senate, 57-43 on a procedural vote, after Democrats argued it was too weak and pushed for mandatory protections instead of trusting the industry to police itself.

The midterms therefore could decide who gets the power. Democratic gains could put more grid-upgrade costs on tech developers, raising project costs just as access to power is constraining new construction.

But Congress is only part of the equation. State regulators, utilities and local governments will still decide where projects connect to the grid and which facilities get built.

"We think the election can have meaningful consequences, but on a highly localized basis," Salvatore said.

#2999. Lumentum CEO touts 'enormous' opportunity in massive AI connectivity deal with Marvell

Marvell Technology's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday.

"You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here."

Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.

Marvell shares slumped 13% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank nearly 19%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch.

Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.

"We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said.

Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.

Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.

This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.

Marvell's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies.

In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers.

"This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them."

Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.

CORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston described the deal as an 'enormous' opportunity. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

#2989. Judge tosses DOJ case against ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden probe

A federal judge on Monday blasted the Department of Justice for "weaponization" as he dismissed its case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress about investigations into Hunter Biden, multiple news outlets reported.

Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, in a hearing in U.S. District Court in Washington, reportedly tore into the DOJ over its "slapdash job" prosecuting ex-officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, saying he was "deeply troubled by what has happened here."

Faruqui said the government lacked probable cause and failed to present evidence that the officials' statements before the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 were knowingly false, MS NOW reported.

He also accused the DOJ of wrongly rushing the case ahead of the midterm election. The situation "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," he said, according to MS NOW.

The judge even apologized to the government's lawyers, calling it "incredibly unfair" that they were assigned to defend the flawed case.

"This does not feel like an investigation," Faruqui reportedly added. "It feels like a broken one-wish willow obsession."

The DOJ, in response to an email sent to its press office, said it "disagrees" with the decision.

"We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation," the agency said in response to CNBC. "The Department's actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law – not politics."

Attorneys for Floris and Benavides praised the judge's decision outside the courthouse later Monday morning.

"This case should never have been brought. The government had no case, as the judge just laid out," a lawyer for Floris said, slamming the prosecution as a "spaghetti-at-the-wall, Hunter-Biden-conspiracy fever dream."

A lawyer for Benavides said they hope the DOJ will not try to keep the case alive by seeking an indictment before a grand jury "where they get to be behind closed doors and get to shape the narrative, and we are unable to present our side."

The DOJ did not take that step when they unveiled the allegations against Floris and Benavides on Oct. 23.

Rather, despite the alleged misconduct taking place years earlier, prosecutors acquired a criminal complaint, which only requires a judge's signature. Criminal complaints are often used to obtain arrest warrant in situations where prosecutors need to move quickly.

Faruqui had flagged that circumstance as unusual, and last week refused to sign off on a superseding complaint that added an obstruction charge against the two ex-officials.

"I'm concerned with your view as to what the law is," the judge told the prosecutors in a hearing last Tuesday. "Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?"

#2987. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.
