Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

"While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," said Mehta.

#2981. Feeling isolated? Half of in-office workers describe their desk jobs as 'remote,' NY Fed survey finds

Many workers across the U.S. are now back in-office a majority of the time, and they are feeling more isolated than ever.

A recent survey from researchers at the New York Fed finds that roughly half of workers based in-office don't describe a daily experience on the job that matches the goal many corporate employers stated in upping in-person mandates.

Whether three-, four- or five-day mandates, companies have cited the importance of creative collaboration for business productivity and growth, as well as mentorship opportunities. Yet workers surveyed by the NY Fed describe endless Zoom calls and Slacks, and little actual face time.

"Days in the office often lack human contact," the researchers write. Specifically, 48.8% of survey respondents said they had no in-person meetings, either with teammates or non-teammates, on the days they were most recently in the office.

There are a variety of reasons for the disconnect between in-office work mandates and actual experience.

Roughly one in four workers are now fully remote, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data cited by the NY Fed, but they say that alone likely "understates the explosion in the experience of remoteness from colleagues."

With teams being spread across more offices — an effect they say has become more pronounced in the post-Covid organizational structure — many workers "no-showing" on mandates, and employers not enforcing mandates strictly, the result for in-office workers, according to the researchers, is that "they commute in just to take Zoom calls and answer Slack messages from their cubicles."

The NY Fed paper, by NY Fed research economist Natalia Emanuel and University of Virginia economics professor Emma Harrington, concludes that "a staggering share of the workforce experiences this form of in-office remote work."

The survey was conducted in September among a final sample of 1,835 college-educated workers. The researchers chose September, they say, to generate a "conservative estimate," since many companies push in-office attendance after summer ends, and the period between Labor Day and Thanksgiving has less remote work than holiday periods.

The survey found that on in-office days, 70.6% of workers had at least one teammate who was not in the office; while half had no in-person meetings with all participants present, and over a third had neither in-person or hybrid meetings.

"Amazingly, 37% of respondents reported that they had at least one meeting that was virtual, even though all the participants were in the same office that day. In short, many workers' commutes are simply yielding a new background for their Zoom calls," they write.

They cite the example of Zoom CEO Eric Yuan, who said in 2023, "On Zoom, it's really hard. We cannot have a great conversation. We cannot debate each other well."

But the researchers conclude, "if the debates in the office are also happening over Zoom, the benefits of the office may not be so large."

The authors say that separate information collected on a Fortune 500 company employee base to which they had personnel data and badge swipe data shows that nearly half of corporate employees have at least one teammate who is out of the office on their in-office days. They say additional data from the BLS's American Time Use Survey similarly show that "Americans now spend more time physically alone on days they go into the office than they did before the pandemic."

Other recent polling data from Gallup found worker sentiment to be at a 15-year low.

The NY Fed authors caution that their research does not capture relationships with non-teammates, or worker's in-person interactions with clients, often outside the office. They also stress that workers who come to the office often cite seeing colleagues as a major draw. "But since the rise of remote work, the office increasingly fails to deliver this benefit," they write.

They contend that the research has practical implications for both employers and employees.

For one, the experience of remote work is much more widespread than understood, which could have many repercussions not being dealt with effectively now, such as mental health issues.

Second, organizational structure post-pandemic may not be optimal for making in-office mandates work. It may, in fact, just lead to more pushback, they write.

But the authors do not conclude employers should give up on the mandates. To the contrary, they write, "ensuring adherence to the policy helps deliver the face-to-face contact that workers crave."

#2974. Wall Street's Fear Index is doing something strange. Here's what it means for stocks

Stocks wrapped their worst week since June on Friday, but a group of the most sophisticated options analysts agree the reaction in the options market was oddly calm.

While the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX), often referred to as a so-called fear index, did touch its highest intraday level since April on Friday, it quickly retreated and closed at 19.4. Its rollover came even as the S&P 500 finished the day down nearly 2%. For that size of a decline in stocks, the 2.2-point move in VIX was "relatively muted," according to SpotGamma's Brent Kochuba, whose analysis suggests VIX should have jumped closer to 2.6 points, based on a study of 126 selloffs since 2018.

Even in the Nasdaq 100 Index, where implied volatility increased for most options contracts, there were key exceptions. Prices on put contracts that are between 20% and 50% out-of-the-money were higher on a volatility basis after the sell-off on Oct. 16, according to data shared by Nasdaq's Kevin Davitt.

So not only did traders not pile into S&P 500 Index options on Friday, they were also especially choosy with which Nasdaq hedges they bought. For example, in the Nasdaq, puts were more expensive two weeks ago, according to Nations Indexes data. And out-of-the-money S&P 500 Index puts "just aren't being chased-into at this moment," writes Nomura managing director Charlie McElligott, indicating investor calm in the face of falling stocks.

"Index options skew hasn't been particularly reactive to the few days of spot equities selloff this week, and even where it has, it's partially a function of call vol getting mushed," McElligot said in a note to clients on Friday.

One explanation for the lack of hedging could be that asset managers are quickly selling stocks instead of using options to protect those stocks from further decline.

One popular chart making the rounds over the weekend came from Morgan Stanley's prime brokerage. According to the firm's data on long-short active managers, total global gross equity exposure is down 8% from its most recent peak, the biggest drawdown in at least ten years.

"Long/short has experienced a massive de-levering event," said Zed Francis, CIO of Chicago-based Convexitas. "Buy the shorts, sell the longs. If you were closer to cash than you were before, no need to hedge. I believe this is the main reason implied volatility has remained quiet during an increased-stress month."

#2973. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

#2968. Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years. Here's how much money is at stake for beneficiaries

Social Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years.

Without intervention before then, the Social Security retirement trust fund, formally known as the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which helps pay benefits to eligible workers and qualifying family members, will run out in the fourth quarter of 2032, the program's trustees said in a June report.

At that time, the trustees project retirement benefits will be cut by 22%.

The Congressional Budget Office has a more dire forecast, anticipating that the retirement trust fund may run out sooner, in mid-2032, and that retirees may see larger benefit cuts, at 26%, upon insolvency.

Beneficiaries may receive an average $500 cut to their monthly benefits across the U.S. based on a 24% benefit reduction, according to a June report from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. In 29 states, retirees would see even bigger average reductions, according to the nonpartisan organization focused on educating the public on fiscal policy issues.

Senators elected this November will be in office in 2032, when the retirement trust fund depletion date hits. Their ability to right the ship is crucial for retirees and the economy. But it's not a sure thing given the political climate inside the beltway.

"The attention on 2032 is appropriate in the sense that that is when beneficiaries and future beneficiaries will see and feel the consequences of inaction," said Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a public policy think tank focused on promoting bipartisan cooperation.

"Nothing gets Congress to move like that type of deadline," he said.

Of course, brinksmanship and political deadlock may stymie efforts. Congress could opt to kick the can down the road, rather than enact changes to shore up Social Security — which may require tax increases, benefit cuts or a combination of both.

If lawmakers decide to combine Social Security's retirement and disability trust funds, the depletion date may move to the third quarter of 2034, when benefits may be cut by 17%, according to Social Security's trustees.

Akabas said any delay by lawmakers would have consequences: Social Security's shortfall would continue to increase.

There could also be consequences for the economy, he said.

In 2023, Social Security benefits generated $2.6 trillion in total economic output and supported more than 12 million jobs, according to 2025 research by the National Institute on Retirement Security, a Washington, D.C., based nonprofit, nonpartisan organization.

A 19% benefit cut could reduce gross domestic product by hundreds of billions of dollars, according to the NIRS research.

Moreover, failing to muster Social Security reform would prompt bond market strain, according to research published in June by George Mason University's Mercatus Center.

Social Security is tied to the bond market because its trust funds are invested in special issue U.S. Treasury bonds.

If Social Security reform is delayed, that may put upward pressure on Treasury yields, with investors wanting higher returns for long-term bonds.

Delayed reform may either prompt higher interest rates and borrowing costs or inflationary adjustments that hurt the value of government liabilities, according to the Mercatus Center research. Those changes may affect household budgets through higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and other types of consumer credit as well as student loans, according to the research.

If interest rates and prices rise, that will interfere with economic growth, Akabas said.

"Those effects are also ones that the American people feel, in addition to adjustments to their benefits," Akabas said.

Heading to the midterms, some Democratic congressional candidates have said they would raise or eliminate the Social Security payroll tax cap so high earners pay more into the program. In 2026, the 6.2% tax paid by both workers and their employers applies to earnings up to $184,500.

Yet it remains to be seen whether Washington leaders will have the political will to address the problem soon. Tax increases, in particular, may not be viewed as politically popular heading into the 2028 presidential election.

As such, payroll taxes are "extraordinarily unlikely" to rise in the next couple of years, said Jessica Riedl, a fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, which provides independent analyses of tax issues. If those tax hikes happen, it would likely be closer to 2032, she said.

"In Washington, they love to wait until the last minute," Riedl said. "There's no interest on either side for these sorts of tax increases in the short term. In the long term, I think everything is on the table."

The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, founded by President Franklin D. Roosevelt's son, former U.S. Rep. James Roosevelt, has scored incumbent lawmakers on whether their votes have protected those programs.

The advocacy organization has also endorsed candidates who support raising payroll taxes and protecting Social Security benefits from cuts. With those endorsements, the NCPSSM gives candidates a set of boxing gloves as a symbol of the fights they'll face in Congress, according to Dan Adcock, the NCPSSM's director of government relations and policy.

The organization is also working to educate voters that the senators elected this year will be among those to deal with Social Security, he said.

"We've been trying to impress upon voters why this is an issue that should be top tier," Adcock said. "They need to be asking candidates about what their plans for the program would be."

#2966. Bucks exercise rookie-scale options on Kel’el Ware, Kasparas Jakučionis

The Milwaukee Bucks will exercise their rookie-scale options on offseason acquisitions Kel'el Ware and Kasparas Jakučionis, according to HoopsHype's Michael Scotto.

Ware, a 22-year-old seven-footer acquired in the trade that sent Giannis Antetokounmpo to the Miami Heat, has played solely in a reserve role for the Bucks to begin the season, averaging a career-high 13.8 PPG to go along with 8.7 RPG and 1.5 stocks (steals plus blocks). But for all his talent and flashes of brilliance, Ware has continued to show the motor and decision-making issues that marred his first two years in the league, leading to career lows in shooting (46.8% overall, 26.1% from three) and minutes (19.7 MPG), despite Myles Turner's struggles and the Bucks' lack of size in the frontcourt.

Jakučionis, also acquired in the Giannis trade—and by all accounts a must-have component of it—has arguably been one of Milwaukee's brightest spots to start the season. Quickly emerging as a Taylor Jenkins favourite, the 6'5" Lithuanian point guard has become the team's sixth man and earned enough trust to feature in many of the team's closing lineups too. So far, the 20-year-old is averaging career highs across the board, including points (8.3 PPG), rebounds (2.8 RPG), assists (4.0 APG), and minutes (22.5 MPG). However, like many of his teammates, he's struggled shooting from distance, hitting just 23.5% of his three-point attempts, down from 42.3% last season.

On-court production aside, Ware and Jakučionis figure to be key parts of the Bucks' present and future, so seeing their rookie-scale options picked up is a positive sign. As per Scotto's reporting, Ware's option for the 2027-28 season comes in at $7.14m while Jakučionis' is for $4.02m.

Here's hoping the pair continue to grow as the season progresses.

#2962. Game Preview: Suns hit the road for rematch against Warriors

Who: Phoenix Suns (1-3) @ Golden State Warriors (4-3)

Watch: Arizona's Family 3TV, Arizona's Family Sports

The Phoenix Suns have the worst defense in the NBA, and tonight they get Steph Curry and Draymond Green on the road.

Nine days ago this matchup felt like relief. Booker dropped 43 on a Warriors team missing its stars, the bench flipped the game, and we all exhaled after Portland. Since then? Phoenix lost in Oklahoma City, lost to Denver on Booker's 30th birthday, and sat on a 1-3 record all weekend. Golden State went the other way and hasn't lost since leaving Phoenix.

So here's where the fanbase is at: nobody's panicking about the offense anymore. We're panicking about the other end. Every opponent has hung 120-plus on this team, and the Warriors just made 22 threes without Steph on the floor.

You do the math on what happens if Phoenix shows up with the same effort on the perimeter.

Golden State rested Curry and Draymond on the front end of the back-to-back against the Clippers, saving both for Phoenix.

Phoenix won the home opener 131-122… still, their only its first win of the season. Devin Booker went for 43 points, 7 rebounds, and 7 assists with only two made threes, didn't miss a shot in the third quarter, and broke the franchise home-opener scoring record held by Eddie Johnson and Charles Barkley.

The real story was the bench. Ryan Dunn, Jordan Goodwin, Collin Gillespie and Luke Kennard were a combined +56 in a 9-point win. Gillespie went scoreless in the first half, then rattled off 9 points in 3 minutes to swing the momentum. Kennard hit big shots in his Suns debut.

Now, the asterisk, and we have to be honest about it. That was Golden State's C team on the second night of a back-to-back: no Curry, no Draymond, no Podziemski, no Horford. It was not an impressive win. And the Warriors will likely want to prove that tonight in front of their home crowd.

Even then, a depleted Warriors group put up 122. The first unit looked discombobulated with sloppy turnovers in the first half, and Booker himself said the second unit had better chemistry than the starters. Rebounding was the other red flag he flagged postgame. These are the two worst defensive rebounding teams in the NBA, with Phoenix at 30 and Golden State at 29 overall.

So now the question is: how does Phoenix stop Stephen Curry? A heavy dosage of Jordan Goodwin could be in order. Even then, good luck.

Stop the ball before it reaches the paint

Phoenix entered last week with a 124.5 defensive rating, dead last in the league, and opponents are now shooting nearly 44% from three against them. The sequence repeats every night: a guard gets beat off the dribble, nobody stops the ball, the forward helps late, and it's a layup or a wide-open corner three. Against Denver, Jamal Murray and Christian Braun went 14-of-18 from deep, and Phoenix allowed 54% from three overall.

Braun was a 23% shooter coming in. Golden State's role guys will get the same invitation if the help keeps collapsing.

Denver shot 30 free throws to Phoenix's 11, and Murray alone took more than the entire Suns roster. Some calls were questionable. Plenty were dumb fouls, technicals, a delay of game, and the Brooks ejection. You can't give Steph free points on top of open threes.

Collin Gillespie had 16 points, 10 assists, and 4 steals against Denver and was +8 in a 7-point loss. Jalen Green had 2 points on 1-of-6 in 25 minutes. The Suns look their best with Gillespie on the floor, period. Against a small, switch-heavy Warriors team, this is also the perfect night to promote Oso. Gillespie said it himself: Oso plays like a point forward and makes the flow easy. Watch how early Jordan Ott staggers and who closes, because that tells you where his head is at.

Somebody has to sacrifice. Devin Booker scored 43 last time against a skeleton crew. He won't get that runway with Draymond, Melton, Yaxel, and others loading up on him.

In that same vein, who steps up? Does Green bounce back off the bench or as a starter? Can Miles Bridges keep attacking downhill as he did in his 24-point, 10-rebound game against Denver instead of settling for threes? It takes a team to win. Hero ball needs to fade, and the hunt every possession should be to get the best possible shot. This is not on one guy. It's on the entire team to buy in.

While the Suns showed some progress in their loss to Denver, their defense is still a major concern. I do not see them winning this one, but I hope to be proven wrong.

#2946. Observations after Sixers beat Bulls to reach East-leading 7-1

Observations after Sixers beat Bulls to reach East-leading 7-1 originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers kept up their hot start to the season Monday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, reaching 7-1 with a 126-107 win against the Bulls.

All five of the Sixers' starters scored in double figures. Tyrese Maxey posted 26 points on 10-for-15 shooting and 11 assists. Jaylen Brown tallied a season-best 25 points and 11 rebounds.

VJ Edgecombe's 21 points were a new season high. LeBron James recorded 15 points, nine assists and seven boards.

Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson had 24 points and seven rebounds.

Joel Embiid (15 points, eight rebounds) had been listed as questionable with an official designation of "right foot plantar fascia injury management." He sat out Saturday on the second night of a back-to-back for the Sixers' win over the Hornets.

"Plantar is a little bit of a come and go type of thing," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse told reporters pregame. "They're just trying to manage it. It's very painful, if you've ever had it. It can kind of come and go out of nowhere. So we're just trying to manage the pain with that, be as smart as we can."

Nurse told reporters that Dominick Barlow is set to see a specialist Tuesday about the back injury that's sidelined him to start the season.

"He's been on court a little bit … not a ton of moving around," Nurse said. "I think they want to get to tomorrow's appointment. Hopefully, it'll be positive and we can get into his workouts a little bit."

The Sixers will begin a three-game road trip Wednesday when they visit the Pistons. Here are observations on their victory Monday:

After Embiid blitzed a Bulls pick-and-roll, Maxey picked off Matas Buzelis' hurried pass to get the Sixers rolling in transition and James jammed home the team's first field goal.

Edgecombe got a slam soon after James grabbed a defensive rebound and the Sixers again pushed the pace. The Sixers scored six quick fast-break points, leading the Bulls to burn an early timeout.

Edgecombe had a dunk-heavy first quarter. He threw down his second when Dean Wade nabbed a steal and dropped off a typically selfless dish to the Sixers' explosive second-year guard, whose slam put the team up 22-13.

The Sixers have an abundance of dangerous options in the open floor, Edgecombe included. As he's already shown with his continued clutch shotmaking, the 21-year-old won't become anything resembling a non-factor offensively this year as a byproduct of the Sixers' enhanced star power.

Over the team's first seven games, Edgecombe had averaged 11.3 points. He scored 11 in the first period on 5-for-5 shooting.

Adem Bona missed a dunk early in the second quarter, which stung a bit more when Jalen Smith drilled a three-pointer seconds later.

Bona remained the Sixers' main backup center. He had a poor first-half stint overall amid a largely negative start to his third season. The 23-year-old big man played well in the Sixers' victory over the Bucks, posting six points, 13 rebounds and three blocks. Outside of that, his season has been sparse on bright moments so far. It's reasonable to wonder when Nurse might turn to alternatives like Jabari Walker, who played a good game Saturday in Charlotte, or try James again at the five.

The Bulls outscored the Sixers by eight points in Bona's first run, cutting their derficit to 40-38. Chicago went in front with a three by former Sixer Buddy Hield.

The Sixers regained the advantage late in the second quarter. Maxey and James each were excellent as passers in the first half, combining for 14 assists and three turnovers. James fired the ball to Wade for a corner three that gave the Sixers a 60-52 lead.

Following a third-quarter Embiid fadeaway jumper and two James lay-ins, the Sixers were up 17 points.

The Bulls cut the Sixers' lead down to 11 points by the start of the fourth quarter. With Bona still struggling and on four fouls, Wade began the fourth at center. Bona then briefly spelled Wade before being whistled for his fifth foul and taking a seat. Embiid ultimately wasn't needed for any of the fourth period and only logged 25 minutes.

The Sixers' lead got as low as eight points, but Chicago did not shoot well enough from three-point range (27 percent) or have sufficient firepower to sustain a meaningful comeback run. The bottom line is the Sixers are in a different class than the Bulls, who fell to 1-6.

As for the Sixers, they'll wake up Tuesday morning at the top of the Eastern Conference standings.

#2943. I bonds now pay 5.51% — but there are trade-offs. What to know before buying

Now that Series I bonds pay higher interest, the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset could be more attractive for certain investors. But I bonds have downsides, and there are alternatives to consider.

Newly purchased I bonds currently pay 5.51% annual interest through April 30, up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through October.

Amid rising inflation, the variable part of I bond interest rose to 4.08%, while the fixed part increased to 1.40%, the highest since 2006. Combined, the 5.51% composite rate is the biggest yield since November 2022.

The new I bond rate is "very attractive," according to Ken Tumin, founder of DepositQuest.com, a blog that tracks I bond rates, among other deposit accounts.

The variable part of I bond interest resets every six months, based on the consumer price index. For the next six months after purchase, I bonds look "very competitive" compared to other shorter-term options for cash, such as savings accounts or certificates of deposit, according to Tumin.

Meanwhile, the I bond's 1.4% fixed rate stays the same for as long as you own it, which could appeal to longer-term investors, he said.

But I bonds aren't right for everyone. Here are some key things to know before purchasing.

Investors can buy $10,000 of electronic I bonds per person per calendar year via their TreasuryDirect account. You can open additional TreasuryDirect accounts for other family members or businesses to buy more.

I bond interest is tax-deferred until redemption and is not subject to state or local taxes. You can also avoid federal taxes if you use the money for qualified education expenses.

But experts say there are some downsides. The funds are locked up for 12 months from purchase, and you'll lose your last three months of interest if you redeem within five years.

Advisors typically recommend keeping at least three to six months of living expenses in cash for emergency savings. I bonds could boost those reserves, experts say, as long as you keep enough readily accessible cash elsewhere.

"I always say [I bonds are] a secondary emergency fund," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, and I bond rates.

Once you own I bonds for five years, you can redeem the money as needed, penalty-free.

With I bond purchase limits, restrictions and some TreasuryDirect complaints, advisors often recommend other options for clients who want to preserve purchasing power.

"For most of my clients, I bonds are more hassle than they're worth," said certified financial planner Eileen Olson, founder of advisory firm Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina. "The amount is too small to matter."

On a $2 million portfolio, the $10,000 annual purchase limit is only 0.5%, and it earns about $550 in a year before federal taxes, she said. "That won't protect anyone's lifestyle from inflation."

Instead, Olson prefers TIPS, which don't have purchase limits and can be bought alongside other assets, outside TreasuryDirect.

TIPS have five-, 10- and 30-year terms, with yields ranging from about 2.3% to above 3% for the 30-year term, as of Nov. 2.

However, the right option depends on your investing goals and timeline, experts say.

"For short-term cash, Treasury bills and high-yield savings are simpler," Olson said.

Also backed by the U.S. government, Treasury bills, or T-bills, have terms ranging from four weeks up to 52 weeks. As of Nov. 2, some T-bill yields were well over 4%.

By comparison, the top 1% average of high-yield savings accounts were paying above 4%, according to rate comparison site DepositAccounts. Some one-year certificates of deposit were also offering rates over 4%, the same day, according to Bankrate.

Money market funds are another option. Some of the biggest funds were paying around 4%, as of Nov. 2, according to Crane Data.

#2941. Jets’ defense has crashed back to earth with critical tests looming

The Jets defense was ranked No. 1 in yards allowed after two games this season.

The defense has crumbled since then, culminating with Sunday's collapse against the Raiders when the Jets became the third team in the last 45 years to score on their first six possessions and still lose, according to ESPN.

The Jets wasted a rare 30-point game from their offense because their defense could not slow down Kirk Cousins and Brock Bowers and they allowed four touchdowns, with three coming in the second half (special teams allowed another).

"Defensively, we got to do a way better job than what we did," Jets coach Aaron Glenn said Monday, "but when you really look at this game, and see what it came down to, it was the third-down penalties that you can't give any offense a second chance to get a drive on you, and those things happened to our defense."

Glenn pointed to the two penalties, which did lead to the Raiders staying on the field and scoring touchdowns, but the problems feel deeper than that. The penalties both came in the third quarter. Brandon Stephens was flagged for holding on third down against Raiders tight end Brock Bowers in the end zone on Las Vegas' first drive of the second half. The Raiders scored moments later.

Raiders tight end Brock Bowers (89) runs the ball against the Jets. Bill Kostroun for NY nPost

Later in the third quarter, Jarvis Brownlee Jr. was called for pass interference on third-and-10 when the Jets should have gotten off the field. That extended a drive that ended with another Raiders touchdown.

Glenn said the Jets will focus on cutting out those critical penalties this week.

"Well you'll address it, first off, and then you look at the technique part of it," Glenn said, "and see how do you fix that, so you don't want that to happen on third down, you don't want it to happen on second down, or first down, so if you can address that and fix the technique part of it, it gives you a chance to be successful in that position."

While the penalties were costly, they hardly tell the full story. The Jets went a second straight week without a takeaway. They still have just one interception this season, which means they have one total interception in 25 games under Glenn.

"Certainly as a defense, you have to find a way to take the ball away," linebacker Demario Davis said. "That changes momentum of the game, whether it's a punch out or an interception. Have to find a way to create disruption when they're putting those drives together by taking the ball away. We just didn't do a good enough job of that and that's one of the things you just have to own, fix and keep moving."

The Jets have allowed 300 yards in five of their last six games after holding their first two opponents under 200 yards. They have given up 100 yards rushing in four of the last six.

The Raiders struggled to get a running game going, but the Jets allowed Bowers to catch seven passes for 92 yards and two touchdowns. Everyone in MetLife Stadium knew the ball was going to Bowers and the Jets could not find a way to stop him.

The Jets barely touched Cousins, who threw three touchdown passes and rushed for another. They sacked Cousins just once and had six hits on him. The Jets were playing without rookie edge rusher David Bailey, but you'd still expect them to get more pressure on Cousins.

Raiders wide receiver Jalen Nailor (9) catches a touchdown pass in front of Jets cornerback Azareye'h Thomas (1). Bill Kostroun for NY Post

"We're not being consistent enough, I think, with disrupting the quarterback," Davis said. "That's a big thing. When we're disrupting the quarterback whether it's hitting him, being in those passing windows, or forcing incomplete passes, we're better."

The Jets needed a stop late in the game and allowed the Raiders to put together a nine-play drive before they kicked a field goal. That left the Jets offense with just 27 seconds and needing a touchdown. Late-game stops have been a struggle for the Jets since the loss to the Bears a month ago. The Bears, Patriots and Dolphins have all had long drives in the fourth quarter to seal wins.

The Jets are also bad at situational football. The Raiders were 7-for-11 converting on third down and they scored touchdowns on all four red zone trips.

Glenn, who is calling the defense, needs to fix things fast. It won't be easy with Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs coming this week, followed by Josh Allen and the Bills next week.

#2939. What we learned as Steph Curry, Warriors erase 17-point deficit to stun Suns

What we learned as Steph Curry, Warriors erase 17-point deficit to stun Suns originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

SAN FRANCISCO – Playing the second night of a back-to-back and their third game in four nights, the Warriors looked exhausted against the Phoenix Suns on Monday night at Chase Center.

Jumping on Steph Curry's back, the Warriors were able to pull off what they couldn't once all last season. They didn't have a single five-game win streak in the 2025-26 season. They do now in the 2026-27 campaign, winning five straight after an 0-3 start to the season, erasing a 17-point deficit to beat the Suns 116-113.

Curry and Draymond Green returned from resting the previous night. Green was ineffective and ejected in the third quarter. Curry started slow and then exploded to score a game-high 34 points.

In his last three games, Curry now has scored 44, 31 and 34 points. He's now averaging exactly 30 points this season at 38 years old in Year 18.

Brandin Podziemski added 20 points, Charles Bassey was a jolt in scoring a career-high 19 points off the bench  and Yaxel Lendeborg followed his 37-point performance with 16 points, five rebounds and five assists.

Here are three takeaways from the Warriors' fifth straight win.

Sometimes games can be as simple as shots falling and not falling. The Warriors became 3-point happy to begin the game, taking seven of their first eight shots beyond the arc and making only two. They shot 33.3 percent overall in the first quarter (8 of 24) and went a lowly 2 of 15 from 3-point range (13.3 percent).

The Suns also made two threes in the first quarter, but the Warriors attempted 10 more than them and trailed by 12 points through the first 12 minutes. When it looked like the game could get out of hand in a 16-point deficit, the Warriors answered with a 12-0 run late in the second quarter. They went 5 of 11 from three in the second quarter while taking care of the ball and made it a six-point game at halftime.

As Curry gets going, everybody else usually follows. That's how it unsurprisingly went against the Suns. The Warriors scored 19 points in the first quarter, 32 in the second and then 42 in the third to make it a tie game entering the fourth quarter. It just so happens that Curry found his flurry in the third quarter, and the Warriors went 5 of 10 on threes in the frame.

The Warriors created good shots and minimized their turnovers for a winning recipe. They made four fewer shots than the Suns, but had two more threes than them, made nine more free throws than them and turned the ball over two fewer times to win each of the final three quarters.

There were various reasons the Warriors chose to sit Curry and Green on the first night of a back-to-back instead of the second. The Warriors had just returned from a three-game road trip, and the they needed all 31 points in 31 minutes from Curry to beat the Los Angeles Lakers. He looked rested right away Monday night too, scoring the first three points of the game for the Warriors.

But Curry didn't make another shot the rest of the quarter, and connected just once more – but not from three – in the first half. Curry went into halftime with nine points on 2-of-7 shooting, doing most of his damage at the free-throw line. Right on cue, Curry made a three 15 seconds into the third quarter.

In the first half, it looked like Curry couldn't find his burst. Then the third quarter started, and Curry scored 18 points in eight-plus minutes. All the sudden he was up to 27 points, and the Warriors found their mojo and momentum.

Golden State's lead was lost with Curry on the bench in the fourth quarter. Curry returned at the 4:48 mark and the Warriors outscored the Suns 12-9 the rest of the way.

On the Warriors' next possession after Green's ejection, Bassey entered and continued the kind of impact he had been making all game. Bassey played through contact for a tip-in layup, and though he missed his free throw, he assisted Curry for a three the next time down the court.

Bassey tied Curry as the Warriors' leading scorer in the first half and was one of their two players to have multiple offensive rebounds. How many other players, outside of Lendeborg, do the Warriors have who possess size and can make plays like these?

Using Lendeborg as a playmaking ball-handler, he and Bassey have created quick chemistry for easy baskets and exciting lobs.

The last game these two teams played each other, Bassey shone off the bench with 10 points and seven rebounds. He also grabbed 10 rebounds Sunday night in a spot start. As a team that lacks size and athleticism, Bassey keeps showing why he might be earning more opportunities.

#2936. As AI becomes more fractured, one name stands out: AMD

As Anthropic rushes to takes its shares public, the AI trade is showing cracks, and they are not confined to fringe players.

We recently wrote about CoreWeave, which fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and its default-swap spreads nearly doubled in October. IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, the contagion reached chipmakers, which makes sense since much of CRWV and IREN's spending is going there. AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research exacerbated data-center fears about the pace of AI spending.

Because when you screen for factors that demonstrably generate outperformance over time, the list narrows quickly. My screen: price above the 200-day moving average; revenue growing at least as fast as the S&P 500 (5%+ per annum); EPS growing at least as fast (7%+); rating upgrades; a PEG below 3; and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%. Of the names reporting in the next two weeks, AMD is effectively the only one that makes the list. Yes, you can (and arguably should, as our staples article described) position your portfolio with slightly less tech exposure than the broad indices provide, but we can't ignore the market's biggest and most transformative sector entirely.

Especially because the growth in this case doesn't just meet my criteria; it blows past them. Consensus for Q3 calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, versus $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year ago. That's YoY growth of nearly 62% and 41%, respectively. The recent drawdown came from a sector selloff, not anything AMD reported, but it shows that if some names in the space get hit, even the larger players are likely to feel it. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

So how do you balance factors we know work for a fast-growing company against a backdrop of cracks in the AI trade? Options.

Owning the stock outright means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move (day of). Earnings are about a week out, and over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window was more than 9%, and the largest move, after the company reported its Q1 26 results, was 38%! Of course, that kind of volatility means options aren't cheap, and that rich premium is also a reason not to simply buy calls.

A call spread risk reversal does both jobs: it reduces risk if the cracks widen, and the short options offset the elevated volatility we would otherwise pay for. The bottom chart shows that, by sacrificing about $1,700 of upside for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and given how jittery this trade has been lately, this is a way to stay in it with considerably less risk. $5,000 less, specifically. Of course, selling that out will tie up some cash, but less so than simply buying the stock. And selling both the out and the call reduces long call purchase by 66%

The Celtics look for their 6th straight win as they travel to Houston to take on the Rockets. This is the second of back to back games for the Celtics and the first back to back set on the road. The Celtics are 1-0 so far in the second of back to back games. This is the first of 2 games between these two teams this season. They will play again on January 11 in Boston.

The Celtics were 1-1 last year against the Rockets, with each team winning on the road. The Celtics are 99-58 ovrerall all time against the Rockets. They are 43-34 when playing at Houston. This will be a tough game against a very good team. The Rockets have won 6 of their first 7 games, losing only at Dallas and beating Dallas, Atlanta and OKC at home and San Antonio, Atlanta and Milwaukee on the road.

The Rockets were a good team last season but have gotten better in the off season. Fred VanVleet has returned from a torn ACL that kept him out last season. They signed Marcus Smart, who will help to bolster their defense. They also signed Bogdan Bogdanovic, who will give them another 3 point shooter. They drafted Bruce Thornton with the 31st pick in the draft. They lost Dorian Finney-Smith and Josh Okogie.

After this game, the Celtics will return home to host Milwaukee before a road trip that will take them through Charlotte, Milwaukee, Philadelphia and Toronto. They play Dallas and Orlando at home before a West coast trip that takes them through Denver, Sacramento, Golden State, and Washington. They then play one game at home against Atlanta before playing at San Antonio and Dallas.

After this game the Rockets will host Minnesota before playing at Phoenix. Next they have a 3 game home stand against Denver, Golden State, and Utah. Then they go on the road for 4 games through Washington, Miami , Indiana, and Denver. Next, they host the LA Clippers, Phoenix, Philadelphia, the LA Lakers, and Toronto.

The Celtics started Derrick White, Jordan Walsh, Paul George, Jayson Tatum and Mitchell Robinson in the first 5 games. In their last game against the Magic, they started White, Gonzalez, George, Tatum and Queta. I'm guessing that Gonzalez once again starts and that Robinson will return to the starting lineup after a game off for rest. Mitchell Robinson missed Sunday's game for rest and I expect him to return for this game. Joe may choose to sit out other players for rest in this game but at this time the injury report is not out. Keys to the GameDefense – Defense is always a key to winning. Players struggle on offense in some games, but they can always play defense. The Rockets have an offensive rating of 121.2 (1st). They have to play harder than the Rockets and play like the team that wants this game more. They also need to carry that aggressiveness through all 4 quarters with no let up. They also need to stay focused on taking good shots and making them. They have to keep their focus on playing team ball.

Depth – The Celtics need to lean on their depth for this game. It is the second of back to back games and so they will need the reserves to play well to take some of the pressure off of the starters. X-FactorsBack to Back Road Game – The Celtics are on the road where they are 1-1 so far, losing to Detroit on opening night and beating the Magic on Monday. The Celtics are playing on the second night of back to back games while the Rockets are at home and rested. The Celtics had to travel, stay in a hotel, play in front of a hostile crowd and on an unfamiliar court while the Rockets should get a boost from being on their home court. They need to shake off the distractions of playing on the road and stay focused on playing team ball.

Coaching – The Rockets are led by former Celtics coach Ime Udoka, who left Boston under less than desirable circumstances. He was suspended for violating team rules and assistant coach Joe Mazzulla was made interim coach. Eventually, Udoka was officially released and Mazzulla was made head coach. I am sure that Udoka would love nothing more than to once again beat the team that let him go after he led that team to the Finals. And, Joe just wants to win every single game no matter who the opposing coach is. Officiating – Officiating is always an x-factor in every game. Every crew officiates differently. Some call it tight, others let them play. The Celtics need to adjust to how the refs are calling the game and not allow bad calls or no calls to take away their focus from playing the game. The Celtics also have to be aware of the new points of emphasis for this season and try to avoid off‑arm push‑offs, reckless closeouts, delays before free throws illegal screens and especially flopping. Paul George was already fined for a flop in the first game and there have been several other flopping calls as well.

#2928. Jim Cramer says these six fashion stocks are buys beyond the AI trade

CNBC's Jim Cramer highlighted six fashion and apparel stocks on Monday for investors looking for alternatives to the struggling AI trade.

While technology stocks have come under pressure in recent weeks, consumer stocks have been resilient. The SPDR S&P Retail ETF (XRT) gained 10% this quarter, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK) fell 11%. Cramer said falling interest rates could provide an additional boost to apparel companies heading into the holiday shopping season.

"Ralph Lauren, Tapestry, Levi's, VF Corp, Kontoor Brands and Reformation are some of the fashion stocks that we think look best right now," the "Mad Money" host said.

Ralph Lauren remains Cramer's favorite apparel stock, thanks to its consistent growth under CEO Patrice Louvet. The company has continued gaining momentum across women's apparel, accessories and outerwear, and has been strengthening its international presence, particularly in Asia. Although the stock pulled back in August and September, it has since recovered, and Cramer is optimistic ahead of Thursday morning's earnings report.

Tapestry, the parent of Coach and Kate Spade, also reports Thursday. Cramer likes Coach's position in the accessible luxury market, particularly its popularity among younger female consumers. However, shares have fallen 20% since the company's August earnings report, when guidance failed to impress investors following a massive multiyear rally. "I hope this Thursday's report can represent the start of a comeback for Tapestry," he said.

Levi Strauss is another potential turnaround story. Shares fell below $20 following disappointing earnings a few weeks ago, but CEO Michelle Gass told Cramer that the company had moved quickly to address inventory shortages in popular styles. The stock has since rebounded more than 20% from its post-earnings low, though Cramer still considers it inexpensive at roughly 14 times earnings, with a 2.8% dividend yield. "I think this is a good option to play the broader strength in denim that we keep hearing about," he said.

VF Corp, which owns The North Face, Vans and Timberland, is showing signs of improvement after years of struggles, particularly at Vans. Cramer pointed to encouraging results from a recent Piper Sandler teen survey and a strong quarterly report as evidence that the sneaker brand's turnaround may be gaining traction. Shares have risen roughly 14% since he recommended the stock about two weeks ago.

Kontoor Brands offers another opportunity tied to denim and corporate restructuring. The company plans to sell its Lee brand for up to $1 billion, allowing it to focus on Wrangler and outdoor apparel maker Helly Hansen. Cramer expects the sale to be followed by substantial share repurchases and said the remaining businesses have room to grow. Shares trade at roughly 14 times earnings and offer a dividend yield near 3%.

Cramer's more speculative pick is Reformation. The women's fashion brand initially struggled after its IPO in late July, but Cramer said it "has great growth, it's profitable, and it has a differentiated shopping experience with a technology kicker." Cramer highlighted the stock in late September; shares surged more than 31% in October.

#2922. Anthropic reports $17 billion in Q3 revenue, purchase commitments of $895.4 billion in revised S-1

Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business.

The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.

Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering. The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year.

During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.

The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.

As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds, and quarterly reports from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns.

The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows, causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.

In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."

Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year.

"As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing.

The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut.

Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors. The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives.

"We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing.

#2921. JJ Redick is again preaching patience while also acknowledging the need for improvement

Although not always the case, most good NBA teams offer indications of their quality quite early in the season. Through seven games, the Los Angeles Lakers have done precisely that (partly thanks to a friendly schedule). They're fourth in the West at 5-2 with the league's third-ranked offense, 18th-ranked defense and seventh-best net rating (plus-7.5), per Cleaning the Glass.

Despite a team's general quality typically revealing — or, sometimes, merely previewing — itself early into the year, the specifics require much more time crystallize. Rotations and schematics change. Players progress or regress. Injuries and trades crop up. Other teams adapt. For any team with lofty end-of-season aspirations, building toward those goals is a long-term process, including the 2026-27 Lakers.

"We want to become a great team. You don't become a great team in six games. We want to become a great team after 82 games and have a chance to go compete for a championship in April and May and June. It's a process to get there," Redick told reporters following Friday's loss to the Golden State Warriors. "We are going to be patient. There's also, along with patience, doing what you're supposed to do. I think as we play more games together, we do more walkthroughs together, we do more film together, we do more practice together, that will all get better."

After overhauling much of the rotation in free agency, led by three new starters, the Lakers will take some time before reaching their final form. Redick understands that and has repeatedly harped on this group's need for a lengthy runway to gel.

Fortunately, the schedule remains fairly light over the next few weeks — a road game against the Detroit Pistons on Sunday should test them, however — even if it includes plenty of postseason hopefuls. A month-long stretch from late November to late December featuring matchups with the San Antonio Spurs, Indiana Pacers Philadelphia 76ers, Houston Rockets (twice), Denver Nuggets (twice) and Minnesota Timberwolves (twice) should give Los Angeles some important insights about its state at that time.

That's still many weeks away, though, so the Lakers will hope all the games, walkthroughs, film sessions and practices they share together before then accelerates their path toward becoming the great team they're aiming to be.

#2916. Intel foundry push faces critical test after stock's 45% plunge in October

As Intel comes off its steepest stock drop since the 1970s due to a worsening outlook for the PC market, the chipmaker is facing intensifying pressure to get its flailing foundry business off the ground.

It's been an elusive task for Intel. The company has spent half a decade, and a good chunk of its $108 billion in capital expenditures over that stretch, trying to challenge Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. But it still has no marquee customer for its most advanced chips and is primarily manufacturing chips for its own products.

Wall Street is losing patience. After the U.S. government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, the stock started to shoot up, ultimately rising sixfold over 10 months before peaking in June. Intel was finally finding its niche in the artificial intelligence boom, delivering central processors used for agentic AI, while optimism simultaneously grew over its fab aspirations.

Intel's story took a dramatic turn for the worse on Thursday, when the company said revenue this quarter will be between $1 billion and $2 billion shy of analysts' estimates as the PC market continues to suffer from soaring costs for memory and other components. Intel still counts on its PC segment for roughly half of its revenue, and consumers are increasingly choosing not to upgrade.

The stock plummeted 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s, capping off a 45% plunge in October, the steepest monthly drop on record, according to FactSet. It's down another 8% in Monday trading.

Intel's investments in the future are supposed to be paying off. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said he sees the global market for server processors increasing as much as five times over the next five years to about $200 billion. Intel's data center business recorded 78% growth in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.3 billion.

However, Intel said it can't make enough chips to fill demand, pointing to industrywide supply constraints for wafers, substrates and memory, many of the same factors hurting PC sales.

That's forcing Tan to make some hard choices. In response to the capacity shortage, Intel said it's shifting some Oregon factory capacity away from making wafers for its advanced 18A chips to make more wafers on an older node, known as Intel 3, used for its data center products.Intel is counting on 18A to attract outside foundry customers, so the shift in resources could complicate that effort. David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who previously spent almost three decades on Intel's board, said the latest moves are hardly welcoming to prospective foundry customers.

"They're concerned that if Intel doesn't actually have excess capacity beyond its own demand, that they're just not a very credible supplier," Yoffie said. If it doesn't find a large-scale foundry customer within a year, "then the stress on Intel's economics are going to start to show even more dramatically," he said.

An Intel spokesperson said in a statement that "customer confidence in Intel Foundry is built on execution."

"We're delivering against our technology roadmap, demonstrating strong performance with 18A and progress on 14A," the spokesperson said, referring to the company's forthcoming chips. "We continue to see strong engagement with customers and remain focused on earning their business through consistent execution."

Intel is best known for its industry-leading central processing units, or CPUs. Graphics processing units from Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices ruled the early AI boom because they excel at handling large workloads for training models and inference for chatbots, while CPUs like Intel's are crucial for running the virtual machines used by agentic apps like Meta's Muse.

As one of the only companies in the world capable of manufacturing and packaging the advanced chips it needs for its own products, Intel has "more control over their destiny" than most chipmakers, Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview.

"If you don't have enough capacity, you leave revenue and money on the table," Klein said.

Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, who was ousted in late 2024, spent his four-year tenure at the company aggressively pursuing foundry investments to catch up after delays on its 7- and 10-nanometer technologies, advanced process nodes that aim to fit more transistors on each chip.

Tan has taken a more cautious approach, limiting spending until customer demand is locked in. He said on Thursday that "a couple customers" would be announced in the coming two quarters.

Intel's 18A chips, for its own use, are in high-volume production out of Arizona, with a second fab in the works. A first structural truss was just installed at Intel's new Ohio facility, although the project is nearly five years behind schedule.

Another roadblock to getting new customers, Yoffie said, is that chipmakers like Broadcom and Qualcomm may hesitate to manufacture chips at a company that's also a competitor on the product side.

"The right solution is for Intel to spin off the foundry business," Yoffie said, calling it "not only the best solution, but maybe the only solution."

AMD reports third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday.

Yoffie said the U.S. needs Intel to succeed.

"Ultimately, TSMC can only create maybe 20-25% of their global capacity in the United States and that will still take several years," he said. "If we have no American foundry and we run into any number of geopolitical problems, supply chain problems like we had under Covid, that is going to be bad for the country and bad for the American semiconductor industry."

#2912. Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar

Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management.

The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year.

It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients.

"Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like."

Stablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours.

As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash.

"Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution."

"This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently."

Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments.

The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD.

RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion.

RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets.

Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline.

Correction: A previous headline misspelled RLUSD.

#2908. Supreme Court rejects DOJ's bid to block California from counting disputed ballots

The Supreme Court, in an order Monday evening, denied the Department of Justice's last-minute request to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from about 20,000 voters who it suggested may not be U.S. citizens.

The one-sentence order came hours after the DOJ sought the injunction, and on the eve of Election Day.

The Supreme Court did not explain its reason for the denial, and it did not note any dissents. The order came after Justice Elena Kagan presented the DOJ's request to the full court, which includes three appointees of President Donald Trump.

The swift ruling was the latest courtroom blow to the Trump administration, which is engaged in multiple other legal fights related to the midterm elections.

Those contests will determine which political party holds majorities in the House and Senate. Pollsters and analysts widely predict Democrats will make significant gains.

On Sunday, a federal judge dismissed a DOJ lawsuit that sought to block Alaska election officials from immediately certifying the result of the U.S. Senate election there if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses that race by a margin that could be attributable to voter confusion about another candidate with his name.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta told CNBC that Monday's denial by the Supreme Court was "completely appropriate, very expected."

"This was a Hail Mary. It was baseless," Bonta said in a phone interview. "And the U.S. Supreme Court's response showed just how baseless it was."

The attorney general noted both the speed of the Supreme Court's order and the fact that it was issued without the court first asking California to respond to the DOJ's request.

"That is very rare," Bonta said, adding that, "We haven't seen this type of order where they didn't even ask for a response since 2018."

The DOJ's application to the Supreme Court came three days after the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals rejected the department's attempt to overturn a federal district court judge's ruling that allowed the California ballots to be counted.

That same day, another federal district judge in a separate case in California barred DOJ from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution for refusing to stop processing ballots or resisting other demands.

During a hearing Monday in that second case, a DOJ lawyer admitted to Judge Trina Thompson that the lists of purported noncitizens on California's voter rolls had a "high error rate," MS NOW reported. But that lawyer also argued the errors are evidence of why election officials need to examine those rolls and make sure that everyone on them is a U.S. citizen.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer, in his application Monday morning asking the Supreme Court to enjoin counting of the mail ballots, said, "In this case, this Office has been informed that the United States has identified more than 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California based on publicly available information at the time that information was received, but who, in the United States' view, are likely not U.S. citizens."

Sauer said "the United States is likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal" of the lower court ruling denying the DOJ's request.

"The district court concluded that the United States lacks Article III standing to bring this suit, but the United States suffers a judicially cognizable 'injury to its sovereignty' from the 'violation of its laws,'" Sauer said in the petition.

"Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back."

The DOJ sued California on Oct. 15 in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles. The complaint sought to prevent state election officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined."

The DOJ previously gave Los Angeles County officials a thumb drive containing names of voters the department suggested could be noncitizens, who by law are barred from voting in federal elections.

Last Wednesday, Judge David Carter denied the DOJ's request that he order California officials to set aside mail ballots from alleged noncitizens named on a list prepared by the Department of Homeland Security, and not count their votes until their citizenship is confirmed.

"This case is about the right of every American citizen to vote in a free and fair election," Carter said in his ruling.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," Carter wrote.

"In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too."

The DOJ then appealed that ruling to the 9th Circuit. A three-judge panel on that court denied the appeal in a 2-1 ruling on Friday

"There is a material risk that granting the United States its requested relief would result in disenfranchisement," said the ruling by the majority, Circuit Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez. Bennett was appointed by Trump, and Sanchez was appointed by former President Joe Biden.

"I think we're continuing to work at it," Payton said. "There were some glimpses yesterday. There were also some looks yesterday that we felt could have been blocked better. We'll continue to work on that, and that's something that we definitely feel like there'll be improvement with."

Until yesterday, I would have disagreed with him. Why? Because of his unwavering commitment to J.K. Dobbins up until halftime on Sunday. I have nothing against Dobbins and appreciated his time in Denver, but its clear he is missing something this year. Something that Jonah Coleman seemed to have.

Payton finally saw it too and the result was a second half emergence of Coleman as a featured back for Denver. He was a big part of their comeback and why I think Payton might be right that the run game might be improving greatly in the coming weeks.

#2905. Michael Carrick looking to rekindle some Old Trafford historical magic against AS Roma to save job

Manchester United welcome AS Roma to Old Trafford in the Champions League tonight.

The Red Devils have three points from a possible nine and desperately need a victory tonight to get their Champions League campaign back on track.

This is due to a 0-2 loss to Atlético Madrid and a 1-4 loss to 1907 Como a couple of weeks ago.

Here are three storylines to get the blood racing.

United have enjoyed some big nights against AS Roma in recent years.

They have won five out of eight matches, losing two and drawing one.

The most famous would be the 7-1 victory over the Romans in 2007, which saw United qualify for the Champions League semi-final.

The now manager, Michael Carrick, was playing in that match and scored two spectacular strikes.

In April 2021, they also took apart the Italian side 6-2 in the Europa League semi-final.

United have played 43 times against Serie A sides, including many famous ties against the likes of Juventus, AC Milan and Inter Milan over the years.

There have been 43 matches between the sides, with United coming out on top 21 times.

There have also been seven draws and 15 defeats for the English side.

The last Italian side to visit Old Trafford was Atalanta, as United won 3-2 in dramatic fashion in 2021 when Cristiano Ronaldo won the match in the dying embers in front of the Stretford End.

Defeats against Atlético and Como were bad enough, but the Reds also set an unwanted record.

"Man United became the first team in UEFA history to concede in the first two minutes of back-to-back major European matches."

They will certainly not want to become the only team to do it three times in a row.
