#2904. CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Nvidia's humanoid push relies on China-made robot hands

Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.

Chinese robot companies still underpin many U.S. tech endeavors, especially when it comes to the pain point of robotic hands. Who is one of the latest on Nvidia's radar?

In just a few months, Nvidia has showcased two humanoid robot training packages: one with mechanical hands from Sharpa, and another with hands from Wuji.

Pan Yunzhe founded Wuji in 2019, eventually moving much of the team to Shenzhen and drawing backers such as Ant Group, HSG and Future Capital, according to PitchBook. A demo video last week claimed a Wuji Hand 2 could autonomously spin a pen, despite interference.

The Wuji Hand 2 made it onto a slide Oct. 21 behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as he told a crowd in Berlin about a new humanoid hardware system for training the robots on Nvidia software. The robot body comes from Agile Robots, which has offices in Germany, China and the U.S.

"It will be the flywheel by which we can accelerate development of robotics," Huang said of the hardware system, called Agile One SN. Agile Robots announced the system, which uses Nvidia's Isaac robotics software and Jetson Thor computing platform.

Research institutions, such as Stanford and ETH Zurich, can likely start using the Agile One SN system in early 2027, according to Nvidia.

Stanford and ETH Zurich were also among the institutions Nvidia named in connection with its first reference humanoid design, announced May 31. That system uses a body from Chinese humanoid company Unitree and mechanical hands from Sharpa. It was scheduled for delivery from late 2026.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether deliveries had begun, or whether the researchers would try both reference robots, or just one.

Sharpa, headquartered in Singapore, was co-founded by David Li, CEO of Shanghai-based lidar company Hesai. Sharpa has said its manufacturing R&D is in Shanghai.

While these are just two of the many robotic hand makers in China — and globally — they've grown so much in prominence that Google DeepMind research lead Keerthana Gopalakrishnan directly compared the two startups in a podcast last month.

Sharpa Wave is a bit stronger than Wuji, which is closer in size to a typical human hand but has the strength of a ten-year-old, she said. It was not clear whether she was testing the Wuji Hand 2 or an earlier version.

In September, humanoid startup JoyIn's Zhu Mingxuan told me she found Wuji's mechanical hands very light and very good at completing tasks, but prone to heating up while doing so. She said Sharpa's performed better, but were far more expensive.

Hardware is limiting humanoid development, and hands are the main challenge, she said. Zhu said she left U.S. humanoid company Figure last year, where she had also worked on models to help humanoid robots mimic human actions.

As China pushes its humanoid industry to develop more core technologies, mechanical hands are one way companies can try to stand out in the robot race.

Consumer electronics company Xiaomi said last week that, by testing its robotic hand in its car factory, it found that most of the tasks it tested required only a specific range of movement.

And in another sign of just how far along the tech may have come in China, Meta has worked with Chinese startup Fourier for a humanoid prototype, The Information reported Oct. 31, citing sources. Neither company immediately responded to a request for comment.

China industrial profits see strongest growth since June

#2903. Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December

Eligible Trump Account holders will begin receiving donated shares of SpaceX stock next month, according to an X post on Friday.

"Robert and I are thrilled that our gift of over 2 million shares of SpaceX stock will be distributed to children's Trump accounts in December!" President and COO Gwynne Shotwell wrote in the post.

The gift from Shotwell and her husband will provide a share apiece to around 2 million Trump Accounts holders ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less, or in ZIP codes with too few residents for a median family income to be reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. These families should receive a notice by Monday, Shotwell wrote on X.

"In a few weeks, an additional gift will be finalized for eligible 11 to 17-year-old children in military families serving overseas, children in foster care, and more children whose MFI is $90,000 or less living in counties near our home in the great state of Texas," she also wrote.

Parents or guardians can check eligibility for the donation through Invest America, a nonprofit advocacy group, and track account activity with the Trump Accounts app.

Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.

Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the U.S. Department of the Treasury.

Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria. In a separate funding announcement in October, Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which may also come via Trump Accounts.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds.

The move to permit stock donations could pave the way for more large-scale philanthropic gifts, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Oct. 8.

On Oct. 29, Bisignano announced his own donation to Trump Accounts for eligible children ages 2 to 8 living in 11234, Bisignano's hometown ZIP code, according to The Bisignano Family Fund.

#2902. Harry Kane hasn’t ruled out playing in Spain, but is happy at Bayern Munich

Harry Kane hasn't ruled out the possibility of playing in Spain someday, but the Bayern Munich striker made it clear that he has no regrets about his journey to Germany.

Kane was asked whether he would have liked to experience Spanish football during his career. The England international admitted that competing in La Liga would have been an appealing opportunity.

"I never really had the chance. Obviously I was at Tottenham a long, long time, and I was happy there, and then when this opportunity came to come to Bayern, it was something I wanted to do straight away," Kane explained (via @iMiaSanMia).

The striker didn't completely close the door on a future move to Spain, either.

"If the opportunity arose at the right time and it was right for me, then for sure, it would have been amazing to play in Spain and play in La Liga and compete against these players," Kane added.

However, any speculation about a potential Spanish adventure needs to be balanced against his satisfaction with life at Bayern.

"Ultimately, everyone's journey leads you to a certain place, and I'm really happy that mine led me to Bayern, because as you've seen, I've been extremely happy here," Kane concluded.

So, while Kane clearly appreciates the appeal of experiencing Spanish football, his comments don't suggest that he is looking for an escape route from Munich. If the right opportunity ever presented itself, he would be open to considering it, but for now, he sounds perfectly content with how his career has unfolded in Germany.

#2900. How to watch Warriors vs. Suns

The Golden State Warriors will look to extend their winning streak to five games when they host the Phoenix Suns on Monday night. The game will be played at 7:00 PM PT in San Francisco and can be watched on NBC Sports Bay Area.

Golden State opened this set of back-to-back games with an impressive 124-112 victory over the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday night. Despite playing without veteran stars Stephen Curry and Draymond Green, who were both held out for rest, the Warriors secured their fourth consecutive win behind a big performance from rookie Yaxel Lendeborg.

After failing to reach double figures in scoring for the first time in his young NBA career against the Los Angeles Lakers on Friday night, Lendeborg bounced back in spectacular fashion. The rookie led all scorers with a career-high 37 points on an efficient 13-of-19 shooting from the field, including 6-of-11 from beyond the arc. His performance marked the most points scored by a Warriors rookie since Curry dropped 42 against the Portland Trail Blazers in 2010.

For years, Golden State's offensive success has largely depended on Curry's brilliance, with the Warriors often needing an unexpected scoring outburst from someone else to help carry the load. However, Lendeborg's emergence as a legitimate offensive threat has given the team another reliable scoring option, easing the burden on Curry and creating a more balanced attack.

One of the biggest beneficiaries has been Brandin Podziemski, who has settled into a complementary role rather than being relied upon as one of the team's primary scoring options. The fourth-year guard has thrived in that role, playing with greater decisiveness while averaging 16.4 points, 5.4 rebounds, and 5.6 assists per game. His ability to contribute in multiple areas has become increasingly valuable as Golden State's new offense continues to take shape.

With Lendeborg providing another dimension to the offense and Podziemski finding his rhythm, the Warriors are beginning to show they have the supporting cast needed to compete at a high level. They'll look to keep that momentum going Monday night against a Phoenix team that beat them just over a week ago behind a 43-point performance from Devin Booker. This time, however, Golden State will look to turn the tables with Curry and Green back in the starting lineup.

Enjoy the game Dub Nation. GO WARRIORS!!!

#2897. OpenAI hires former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for national security role

OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company.

Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position.

He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology.

"National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security.

The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement.

Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine.

At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program.

#2896. AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.

Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming.

Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.

Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms' plans for a $95 billion stock offering, announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off.

Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief.

"Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said.

A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.

The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."

Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%.

"It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."

Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending.

Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to continue.

Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.

S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027.

More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."

Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said.

CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P.

"It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one."

One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.

"There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday.

S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added.

Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.

Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.

"They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers.

"The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."

Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Oracle's investment-grade credit rating is BBB-, according to S&P. A previous version mischaracterized the company's credit rating.

#2893. Trump focuses on Reflecting Pool in final public speech before midterms

President Donald Trump began his final scheduled in-person speech before Tuesday's Election Day with a lengthy disquisition about his efforts to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other sites in Washington.

"Today I'm thrilled to announce the official opening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool," Trump said Monday afternoon in front of the water feature, which was fenced off for months amid a problem-plagued renovation the president had ordered.

The speech, which lasted nearly an hour, was expected to serve as Trump's "closing argument" on the midterms before millions of voters head to the polls to determine which party will control the House and Senate in the next Congress.

But Trump kicked off his remarks with more than 20 minutes of commentary that focused largely on the Reflecting Pool, along with his administration's work on refurbishing other Washington-area monuments and cracking down on crime in the nation's capital.

"The pool is now better and more beautiful than it's ever been before, and we're very proud of it," Trump said, before repeating unfounded claims that vandals were responsible for damaging the pool and delaying repairs.

U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro told a court July 31 that the damage was caused by a contractor's botched installation. Trump lashed out at Pirro over the admission and has continued to claim vandals were to blame.

Trump's first explicit reference to the midterms came around the 23-minute mark.

"As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime," Trump said.

"The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history," he said.

He touted his administration's record and lashed out at some Democratic candidates by name, including Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. He also repeated his controversial claim that if Republicans win, "everybody is going to get $5,000."

"We have to keep our Congress strong, free," Trump said. "America is ready to go. They're ready to vote. I hope they're ready to do the right thing."

But Trump, as he has done in other recent remarks, seemed to acknowledge that Democrats had an advantage — at least when looking to historical trends that show the president's party tends to underperform in midterm elections.

"For some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms. But we gave this a very strong shot," he said.

Later in the speech, Trump continued discussing the pool, as well as his push to erect a massive triumphal arch in Washington and his plans to build a promenade along the Potomac River.

He also said the government planned to build a "National Garden of American Heroes," comprising "250 to 500 great American heroes in statue form." And he talked about ongoing efforts to renovate a public golf course in Washington that is subject to legal challenges.

#2891. Te’Cory Couch played like wily veteran for Bills in win over Ravens

One of the biggest individual revelations from the Buffalo Bills' win over the Ravens in Week 8 was the stellar play of Te'Cory Couch, the nickel corner signed from the practice squad before this contest who thrived in slot throughout.

He was a component of a much more connected, in-sync back seven that communicated significantly better than the vast majority of Buffalo's first six contests, particularly in zone and when the Ravens attempted to confuse man-to-man assignments with motions and stacked formations.

While I'm on the topic of pre-snap movement and bunch formations, check this first play from Couch that exemplified his discipline and the improved passing off in zone from Buffalo's linebackers and defensive backs.

At the snap, you'll notice Rashod Bateman in motion. With that motion, Baltimore wanted to widen the path of his vertical route in case Davison Igbinosun jumped the intermediate out-breaker run by Mark Andrews.

The route concept also featured Zay Flowers working across the middle underneath, and it would've been easy for Couch — aligned in the slot near the bottom of the screen — to jump that slant.

Watch as he passed off Flowers to Terrel Bernard before sinking to occupy the area of Andrews' out-breaker:

Absolutely textbook. Couple that with Igbinosun staying home in his deep outside fourth of the field, and there was simply nowhere to throw the football.

Now, sure — that play was a simple example of everyone staying true to their zones, but oftentimes offenses bank on one back seven player getting greedy or taking one false step … and that's when a pass-catching option comes open.

Fine dedication to his zone from Couch there, especially for someone with very little experience.

Couch manned up well too, even against Flowers on a few occasions.

Here, the Bills were in straight-up man across the board, and notice how Couch raised his arm before the snap. I can't say for sure what that indicated, but I love that he took charge on the communication front, even if it was in visual form.

The Ravens snapped the ball with motion, and attempted to cause natural picks at the bottom of the screen with Andrews, Bateman, and Flowers.

Couch got physical with Flowers during the allowed five yards beyond the of scrimmage before releasing his hands and running with him as the lightning-quick separator ran a deep over across the field:

This next play from Couch was low-key outstanding, and it served as a fine demonstration of how abruptly defenders must adjust pre and post snap.

A split second before the snap, the Ravens sent Andrews in motion toward the sideline, which widened Couch as the ball reached the quarterback in the shotgun.

Because his assignment was the short zone underneath on his side of the field, Couch got a shove on Bateman to disrupt his route timing before turning his attention into the backfield. Notice how quickly he recognized screen, avoided a block from an offensive lineman, and got a hand on Justice Hill to trip him before the veteran back could flip on the afterburners:

With Deone Walker bowled over by two Ravens blockers, the 5'10", 185-pounder was the only Bills defender still standing within 10-15 yards of Hill when he caught the football.

Outstanding play from the 27-year-old defensive back.

Here, in the low red zone, Couch, Damar Hamlin, and Igbinosun avoided collisions at the top of the screen and Couch didn't vacate keeping inside leverage on the inside receiver as Flowers and Bateman approached the goal line:

He then quickly and effortlessly flipped his hips to follow Flowers across the back of the end zone:

Very calm rep there from Couch again, when a lot of inexperienced defensive backs would've panicked or, more simply, not had enough juice to stay with the speedy Flowers across the field.

This would not be a proper film session on an scrappy, upstart defensive back if it did not feature an open-field tackle.

Nothing schematically intricate here… just Couch (near the bottom of the screen) planting and driving from his short zone to stick Andrews before he could turn up field to move the chains:

Yes, of course… the Ravens were massively short-handed at the game's most vital position against the Bills. But there's no doubting Buffalo's secondary played much more like a cohesive unit against Baltimore than at any stage of the past month, if not the entire season to date.

#2890. Spurs' five-game winning streak sets them apart from rest of NBA

The Spurs' 119-97 victory over Utah at the Frost Bank Center on Monday night hiked their winning streak to five games and gave them six different winning streaks of five-plus games over the last two seasons, most of any NBA team.

For the players who survived the back-to-back 22-win seasons in 2022-23 and 2023-24, it's quite an achievement.

"It's just a testament to pounding the rock," eighth-year forward Keldon Johnson said after finishing with 15 points and seven rebounds, both season highs for the reigning NBA Sixth Man of the Year.

"We continued to pound the rock (in those lean years). We continued to stay with it, and the tide turned. We just got to continue to build on those habits we have started. And every day keep coming in and putting our time in, putting that effort in, locking in and getting better each and every day."

Along those lines, Johnson believes the defending Western Conference champions have a long way to go until they hit their stride this season.

"Not comforting at all," Johnson said of the winning streak. "It's a long season, 82 games. We got to continue to get better. Do I feel as though we're playing to our standards? At times, yes. But do I feel like we could do better? Yes. I feel like we have a lot of room for improvement. I feel like we have not yet played our best brand of basketball and we just got to continue to stack days."

New York and Oklahoma City each have five different winning streaks of five-plus games over the last two seasons to rank second behind the Spurs, according to Elias Sports.

#2889. Australia hikes rates to 18-year high to fight inflation

Australia's central bank raised its benchmark cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since November 2008.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's move was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year.

In its statement, the RBA said that the move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold.

This also comes as the country continues to grapple with high inflation, with the consumer price index rising 4.3% in September, up from 4% in August and marking its highest level since March.

The central bank also said inflation is now expected to "remain elevated through much of 2027," and not expected to fall back into its 2%-3% target range till late 2027, three quarters later than previously forecast.

This was due to higher fuel and other commodity prices, in addition to factors including AI-related investment, which is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, the RBA said.

In its September decision, RBA governor Michelle Bullock said that inflation is "too high," driven by higher oil prices from the Iran War and stronger domestic spending.

"We're seeing signs that upside risks to inflation are materializing," she added, saying that additional hikes will come "if that's what's needed to get inflation down."

Growth has slowed in the first two quarters of 2026. Australia's GDP rose 2.1% in the June quarter compared to a year earlier, down from 2.5% in the March quarter.

The RBA is trying to bring inflation back under control while higher borrowing costs and cost-of-living pressures weigh on households and activity.

When asked if she sees a recession for Australia, Bullock said that it is "not our base case at the moment."

#2887. 2026 NFL Trade Deadline Preview: Jonathan Taylor, Brian Thomas Jr. headline top trade candidates

The NFL trade deadline is next Tuesday, and several big dominoes have already fallen. The Bears went all in on their current window by trading two first-round picks for Jeffery Simmons. The Colts, meanwhile, are calling it quits on 2026 and sent DeForest Buckner to San Francisco and Quenton Nelson to Seattle. I've listed some of the biggest names still on the trade block. The list is loosely ordered by how likely I think a player is to be moved.

The Colts are tearing apart their roster and selling every scrap to the highest bidder. Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner have already been moved. Taylor could be next. His numbers this year are universally down. He's averaging fewer rush yards over expected and yards after contact. His breakaway way is also down. I wouldn't really take those as indications of anything other than the sorry state of the Colts' offense. Taylor was sixth in the league in YAC per carry while comfortably leading the league in rush attempts when the offense was humming last year.

The Seahawks and Broncos are two of the most common destinations for Taylor via recent rumors. Both teams could desperately use an infusion of run-game talent, but help is already on the way. Jonah Coleman returned to the lineup in Week 7 and then broke out in Week 8 with 104 total yards and a touchdown. The Broncos have also invested heavily in the running back position with Coleman and RJ Harvey over the past two years. They even brought J.K. Dobbins back on a two-year deal in the offseason. The Seahawks, on the other hand, spent a first-round pick on a running back six months ago. Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet are both healthy after stints on injured reserve.

The Vikings are the holy grail of landing spots. To their own detriment, they have money-balled their backfield over the past few years, settling for another round of Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason in 2026. The Kyler Murray experiment has failed, but Minnesota's defense has dragged the dilapidated offense to a 6-1 record. Taylor would round out the team's identity as an old-school, physical title contender. The 49ers paid second, third, fourth, and fifth-round picks to land Christian McCaffrey and the Colts are reportedly looking for a similar haul. Fortunately for Minnesota, they have an extra third-round pick and two extra picks in the fifth in next year's draft.

The Colts have not been able to get Downs going in the absence of Alec Pierce and he's set to hit free agency in the spring. As Jakob Sanderson points out, Downs would be a great fit for the Chiefs.

To his point about Downs' ability to beat man coverage, Xavier Worthy leads the Chiefs in PFF receiving grade versus man coverage at 72.1. Downs is 17th in the NFL at 83.4. After throwing in the towel on 2026, there's no reason for the Colts not to send Downs to a team that can make better use of his skills.

Ian Rapoport has already implied that this deal might be in the works.

However, more recent reports out of LA suggest that the 0-7 Chargers are not selling, despite their season being the most over a season has ever been. Mack is several years removed from his prime. He posted 17 sacks in 2023 and has managed 14.5 sacks in 35 subsequent games. On the other hand, he's still a solid option, and the ceiling might be there for another team to rediscover. It's hard to believe the Chargers won't even listen to offers from a team like Chicago or Buffalo. The Bills have a penchant for splashy pass-rush acquisitions and their defense currently ranks 26th in EPA per dropback allowed

Thomas Jr. got back on the board with a touchdown in Week 8, but it was his only catch of the day. He has caught more than one pass in just three games this year and has yet to reach four receptions in a week. His route rate also sits at a paltry 54 percent. A former first-round pick with a 1,300-yard season on his resume is barely on the field for half of his offense's passing plays. It's time for both sides to part ways. Even though that breakout season was all the way back in 2024, GM James Gladstone's phone is going to blow up with BTJ inquiries this week. The Chiefs have already been linked to him, and if they can get the 2024 version of Thomas Jr., we might just see a return of the Patrick Mahomes deep ball.

The Rams, 49ers, and Seahawks have all been rumored as potential landing spots. While all three need another starting wide receiver, they're also teams that care about run-blocking and winning hard-fought passes over the middle of the field, something BTJ has struggled with for years.

For my money, the Commanders are a far more interesting option. Since Brian Thomas Jr. entered the league, Terry McLaurin is one of his closest comparable players by several metrics.

They are both boundary field-stretchers who have earned targets at a high clip despite their downfield roles. McLaurin is done for the year with a knee injury, but the Commanders are still in the playoff hunt. BTJ also caught passes from Jayden Daniels at LSU, hopefully creating more chemistry between the two than BTJ ever developed with Trevor Lawrence.

The Eagles have had a will-they-won't-they relationship with Goedert for years. It's time to pull the plug. He's on an expiring contract and the team spent a Day Two pick on Eli Stowers in April. Stowers recently returned to the lineup and popped for 53 yards on three catches in Week 8. The rookie needs more reps to develop as a pass-catcher and a blocker, while Goedert, at 31 years old, is likely playing in his final games as an Eagle. The Broncos and Bucs are contending teams that have gotten next to nothing from their veteran tight ends this year. Both could be on the shortlist of landing spots for Goedert.

Dickerson has missed most of the 2026 season while on injured reserve. He's nearing the end of his 21-day practice window, so he should be on the active roster and able to play in Week 9. It seems like he's ready to be done with the Eagles.

Philly restructured Dickerson's deal this offseason to make more of his money incentive-based. They also took off the final season of his four-year deal entirely. His contract is now more attractive to other teams, and the cap maneuvers certainly didn't strengthen the relationship between Dickerson and the front office. This is a move where the split is likely in the best interest of both parties. The Packers and Vikings have dealt with interior offensive line injuries and could use some more firepower in the trenches as they fight for NFC North supremacy.

Cornerback Riq Woolen is the final name to watch for the Eagles. They signed him to a one-year, prove-it deal in the offseason. He has played solid football for the Birds, starting all seven games with six pass breakups and a forced fumble. There's simply no need for a 2-6 Eagles team to hold on to his expiring deal. The Panthers and Lions are among several contenders who should be in the market for a starting cornerback ahead of the deadline.

Pollard is playing like a man who wants to get traded (complimentary). He has 46 carries for 146 yards and five touchdowns over his past two games. The breakout has been appreciated by Titans fans, but it shouldn't factor into the team's long-term plans. Pollard is 29 years old and is set to become a free agent at the end of the season. Even in his two breakout games, the Titans failed to bring home a win. Pollard isn't a game-changing back like Jonathan Taylor, but he brings an element of stability to a backfield that a few contenders might want. The most obvious landing spot is Green Bay. Josh Jacobs' availability is once again in question after more allegations of domestic violence were uncovered. The league is currently looking into them, though it's unclear if a suspension will come anytime soon. If the Packers want some insurance for the remainder of the year, Pollard could be had for a reasonable price.

If the Titans want to keep their ground game intact to help Cam Ward's development, Tyjae Spears could be on the block. Spears is also in a contract year and his role has dwindled in his fourth season. Rookie Nick Singleton could also be developed into Spears' replacement. Spears needs to get healthy before a team will scoop him up, but he is at least worth a look for a team that wants a third-down specialist.

This section is going to be a catch-all for veteran wideouts who are doing absolutely nothing right now but apparently have some interest on the trade market. That includes Ridley, Jerry Jeudy, and Hollywood Brown. Not a single one of them is averaging even one yard per route, which is already a pretty dismal mark. The Browns are somehow contenders, so even with their wealth of young pass-catchers, they may not be that inclined to trade away receiver depth.

The Titans just played in an overtime thriller with the Bengals that featured 79 total points and arguably the best performance of Cam Ward's career. Ridley caught one pass. He averaged 1.9 YPRR in 2025 and 2024 and posted back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons before missing most of last year with an injury. He's probably on his way out of the league, but maybe the 31-year-old has a little more in the tank and just needs to land in a better offensive environment.

Like Ridley, Brown shouldn't cost much to acquire. He's little more than a depth option at this point in his career, but a team with injury issues at wideout like the Broncos could value his experience and straight-line speed.

Jauan Jennings was originally a perfect fit for this section, but he nixxed a trade back to San Francisco, preferring to stay with the Vikings.

Barring a change of heart, he'll remain in Minnesota.

The Cardinals have already signaled the end of their veteran quarterback. Brissett was benched for Gardner Minshew last week and Day Two rookie Carson Beck is waiting for his turn to take the field. Brissett hasn't been awful this year. He's 24th in EPA per play and 21st in completion percent over expected, but it's not a profile most teams care to trade for. The Ravens, however, are in a unique spot. They're 4-4 and only two games back from the Steelers in the AFC North race. They're also down to their third-string quarterback after Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley suffered long-term injuries in Week 8. If they want any shot at pursuing a playoff bid, they need to make an addition at quarterback. Brissett is likely the best option available, and he shouldn't cost them much.

The Ravens could also pursue one of the Bears' backups. Baltimore OC Declan Doyle coached both Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent last year, meaning they have enough familiarity with his scheme to start as soon as Week 10.

Sweat leaked to reporters throughout the offseason that he was unhappy with life in Arizona. The trade rumors then started to swirl and Sweat spent the entire training camp on the PUP list, likely hoping the Cardinals would move him before the start of the year. Arizona GM Monti Ossenfort was steadfast in his refusal to trade Sweat, but the rumor mill is churning once again now that the 3-5 Cardinals are in last place in the NFC West. Sweat has three sacks on 15 pressures in what looks like a down year, but it's understandable to expect his numbers to improve if he gets out of Arizona. With Sweat simply not wanting to play for the Cardinals anymore, moving him looks like a no-brainer.

Things are totally normal for the Cardinals right now.

Baker reportedly hasn't requested a trade, though he hasn't told the Cardinals he would refuse a deal either. This move would be a tougher sell for the franchise. He has arguably been the face of their defense for the past decade and is still playing at a high level. Baker has one interception, one forced fumble, and 3.5 sacks through eight games. He's the only safety with more than two sacks.

The Bills are again an interesting landing spot. Their secondary is arguably a bigger issue than their pass-rush, and Baker would give the team a dynamic safety at a time when that archetype has become extremely coveted.

The Jets would love to be sellers at the deadline, but their biggest names are largely on offense, and it's hard to justify getting rid of young weapons that a rookie quarterback will likely be throwing to next year. Instead, it makes more sense to see what they can get for players on the other side of the ball.

McDonald's role has plummeted with the addition of David Bailey this year. His snap share is below 50 percent for the first time since his rookie season and he has made just two starts in eight appearances. McDonald's 14.8 percent pass-rush win-rate, as charted by PFF, is the 27th-best mark among all EDGE defenders. McDonald isn't the splashiest move a contending team can make, but he's good enough to start for several teams and would make an excellent pass-rush specialist on deeper rosters. The Bengals and Bears could both use McDonald to round out their front seven.

Cousins has been the subject of trade rumors from the moment he took the field in Week 1, but he's playing too well to be moved in the next week. He's ninth in EPA and second in passing touchdowns. At 4-4, the Raiders are still very live in the hunt for a playoff spot. They're even still in the mix to win the AFC West. Maybe if Cousins implodes versus the 49ers and gets benched mid-game a move could be on the table, but that seems far-fetched at this point.

Barkley told reporters that the team informed him he will not be traded, so this one is off the table unless someone shows up to Howie Roseman with an offer he can't refuse.

With Jonathan Taylor being made far more available by the Colts, it's hard to imagine a team going out of their way to pursue Barkley. Denver and Minnesota would both be interesting landing spots, but Barkley escaping the Eagles' fledgling offense is a pipe dream at this point.

#2886. Trail Blazers Improve to 5-1 With Impressive Comeback Win Over Nuggets

The Portland Trail Blazers have moved to 5-1 on the season, including 4-0 on the road, after overcoming a 12-point first-quarter deficit and an eight-point halftime deficit in a 118-110 victory over the Denver Nuggets on Monday night.

Portland trailed for most of the first three quarters before Jrue Holiday gave the Blazers their first lead late in the third period. Denver briefly reclaimed the advantage, but Portland continued to fight and eventually took control down the stretch.

A 9-2 run in the fourth quarter helped the Blazers establish momentum and build an advantage that ultimately proved to be the difference. Denver did fight back to get within three points in the final minutes, but Toumani Camara hit a huge corner 3-pointer with just over a minute remaining to help seal the victory.

Deni Avdija was phenomenal in this game, continuing to step up in Ja Morant's absence. He finished with 28 points and five assists, leading the way offensively for Portland and providing a consistent scoring presence throughout the night.

Damian Lillard added 20 points, giving the Blazers another dynamic perimeter scoring option. Donovan Clingan had a massive game in the paint, finishing with 17 points, 18 rebounds and four blocks while making his presence felt on both ends of the floor.

Holiday was another player who stepped up in the absence of Morant, nearly recording a triple-double with 17 points, 10 assists and eight rebounds. His ability to facilitate the offense while also contributing as a scorer and rebounder was critical to Portland's success.

For Denver, Jamal Murray had a strong performance with 35 points, while Nikola Jokic finished with 26 points, nine rebounds and eight assists. While those are still impressive numbers, it's a relatively average performance by Jokic's standards, and the Blazers did a good job limiting his overall impact.

Both inside and out, Portland found ways to control this game, especially in the second half. The Blazers dominated on the glass, grabbing 21 offensive rebounds compared to Denver's nine, creating additional second-chance opportunities throughout the night.

Portland also connected on 15 3-pointers compared to just nine for Denver, showcasing the team's ability to generate offense in multiple ways.

It was an impressive inside-out performance from the Blazers and arguably one of their best wins of the young season. At 5-1, Portland is quickly establishing itself as one of the teams to beat in the Western Conference.

With a matchup against the Phoenix Suns coming Wednesday, the Blazers will have another opportunity to move to 6-1 and continue climbing the Western Conference standings.

#2885. Yaxel Lendeborg declares himself to be an ethical hooper

Golden State rookie forward Lendebrog really Yaxcelled last night in his 37-point, 4 rebound, 6 assist effort in the Warriors' 124-112 win over the Clippers. After the game, he confessed that he caused himself some grief by briefly pursuing a 40-point night.

I've never been a stat chaser in my life. […] I'm a guy that loves ethical hoops. I'm a guy that loves efficient basketball and I kind of, like, didn't do for that the last 2-3 minutes. […] If it comes to me, it does. If I don't get it, then I wasn't meant to get it that day.

He correctly noted that after he did try to take some threes to get there the Clippers came roaring back late. I will point out, though, that he was being egged on largely by his teammates, specifically De'Anthony Melton, and it's here that I will put a pin in praising the rookie for speaking with a degree of humility and poise that makes him extremely likable.

Melton gets that not many opportunities like a 40-point night come along in a players' career — unless they happen to wind up like LeBron James, etc. — and was, in my mind, simply pushing his teammate to grab an achievement that was in a bucket's reach. I don't see a problem with that, and it's a credit to Melton for being supportive of a rookie teammate rather than antagonistic. Last week, Take Two posted a video of Yaxel being interviewed by some NBA vets (Drew Gooden and Aaron Gordon) and they made it clear that the game is a lot different today than it was when they got started, specifically in the arena of rookie hazing; but, you never know with these things. It's at least a positive to see that his teammates like him as much as the fans have started to.

But getting back to Yaxel's comments after the game. This is some special stuff. He's certainly making strides on the court, but this is, what, his third post-game presser with some memorable commentary? "Lost all respect" for Luka, "try not to wet the bed" after the Luka rematch, and last night? We are not even 10 games into the season!

It sure does feel like we're on the ground floor of… something. Hopefully, something special. At least, that's how it's trending. But "ethical hoops" is an interesting self-tag. The game'll humble you, the notion of ethical hooping is tricky in its own right — it is, effectively, a smarty pants way of saying "not a ball hog" — and players and fans are always looking for a vector for their venom. How he reacts to the jeers and mockery will be the real test of character, because how he's playing all but guarantees a backlash.

In the meantime… my goodness, what a cool rookie.

#2884. Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows

Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.

The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.

A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.

Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week.

"There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."

Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.

Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control.

"If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.

Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year.

Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance.

The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.

Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.

Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.

The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.

But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment.

The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates.

"Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note.

If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge.

— CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.

#2883. We’re about to find out just how different these Giants are with chance to end ugly Eagles history

Now we shall see how different all this really is.

John Harbaugh has already turned the franchise around. Exactly how far around is an ongoing saga and the next stop on the trail is Philadelphia. Where Giants head coaches go and lose.

Tom Coughlin in 2014 and 2015. Ben McAdoo in 2016 and 2017. Pat Shurmur in 2018 and 2019. Joe Judge in 2020 and 2021. Brian Daboll in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.

Make it 13 consecutive losses for the Giants at Lincoln Financial Field. The last time the Giants won in Philly was Oct. 27, 2013, as Josh Brown's five field goals accounted for all their points in a 15-7 victory, with the Eagles losing quarterback Michael Vick to a hamstring injury, forcing Matt Barkley onto the field. The Eagles won the NFC East that season. The Giants finished third.

This Sunday, Harbaugh takes his first-place squad into the Linc, heading in at 4-2-1 fresh off the bye week, with a new quarterback (J.J. McCarthy) providing even more fuel to the fire Harbaugh is stoking. What has already transpired shows the value of a proven head coach exerting his influence on and off the field.

Let us count the Sundays when there might as well be neon lights flashing "This Is Not The Same'' since Harbaugh took over. Beating the Cowboys in Week 1 — the Giants had lost 10 of 11 season openers to Dallas. Winning the first three games of the season at home — they had not accomplished that in 18 years. Winning on the road in Houston as a 10.5-point underdog.

What comes next is not the most severe football challenge but it is an emotional and psychological hurdle, considering what the rival Eagles have inflicted upon the Giants and their fans for more than a decade.

New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy (18) throws a pass under pressure from Houston Texans defensive end Will Anderson Jr. (51) on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Getty Images

Yes, the Eagles at 2-6 are depleted and a mess. Yes, they lost their quarterback, Jalen Hurts, for the remainder of the season. Yes, long gone is their offensive line dominance. Yes, Saquon Barkley is hurting. Yes, the Birds are on a six-game losing streak, their longest skid since 2012, when they dropped eight straight in Andy Reid's 14th and final year as the Eagles' head coach.

Yes, the Giants are actually favored, on the road, by 1.5 points. Given their history in their least-favorite venue, that spread has more to do with the demise of the Eagles than any perceived ascension by the Giants.

"Philly is a very raucous atmosphere to play in, the fans are super similar to our fans up here,'' guard Jon Runyan Jr. told The Post on Monday after practice. "The only difference is they've had something to cheer about the last couple of years recently. I'm hoping the tables turn a little bit. I feel like they have. It's up to us to go down there and take care of business. I think we have what we need. We split with them last year so I think we're building in the right direction.''

Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley celebrates with quarterback Tanner McKee after a touchdown against the Washington Commanders on Nov. 1, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The baker's dozen worth of consecutive losses at the Linc came in all shapes and sizes. There was an assortment of blowouts — 27-0 in 2014, 34-10 in 2021, 38-20 in 2025. There was one playoff matchup, coming after the 2022 season when the Giants were on the way up in Daboll's first year. That was a 38-7 Eagles smackdown. There was a 23-17 overtime loss in 2019 — Carson Wentz to Zach Ertz for the deciding points. There were several down-to-the-wire setbacks — 27-24 in 2017 (thanks to a 61-yard field goal by Jake Elliott) and 25-22 in 2018 — an Elliott field goal with 22 seconds left. There was a 22-21 loss in 2020 when the Giants blew a 21-10 lead in the final 4:38, which included a terrible dropped pass by tight end Evan Engram.

Most recently, there was Eagles 38, Giants 20 in 2025, as Barkley took it 65 yards on his first touch and Jaxson Dart was introduced to a Giants life in Philly.

Harbaugh said he did not know about the long Giants losing streak in Philly and added, "and I probably didn't need to know that,'' before breaking out laughing.

"Yeah,'' he said, "we don't care, we don't care about that.''

None of this, of course, is on Harbaugh, new on the scene. Still, the dreary Giants history at the Linc is a reality he sort of inherits.

New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh looks on during the second quarter against the Houston Texans in Houston, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Getty Images

"I'm trying to think of the analogy because inherit is an interesting word,'' Harbaugh said playfully. "You're sitting there, you're sitting at one of those, I've only seen them in movies where they all go into the lawyer's office and they read the will, right? What would that be akin to a 13-game losing streak that you inherit?''

How about achieving a one-game winning streak in Philly?

Harbaugh was 15-3 coming out of the bye week in his 18 years with the Ravens, and the Eagles are sagging but there are no sure things. Not anywhere. Especially not in Philadelphia. Especially when it comes to the Giants.

#2882. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

The Memphis Tigers took down No. 18 Iowa State in an upset win. The game took place on November 2nd in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, at the Sanford Pentagon. The Tigers won by a score of 80-76, giving them the first upset of the college basketball season. Iowa State was a team that was expected to win with an experienced roster.

GettyFAYETTEVILLE, ARKANSAS – OCTOBER 28: Tylik Weeks #4 of the Memphis Tigers goes up for a dunk in the second half against Billy Richmond III #24 of the Arkansas Razorbacks at Bud Walton Arena on October 28, 2026 in Fayetteville, Arkansas. However, the Tigers' 45% shooting from three negated those points in the paint.

Jayden Reid of Memphis led all scorers with 26 points and shot efficiently. He was 6/11 and made both of his three-point attempts. The big thing was that he was aggressive and got to the line; he shot 14 free throws and made 12 of them. Luke Almodovar added 18 points and 8 rebounds, and Rihards Vavers had 15 points. Those three carried the bulk of the scoring, which is what they needed.

Reid hit a big three down the stretch with 38 seconds left to give them a five-point lead. He also hit two big free throws with 20 seconds left to make it a six-point game. From start to finish, he made big plays and was aggressive. This was a good team win for the Tigers, who showed how good they could be this season.

A win like this could be huge for an unranked Memphis team. This could give them confidence going forward. To win a ranked game in your first game of the season is huge. This gives Coach Penny Hardaway something to build on with this team. Reid showed what he is capable of and that he is a big-time performer. This team could emerge as a legitimate American Conference contender.

However, they showed heart and resiliency in this game. They fought from beginning to end and never let up. This is an inspiring win for the Tigers.

This is a win that they should feel good about; they beat a really good Iowa State team. This gives hope to the Tigers fanbase and to the players. They could be onto something if they get another big win. This is a team capable of having a big year.

#2880. North Korea denies links to Binance hack as researchers trace stolen billions

North Korea rejected allegations linking Pyongyang to the estimated $6.3 billion Binance hack, calling the accusation a “grave political provocation,” according to state media.

Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denounced the FBI's attribution of the attack to North Korea-linked hacking group TraderTraitor, Yohnap reported Tuesday, citing the state-run Korean Central News Agency.

Blockchain analytics firms including Elliptic and Chainalysis have also linked the attack and subsequent movement of the stolen funds to North Korea-linked actors.

"The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state', claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," Kim said, according to KCNA.

She accused Washington of misleading international public opinion by portraying cybercrimes around the world as the work of North Korea.

Separately, Binance said Tuesday it would begin progressively reopening withdrawals for additional crypto assets across more networks, expanding its phased restoration of services following last week's hack.

The denial comes as blockchain analytics firms trace billions of dollars in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance through thousands of wallets across multiple blockchains.

Elliptic and Chainalysis said hackers linked to North Korea have used increasingly complex techniques to obscure the trail of the funds.

In the first four days after the attack, the hackers used roughly 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains and conducted more than 40,000 transactions, Elliptic said in a report Monday. The activity appeared highly complex and automated, with an average of one new wallet used every 25 seconds.

Much of the laundering activity initially took place on the Tron blockchain, where stolen funds were distributed across about 7,700 addresses before being moved to Ethereum through cross-chain bridges, according to Elliptic. At least $147 million had been transferred out of Tron through such bridges.

The hackers also used decentralized exchanges to swap stolen stablecoins into cryptocurrencies that cannot be frozen by their issuers, including ether. Elliptic said roughly $786 million in stablecoins was converted before issuers including Tether and Circle froze the remaining assets.

The laundering operation has since expanded to other blockchains, including Solana. Chainalysis said North Korea-linked actors had begun a new phase of laundering after moving more than $500 million through intermediary wallets on Tron.

Elliptic also identified the first signs of bitcoin mixing, a technique designed to make transactions harder to trace. About 28 bitcoin, worth $2.2 million, had passed through 18 mixing transactions as of early Monday, the firm said.

Despite the extensive movement of funds, about $2.85 billion — or 44% of exactly $6.43 billion stolen as reported by Elliptic — has been frozen or seized, while roughly $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly in bitcoin and ether.

The firm said only a negligible amount of stolen funds appeared to have been cashed out, with most of the activity involving transfers or conversions between cryptocurrencies rather than exchanges into spendable funds.

Elliptic said the laundering has moved slower than after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, when North Korean hackers moved all the stolen ether within 10 days. It expects the remaining funds to be gradually converted into bitcoin and potentially cashed out through over-the-counter brokers and exchanges over several months.

Binance added it has covered about 95% of the affected amount, with the remaining 5% consisting of less liquid tokens that take longer to source. The exchange said it was working with industry partners to acquire the remaining assets.

#2878. Palantir reports booming U.S. commercial revenue growth, topping government for first time

Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time as businesses adopt more of the company's artificial intelligence tools.

Shares dipped about 3% in extended trading.

Here's how the company did compared to LSEG estimates:

Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share.

"I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," CEO Alex Karp told CNBC's Seema Mody in an interview, adding that the business is succeeding without salespeople.

Palantir has long been known for its strength in the government sector, but its commercial segment caught up in Q3.

U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which was up 96%. The company's U.S. commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years.

Palantir lifted its guidance, saying it now expects U.S. commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion for the full year. Last quarter, the company boosted its forecast to $3.42 billion. The company projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026.

Karp has openly supported the use of open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, which he told CNBC earlier this year are forcing businesses to sell their data sovereignty. Karp, on Monday, also reiterated recent calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability.

In September, Karp joined major tech CEOs at the White House as calls for regulation mounted following claims from AI researchers that the technology has a more than 10% of killing humanity.

"My message to everybody is: Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI," he told CNBC. "The future is here. The political ramifications of it are here."

#2874. Giants plan to listen to any and all trade calls with NFC East up for grabs

John Harbaugh sounds interested in changing the name of Carly Rae Jepsen's hit song "Call Me Maybe" to "Call Us Definitely."

The Giants are looking to be aggressive at the trade deadline and are open to hearing from any owner, general manager or head coach with a difference-making player to offer.

"I'll put it out there: We're open for any calls," an exceptionally loose Harbaugh said as the Giants returned from their bye week. "Anybody that wants to call us, call. There's a song like that."

Harbaugh confirmed that he left an unreturned voicemail last week for Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk, inquiring about Jeffery Simmons' availability before he was dealt to the Bears. It became a big story because standard operating procedure is trade discussions usually occur between general managers.

"We're not part of any secret society oath that says you can only talk to somebody," Harbaugh said. "We're not in that. We didn't get memoed on that. We're not in that agreement. So, anybody can call us. We won't be adhering to that particular agreement."

The biggest name connected to the Giants is running back Jonathan Taylor, though Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson's season-ending injury has raised the question of whether Derrick Henry could become available.

New York Giants general manager Joe Schoen and head coach John Harbaugh at practice. Noah K. Murray for NY Post

Just two weeks ago — before Cam Skattebo's first career 100-yard game led a balanced attack with four rushing touchdowns against the Texans — Harbaugh said he would love to be in a "Derrick Henry or Saquon Barkley circumstance," with an elite workhorse rusher.

So, do Harbaugh's ties to Baltimore — where he worked for 18 seasons alongside general manager Eric DeCosta before he was fired — make it easier or trickier to trade with the Ravens? He called owner Steve Bisciotti "a great friend."

"I don't know the answer to that because I think in some ways it makes it easier because it's an easy call to friends, and I think that's part of it around the league," Harbaugh said.

Running back Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts runs the ball. Getty Images

"People on every level make calls to people on every level because they know them. And how we do it here … is it's transparent in our building. We're turning over every stone. We're making every call. We're getting all the information we can possibly get at all times, and we are not apologizing for that at any point in time ever."

With their eyes set on winning the NFC East for the first time since 2011, the Giants also figure to be in the market for defensive tackles, edge rushers and receivers. It's "always the goal" to add significant players.

Taylor and Henry both are under contract beyond this season. That's different than renting the Titans' Tony Pollard or Seahawks' Zach Charbonnet — both of whom are 2027 free agents.

Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball as Damar Hamlin #3 of the Buffalo Bills makes a tackle. Getty Images

"For me, it wouldn't want to be a one-and-done kind of thing," Harbaugh said. "You want to have a short-term and a long-term win if you're going to do it with draft capital."

The Giants hold first-, second- and third-round picks and two sixth-rounders in the 2027 draft. There is a chance of getting a compensatory fourth-round pick, but that won't be determined until February and thus cannot be traded now.

"It's hard to find players that can make you better because we have good players — very good players," Harbaugh said. "So, it's got to be something that is a need, that fits your financial profile, that fits your price tag. We're not loaded with 12 or 13 draft picks where we've got draft capital to burn. So, we have to be smart shoppers that way."

Does that pull mortgaging 2028 draft capital into the equation?

"Yeah, it's easier to put it on the credit card," Harbaugh quipped. "It's always an easier spend."

Harbaugh warned against connecting the dots in his call about Simmons — who was traded for two first-round picks — to the price that the Giants were willing to pay for him or another player.

Calls around the league also are worthy to find out a player's character as the Giants try not to mess up their locker room vibes. Harbaugh admitted that, as a long-timer at league meetings on league committees he knows more NFL owners than he does current general managers who are peers of Joe Schoen's.

"We have got a great camaraderie, a great brotherhood, synergy," Harbaugh said. "You want to take that into account, even to the point where you probably talk to some of your [leaders] before you did something like that. Make sure that everybody understands, and they're kind of on board with it."

The U.S. reportedly carried out strikes against Iran on Monday even as Vice President JD Vance expressed hopes of reaching a "negotiated settlement" with Tehran.

America attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, which added that Washington has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks. The military campaign against Iran has been kept quiet on purpose so as not to signal any intention of major combat escalation, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.

Qeshm Island, off Iran's southern coast, is the largest island in the Persian Gulf. Located near the Strait of Hormuz, it has emerged as a potential U.S. target amid reports that anti-ship missiles, mines, drones and attack craft are being kept there in underground tunnels.

President Donald Trump's administration has been talking down risks of an all-out war with Iran, with Vance being the latest to claim "good progress" in talks with Iran.

"The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement," Vance told CNN on Monday.

He added, though, that Iranians are "unpredictable" and Trump retains "kinetic and non-kinetic" options against Tehran. Vance said that Washington has not set any deadline for reaching a peace deal with Iran.

Trump said earlier Monday that the U.S. had to go to war with Iran to stop the country from having "a nuclear weapon," that "we're not going to allow Iran ever to have a nuclear weapon. And they understand that."

Last month, the president had said the U.S. will not attack Iran before the midterm elections, after polls ahead of the ballot showed that support for the war had dwindled, with only 31% of Americans supporting the military action.

Trump told Fox News in an interview Monday night that the U.S. had to take a "little detour" to Iran to stop the country from having nuclear weapons.

The president said that the U.S. has bombed out all of Iran's potential nuclear power, but he might target Pickaxe Mountain next. Located south of Iran's Natanz enrichment plant, Pickaxe Mountain houses an underground nuclear facility.

"We might have to go after Pickaxe, but that's not a big deal," Trump said, adding the U.S. could destroy it in one hour.

On Nov. 1, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had also said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.

#2865. When will Myles Garrett return? Injury update on Rams star pass rusher

The Los Angeles Rams might soon be getting a major boost to their pass rush.

Myles Garrett is returning to practice this week, head coach Sean McVay announced during his media availability on Monday, Nov. 2. While McVay was noncommittal about setting a deadline for the superstar defensive end's return to the field, the team is opening Garrett's 21-day practice window ahead of Sunday's Week 9 matchup with the Washington Commanders after missing nearly two months since undergoing arthroscopic surgery on his left knee.

Donald missed the Rams' season opener in Melbourne, Australia, where Garrett struggled and admitted afterwards that he was more focused on protecting his ailing knee.

The two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year underwent surgery shortly after the Rams returned home and has been on injured reserve in the seven weeks since.

Having a healthy Garrett back in the fold could unlock another level from Chris Shula's defense. Opposing offensive lines would now have less room to key in on stopping Donald, which would create more 1-on-1s for Donald, Garrett and the rest of the Rams' defensive front. That could translate into generating more pressure while calling less blitzes, which could then free up Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson and Kamren Curl to spend more time in coverage.

"We are excited anytime we get anyone back, especially a guy like Myles," McDuffie told reporters. "Just getting him back on the practice field will be really good. Just knowing we're getting him back to a defense that is going uphill is awesome."

The Rams got off to a slow 2-4 start but are coming off back-to-back wins for the first time this season to get back to .500. McVay's teams have had a habit in recent years of getting stronger down the stretch, and getting a guy like Garrett back sooner could once again make them a team to look out for.
