#2864. Oregon men's basketball shines in season-opening win

Oregon's new coach and unrecognizable men's basketball roster made a pretty good first impression.

The Ducks took it to Montana and looked good doing it, winning their season-opener 87-69 on Nov. 2 in front of an announced crowd of 4,067 at Matthew Knight Arena.

Tyrone Riley IV led Oregon with 17 points, Malique Ewin had 14 points and 13 rebounds and five Ducks scored in double figures.

"Everybody was eating today," forward Taylor Bol Bowen said as he glanced over the stats sheet. "I don't think we saw a lot of bad shots."

The game marked the debut for interim head coach Tony Stubblefield, who took over for Dana Altman when the former coach retired Oct. 7 after 16 years at Oregon.

The Ducks also debuted 11 new players – nine transfers and two freshmen – with five of them making their first starts in a regular-season game.

Fred Payne opened at point guard and scored 12 with five assists, Riley was at guard, Andrew Meadow was at small forward and scored 14, and Bol Bowen and Ewin were in the post. Collectively that group scored 63 and shot 57.7% from the field (26 for 45).

They were among a group that entertained the small crowd with an up-and-down playing style highlighted by dunks, transition baskets and efficient offense.

"We have so many different weapons," Meadow said. "If we can all play together like we showed tonight, we can just keep having different guys have big nights on different nights."

The Ducks shot 60.3% (35 for 58) from the field, dominated inside with 54 points in the paint. They also had 21 assists, and outrebounded the Grizzlies 37-26.

Ten players scored for Oregon, including reserve point guard Wei Lin, who had 10 points off the bench.

"I keep telling out guys our strength is in numbers, and I think we have a lot of depth on this team," Stubblefield said. "I think over the course of 40 minutes we can wear a lot of teams out."

Montana started the game 4-for-4 from 3-point range to take a 12-4 lead at the 17:00-minute mark of the first half. But the Ducks settled in and were up 40-31 at halftime.

Their lead grew to 15 points – 53-38 – four minutes into the second half before the Grizzlies started chipping away until a 3-pointer by Jordan Clark tied the score 57-57 with 10:41 to play.

Clark's 3 was one of 13 deep shots made by Montana on 30 attempts.

The Ducks didn't get rattled after losing their double-digit advantage. Instead, they responded with a game-closing 30-12 run. Riley scored eight during that stretch and 14 of those points came in transition for the Ducks.

"It's a game of runs over the course of 40 minutes, teams are going to go on runs but I thought our guys were resilient," Stubblefield said. "I thought they responded very well and then I think we got to their legs a little bit. I think they got a little fatigued over the course of the last eight or nine minutes."

The Ducks will play their next three at Matthew Knight Arena, beginning with a 3 p.m. game Friday against Eastern Washington as part of a doubleheader with the Oregon women's team, which plays Washington State at 7 p.m.

Chris Hansen covers University of Oregon football, men's basketball, track and field, cross country and softball for The Register-Guard. You can reach him at chansen@registerguard.com.

#2861. $6.3 billion Binance hack is largest crypto theft on record

Binance said Friday that a security incident impacted about $6.3 billion in client assets, with around $3 billion frozen on-chain, marking the largest crypto hack on record.

The company later added it began recovering assets impacted by the breach after pledging to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, which the company created in 2018 as a protection for clients in the event of a hack.

It wasn't clear how the attack took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.

The FBI said Friday it was aware of the incident and was in touch with "relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate ​potential impacts, ​and ⁠coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

It wasn't clear either who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said in a post.

Blockchain data platform Chainalysis also said this appears "be the work of North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor. This group has repeatedly targeted the cryptocurrency industry, exchanges, DeFi protocols, and investors, to raise funds for the regime. We base our intelligence assessment on on-chain activity observed in the hours following the hack."

Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while it overhauls its withdrawal security systems and has revoked the affected address authorizations, Teng said. The exchange is also working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds, while deposits remain unaffected.

Binance co-founder Yi He said deposits remained unaffected and continued to operate normally, while the exchange was working on enhancements to its withdrawal service and related address controls. It expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours.

"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified," Binance said.

The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group, Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack.

Exploits are not uncommon in the crypto space. In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack. More recently, Bitget lost more than $350 million worth of digital assets in a cyber theft incident. Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges.

This week's breach "proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets earlier this month," Michael Selig, chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said Friday in a CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview. The U.S. derivatives regulator on Oct. 5 proposed a framework that would effectively put crypto exchanges under federal government oversight — after Congress failed to approve legislation to regulate the asset.

"The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets here in the United States. We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cyber security safeguards that we have in our markets today," he said.

Bitcoin fell more than 4% to $77,187.60 on Friday as the hack weighed on crypto markets.

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social media post that the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. USDT stablecoin issuer Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino also said in on X that his firm had frozen more than 1.5 billion of its stablecoin that may have been related to a potential breach.

Jack McDonald, Ripple's senior vice president of stablecoins, said it was actively freezing affected funds held in RLUSD, its U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin.

Closing out the second half of the Monday night matchup against the Chicago Bulls, the Philadelphia 76ers left fans wondering about Joel Embiid's status.

Each 76ers player cleared double-digit minutes in the final two quarters of the November 2 matchup. Well, all except Joel Embiid.

GettyPHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA – OCTOBER 30: Joel Embiid #21 of the Philadelphia 76ers in action during an Emirates NBA Cup game against the New York Knicks at Xfinity Mobile Arena on October 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. During the second half, Embiid checked in for just over eight minutes of action. He finished the game with 24 minutes of playing time.

Embiid was the only starter who failed to see a 30-minute shift against the struggling Bulls on Monday night.

Considering Embiid's injury history, any mysterious absence comes with plenty of worry. But 76ers fans were warned about Embiid's setback going into Monday's game.

Before Monday's action, the 76ers listed Embiid as questionable to play due to right foot plantar fascia injury management.

The Sixers ultimately cleared him for action after head coach Nick Nurse explained that it's an ongoing setback.

"Nick Nurse says the pain comes and goes for Jo. That's just how it is with plantar fascia. They're trying to manage it," Sixers Wire's Ky Carlin reported on X.

"Again, like we talked about pregame, just managing that and trying to be smart with it."

Embiid finished his 24-minute showing by shooting 5-for-11 from the field, and going 5-for-6 from the charity stripe. He produced a total of 15 points, eight rebounds, and three assists.

After the 76ers defeated the Bulls 126-107 at home, they'll hit the road to fire up a road trip, starting with a game against the Detroit Pistons on Wednesday, November 4. Embiid's status for that game is currently unclear.

JuJu Watkins didn't hold back her emotions after ending a 588-day absence by making her return from injury in the No. 3 USC Trojans' 100-68 blowout win over the UNLV Rebels on Monday night.

Watkins started the fourth season of her collegiate career with the Trojans, the third that sees her on the court. She suffered a torn ACL during the second round of the 2025 NCAA Tournament, an injury that sidelined her for the entire 2025-26 campaign.

Watkins prepared herself to return in full force, which she successfully pulled off. In 25 minutes of action, she finished with a stat line of 21 points, five rebounds, two assists, and two steals. She reflected on her return from injury after the game, expressing immense gratitude that she got to come back to the court with her teammates.

#2847. How Jon Ossoff Could Accidentally Become Georgia Football’s Biggest Economic Threat

ATHENS, Ga. — Georgia football has survived Alabama, Nick Saban, conference realignment and the occasional questionable fourth-quarter decision.

But there could be a new threat to the Bulldogs' long-term economic dominance.

The Georgia senator probably isn't spending much time thinking about Kirby Smart's recruiting budget. He has bigger things to worry about in Washington with his interests. Still, it's worth considering how one unlikely political development could send shockwaves through the Georgia football economy.

For starters, imagine a world where Ossoff somehow becomes involved in college athletics reform.

Suddenly, the Bulldogs could face a new federal commission studying NIL spending, transfer portal economics and why a 19-year-old backup linebacker needs a luxury apartment.

Georgia's football economy depends on an enormous ecosystem. Hotels fill up on game weekends. Restaurants cash in. Merchants sell thousands of red-and-black shirts. Gas stations around Athens practically become financial institutions on Saturdays.

And then there is the recruiting business.

If Ossoff ever decided that college football's financial system needed more government oversight, the Bulldogs could find themselves answering questions nobody in Athens wants to hear.

Why does a five-star recruit have a better housing arrangement than most assistant professors?

Ossoff is anti-football. This does not bode well for the inventor of the sport.

Why does a Saturday afternoon football game generate enough economic activity to make a small town look like a financial district?

And who approved the price of a hot dog inside Sanford Stadium?

There is also the possibility of an Ossoff-led national initiative to promote Georgia Tech football.

That might be the most dangerous scenario of all.

Imagine federal money going toward improving the Yellow Jackets' recruiting infrastructure, expanding their NIL operation and funding a comprehensive campaign to make Atlanta a legitimate college football destination again.

Of course, none of this is actually happening. There is no evidence Ossoff has a plan to interfere with Georgia football, and the Bulldogs' economic future is not hanging on a Senate committee.

But if Georgia ever starts losing recruiting battles because Washington suddenly develops an interest in college football economics, Bulldogs fans will know exactly where to direct their frustration.

For now, Kirby Smart can sleep comfortably.

The biggest threat to Georgia football remains the same as ever: somebody eventually has to play Alabama.
